nodes.v: Ran 2026-11-06 on Apple Silicon (linux/arm64 Docker 29.5.2, nav-sitl-px4:v1.17.0 built from samples/sitl-docker, companion in nav-sitl-client:latest with Python 3.12 + pymavlink 2.4.50). Reference pair (coherent 1 m/s, seed 7): velocity-test alarm 3.0 s after onset, EKF2_GPS_CTRL=0 + EKF2_EV_CTRL=5 echoed within 0.03 s, max cross-track deviation 7.8 m with the monitor vs 75.0 m without, EKF2 error 8.2 m vs 105.7 m, EKF2 GPS_GLITCH never set and eph 0.22 m while 106 m off; ArduPilot reference 3.0 s, 6.8 m vs 75.0 m. 20-flight sweep (2 seeds x position/coherent x 1/3 m/s + no-spoof, monitor and shadow, 2012 s wall in 3 lanes): all completed; monitor deviation 7-9 m except position 1 m/s (22 m); without monitor 75 m at 1 m/s and 108-152 m at 3 m/s even though EKF2 flagged GPS_GLITCH; 1 SS false alarm in 2 no-spoof monitor flights. 6 unit tests pass in the venv; 3 pass and 3 skip under plain python3. Not tested: speedup, amd64, PX4 main, aux global position over DDS, host-side MAVLink (did not get replies through a published UDP port).

nodes.n: GNSS jammer geolocation from DF bearings to TAK
nodes.s: Locates a GNSS interference source from KrakenSDR-style direction-of-arrival bearings taken at two fixed sites and one moving vehicle, with noise and multipath outliers. A stdlib robust least-squares triangulation (RANSAC + Gauss-Newton + outlier rejection) runs alongside Stone Soup particle filter and UKF estimators; the fix and its 95% error ellipse go out as Cursor-on-Target events (point + u-d-c-e ellipse) so the emitter can be reported on ATAK/WinTAK. An adapter reads the real krakensdr_doa JSON (websocket) and CSV (DOA_value.html) outputs with the bearing convention taken from its source.
nodes.v: Ran 2026-11-06: 11 unittest cases OK with python3.14.7 stdlib (geo, Kraken JSON/CSV parsing incl. HTTP poll against a local server, triangulation, ellipse, CoT build, UDP send to localhost); locate.py --method all ran with Python 3.12.14 + stonesoup 1.9.1 on synthetic data, outputs in README. Not run: a live KrakenSDR, the websocket listener (needs websockets), and rendering of the CoT ellipse on an ATAK/WinTAK client (ellipse angle convention unverified).

nodes.n: Low-cost GNSS jammer sensor network: u-blox telemetry => localization => TAK and dashboard
nodes.s: End-to-end stdlib pipeline for the 'cheap receivers detect and localize a GNSS jammer and put it on a COP' problem. Simulated u-blox-class nodes (static surveyed sites plus vehicles that lose GNSS and fall back to dead reckoning) report the fields pyubx2 exposes (NAV-PVT fix, per-SV C/N0 drop, MON-RF agcCnt / jamInd / jammingState) as compact JSON on an MQTT-shaped topic schema. The aggregator inverts the C/N0 drop with the standard effective-C/N0 relation (J = Q Rc N0 (10^(D/10) - 1), SV-independent) and the AGC reduction into jammer power at each node, with censored 'clear' and 'all SVs lost' observations. Three localizers: weighted centroid, multistart Levenberg-Marquardt RSS least squares with unknown power (and a BIC test for two jammers), and a grid likelihood over position and power with Bayesian update over time, motion diffusion for a moving jammer, and bookkeeping that counts static-node evidence once. DF bearings from the KrakenSDR sample are triangulated with its own code and optionally fused into the grid. Propagation truth is log-distance path loss with 4-D correlated link shadowing and optional building blockage. Outputs: CoT point + 95% ellipse via tak_out.py / cot.py, sensor-node CoT, and navdash/1 tracks + zones (ellipse, model fix-loss radius, nodes) for templates/demo-dashboard. Includes a Monte Carlo of error vs node count, density and shadowing sigma, and a hardware section limited to documented u-blox monitoring fields.
nodes.v: Ran 2026-11-06 on Python 3.14.7, stdlib only: 16 unittest cases OK (physics inversions and SV-independence, shadow field statistics, building clip, protocol validation incl. 8 malformed cases and topic mismatch, censored measurement kinds, noiseless LS / grid / centroid, k=2 selected only when two sources exist, no estimate without a jammer, motion diffusion, HTTP round trip with a bad line returning 207, CoT and zones from the server, ellipse ring geometry); 6 hand mutations (censor sign, Q in the inversion, BIC always/never k=2, lower censor off, LS ignoring censoring) each fail 1-5 tests. demo.py ran all three scenarios plus a buildings variant; HTTP path gives identical results to in-process; stdin path ran on 2548 dumped messages. evaluate.py ran 40 trials per configuration (~2 min). All data synthetic: no real receiver, no real jammer, no MQTT broker, no TAK client rendering of the ellipse. Model constants (noise figure, tracking threshold, AGC counts per dB, path-loss exponent) are assumptions stated in jsn_model.py.

nodes.n: Querying the hub from LLM agents via MCP
nodes.s: A stdlib-only MCP stdio server (tools/mcp_server.py) exposes search, show, concept and neighbors over the hub's index and graph so Claude Code, Cursor and other MCP clients can query it as tools. The README covers client registration, a navigation path for agents (llms.txt, INDEX.md, concept pages, records.jsonl) and prompt recipes.

nodes.n: LLM mission agent: a safety-gated MAVLink MCP server flying ArduPilot SITL
nodes.s: A small MCP server (stdio JSON-RPC 2.0, pymavlink) that lets Claude Code or any MCP client read and fly an ArduCopter: get_state, get_nav_health (EKF flags, variances, GNSS fix/sats/HDOP => nominal/degraded/lost), arm_takeoff, goto, set_mode, plan_survey, upload_mission and set_ekf_source_set. Every command passes a configurable polygon geofence (target and straight path, with margin), an altitude band and a mode allowlist, can run in dry-run mode and is appended to a JSONL command log. A scripted client flew it against ArduPilot SITL in Docker: geofence and altitude rejections, takeoff, goto, a lawnmower survey in AUTO, simulated GPS loss, switch to the vision (ExternalNav) source set and RTL to landing. Includes registration next to the navigation-index MCP server, prompt recipes, a Claude tool-use loop and a comparison with MAVLinkMCP.
nodes.v: Ran on 2026-11-06 against ArduCopter Copter-4.6.3 SITL in Docker (samples/sitl-docker image, linux/arm64) with pymavlink 2.4.50 on python3.13 (uv venv): scripted MCP client drove the server through fence and altitude rejections, arm_takeoff to 20 m, goto (arrived), plan_survey + upload_mission (12 items, AUTO), SIM_GPS_DISABLE=1 => get_nav_health degraded (gnss_ok false), set_ekf_source_set 2 (ExternalNav) accepted, RTL to landing and disarm; dry-run scenario also run. Transcripts in example_output/. 24 stdlib unit tests pass on python3.14.7. agent_loop.py was not run against the API (no ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in the environment); the Claude Code registration commands were not executed.

nodes.n: MagNav.jl quickstart: Tolles-Lawson and EKF on the SGL 2020 flight
nodes.s: A Julia walkthrough with MagNav.jl that downloads the public SGL 2020 challenge flight and Ottawa anomaly maps, compensates the scalar magnetometer with Tolles-Lawson on a calibration box, and runs the MagNav EKF against the map, printing INS-only vs EKF error and the CRLB. The README explains why magnetic anomaly navigation resists jamming and spoofing, and where it breaks down (map coverage, altitude, aircraft noise, temporal variation).
nodes.v: Ran on 2026-11-06 in the julia:1.11 Docker image (Julia 1.11.9, linux/arm64) with MagNav.jl v1.3.5, CSV v1.3.0, DataFrames v1.8.2 and FFTA pinned to 0.2.1 (FFTA 0.3.2 breaks precompilation of GlobalSensitivity): EKF DRMS 31.2 m vs INS-only final error 218.8 m on line 1006.08 with map Eastern_395. Output in README. Artifacts downloaded: sgl_2020_train ~563 MB and ottawa_area_maps ~1.2 GB on disk, plus EMAG2 ~0.5 GB pulled during precompile.

nodes.n: GNSS spoofing signatures in real AIS tracks: detectors, injected ground truth, GeoJSON and CoT
nodes.s: Shore-side detection of GNSS spoofing from the AIS picture, on real Danish Maritime Authority AIS (partial HTTP-range download of a daily file, ~4.4 h, 1.7 M fixes, 2.5-3 k vessels). Stdlib detectors for teleports, vessel-type speed limits, position-derived vs reported SOG/COG/heading, turn radius vs ship length, loitering-while-underway, crop-circle clusters of vessels on one point, on-land positions (Natural Earth 10m, eroded) and MMSI anomalies including one MMSI on two transmitters. Offset, drift, single-circle and group crop-circle episodes are injected into real tracks to measure recall and time-to-detect (offsets >= 2 km and circles ~0.9-1.0 recall, median TTD 5-17 s; slow 1-2 m/s drift ~0.1). Alerts on unaltered data are broken down by hand (coastline artifacts, a real MMSI conflict, an inland Class B report). pyais handles raw NMEA decode and an encode/decode round trip; flagged vessels export as GeoJSON and Cursor-on-Target via the mavlink-to-tak-cot builder. Public incidents (Black Sea 2017, C4ADS 2019, SkyTruth 2025, Baltic 2025) are cited.
nodes.v: Ran 2026-11-06: run.py with python 3.12.14 (pyais 3.3.1, pandas 3.1.1, shapely 2.2.0, pyshp 3.1.6) on DMA AIS 2026-11-03 and 2026-10-20 (first ~100 MB of each zip), 3 injection seeds per day, plus a pyais NMEA encode/decode round trip with identical scores; nmea_io.py stats on the pyais tests/nmea-sample file; 19 stdlib unit tests pass on python 3.14.7, and disabling the jump, cluster, turn, on-land or SOG checks makes tests fail. Not done: CoT shown in an ATAK/WinTAK client, live NMEA stream ingestion (Kystverket stream unreachable from this network), NOAA MarineCadastre data. No real spoofing event was found in the 8.8 h analysed; detection numbers come from injected episodes.

nodes.n: OSINT interference map from free data: ADS-B NACp hexes and Sentinel-1 C-band RFI over Kaliningrad / the SE Baltic
nodes.s: Two no-login OSINT layers for the same area and morning (2026-10-01, SE Baltic around Kaliningrad). ADS-B: the ADS-B Exchange free readsb-hist sample (1st of each month) is cut to a bbox and binned into H3 hexes with the GPSJam percentage formula on aircraft-reported NACp. Sentinel-1: an 18-scene GRD stack of one relative orbit from Microsoft Planetary Computer, scored two ways - ESA's own per-swath RFI annotation (rfiDetected, KL divergence, in-band/out-band power) and a port of zephr-xyz/sentinel1-rfi-detection's temporal z-score on VH backscatter. Outputs a GeoJSON loadable by templates/demo-dashboard, navdash/1 point tracks of the aircraft reports, and a PNG map.

nodes.n: Galileo OSNMA authentication as a spoofing defence: real recording, file-level attacks, scorer adapter
nodes.s: Runs unmodified OSNMAlib on the real Galileo I/NAV recording bundled with it (Septentrio SBF, 2025-12-12, 76 min) clean and under 10 file-level manipulations: replay without an independent clock, meaconing at 3 s, replay at 60 s and 1 h with an independent clock, forged ephemeris from cold start and after authentication, a spoofer with random keys and tags, OSNMA stripping, a GST shift and a Merkle-only cold start. Shows which attacks OSNMA catches (forged data, keyless spoofing, GST shift, replay beyond the time bound with an independent clock) and which it misses (replay with no independent clock, meaconing inside the bound, ranging attacks with genuine data, and a same-IOD forgery after authentication that OSNMAlib keeps reporting as authenticated). A stdlib adapter subclasses the gnss-interference-monitor scorer and adds six OSNMA detectors with not-measured handling. Includes a Docker recipe for GNSS-SDR 0.0.20 decoding an OSNMA-SDR-SIM IQ file, and operational requirements (time sync, cold/warm start, u-blox and Septentrio support). File-based only, no RF.
nodes.v: Ran 2026-11-06. OSNMAlib (commit 25aa61de, Python 3.12.14) on its bundled real SBF recording: full 76 min clean = 56 KROOT, 962 TESLA keys, 4711 tags authenticated, 0 failures; 11 scenarios on 20 min: replay with no independent clock and 3 s meaconing authenticate normally; 60 s replay leaves only ADKD12; 1 h replay authenticates nothing without any failure; forged OMEGA_0 bit = 277 tag failures; random keys/tags = 97 key-chain failures; stripping = silent loss; 120 s GST shift = 590 rejected pages + 73 key failures; Merkle-only cold start never authenticates (no DSM-PKR in 76 min); a same-IOD forgery after authentication stayed 'authenticated' for 10 min (OSNMAlib freezes the authenticated stream). 15 tests pass with OSNMAlib, 14 + 1 skipped stdlib-only on Python 3.14.7; mutating each OSNMA detector or the weak-signal guard fails 1-2 tests. GNSS-SDR 0.0.20 (Debian trixie) in Docker on OSNMA-SDR-SIM E1 files (600 s, 6.2 GB): fixes computed, strict mode rejects the replayed file on time; with cross_auth_mode=1 KROOT signature and 6 TESLA keys verified but no tag or nav data authenticated (cause not found); fix lands ~3000 km from the configured sim location (not investigated). Not verified: GNSS-SDR tag/data authentication, re-tagging with disclosed keys, live receivers (u-blox/Septentrio support is from vendor and third-party pages), hot-start TTFAF.

nodes.n: PX4 SITL GPS denial: inject, measure drift, recover
nodes.s: Flies a square mission in PX4 SITL (SIH quadrotor, headless; Gazebo also works per PX4 docs), denies GPS mid-mission, logs EKF2 health and estimated vs ground-truth position, then restores GPS and returns home. GPS denial tries MAVSDK failure injection and falls back to SIM_GPS_USED=0 because PX4 v1.17 SIH does not acknowledge GPS failure injection. A stdlib analyzer reports per-phase horizontal drift and time to a 5 m error.
nodes.v: Ran on 2026-11-06 against PX4 v1.17.0 SIH (sihsim_quadx) in Docker from samples/sitl-docker (linux/arm64) with mavsdk-grpc 4.0.5 (its bundled mavsdk_server runs on linux aarch64; the macOS arm64 wheel binary starts but was not flown). Two flights of the same 15 s GPS denial (fresh containers each): run A 8.37 m max horizontal error and 12.7 s to 5 m, run B 17.71 m and 8.5 s (drift.py on the MAVSDK logs, output in README). ulog_drift.py (pyulog 1.3.0) ran on the run B .ulg: 18.30 m max during denial, 7.8 s to 5 m, agreeing with the MAVSDK log at ~125 Hz. MAV_CMD_INJECT_FAILURE for GPS timed out (no ACK) on this target. drift.py tests (4) pass. Not run: gz_x500 (Gazebo).

nodes.n: Real attack replay: Jammertest 2024 u-blox logs through the GNSS interference monitor, with RTKLIB SPP
nodes.s: Replays 7 public u-blox logs from Jammertest 2024 (University of Vaasa VAARA dataset, about 13 h, 21 labelled test slots: drive-by and convoy jamming, motorcade spoofing, time-offset and pseudorange-ramp spoofing at Bleik, jamming-then-spoofing) through the unmodified gnss-interference-monitor scorer. A stdlib adapter frames mixed UBX + NMEA (the logs have no UBX NAV messages and break pyubx2), builds epochs from GGA/RMC/GSV with L1-band C/N0 only, and reconstructs a monotonic time axis so receiver time jumps reach clock_jump. Labels come from the VAARA field log plus two tests recovered from the 2024 NPRA plan shifted by the observed 50 min offset. Reports per test detected / time to detect / detector, alarm time in quiet and unlogged spans, for the shipped scorer and four variants, and RTKLIB SPP error (Docker) with logged vs IGS broadcast ephemerides. Findings: the constant-velocity pos_drift latches on a driving car; a cn0_rise sub-alert freezes the C/N0 baseline for good and hides later drops; staircase power evades cn0_drop; spoofing mostly appeared as a C/N0 drop while the receiver kept its true fix; spoofer ephemerides poison post-processing with the logged nav file.
nodes.v: Ran 2026-11-06. replay.py (Python 3.14.7, stdlib) on 7 VAARA u-blox logs downloaded by fetch_data.sh (64 MB .xz): 21 labelled slots (20 attack, 1 quiet), shipped scorer and variants B/C/D/F; result JSON in results/. RTKLIB demo5 v2.5.1 SPP in the rtklib-demo5 Docker image (built from samples/gnss-rinex-processing/docker, 91 s) on 3 logs with logged nav and with IGS BRDC from the BKG mirror; spp_eval.py numbers in results/. 13 tests on a synthetic VAARA-shaped stream: OK (1 skipped) on /opt/homebrew/bin/python3 3.14.7 without packages, OK with pyubx2 1.4.1 on Python 3.13.15; 4 single mutations each fail 1-3 tests. Not verified: test windows beyond the VAARA field log (2.4.2/2.4.3 are plan-shifted guesses), receiver truth beyond self-referenced medians, phone logs, MON-SPAN, OSNMA on the logged Galileo data, any scorer change (the baseline fix is a runtime what-if only).

nodes.n: Relative navigation benchmark on real data: KISS-ICP lidar odometry, OpenVINS VIO, mono and nadir VO, scored with evo
nodes.s: One command per part. KISS-ICP (pip) on KITTI odometry 04 from the raw drive, scored against KITTI odometry GT and OXTS; OpenVINS v2.7 stereo-inertial (ROS 1 serial mode, Docker, arm64) and an OpenCV mono VO baseline on UZH-FPV indoor_forward_3; frame-to-frame nadir VO over 9 km of VPAIR light-aircraft imagery at about 320 m AGL, image-only versus attitude-aided with a yaw-bias sensitivity. Every trajectory is written as TUM and navdash/1 JSONL for templates/demo-dashboard, and the fitted scale / heading / noise of each odometry is plugged into the altpnt-integrity sample as its relative source.
nodes.v: Ran on 2026-11-06, Apple M2 Max, python3.12 venv (kiss-icp 1.3.0, evo 1.38.1, opencv 5.0.0.93, rosbags 0.11.9) and OpenVINS v2.7 built from source in a ros:noetic-perception arm64 image under colima (4 vCPU). KITTI 04: KISS-ICP ATE 0.23 m, KITTI t_rel 0.41 %, final drift 0.12 % of 394 m. UZH-FPV indoor_forward_3 (49.5 s GT window, 278 m): OpenVINS ATE 0.36 m, final drift 0.26 %; mono VO with a GT scale oracle ATE 0.80 m. VPAIR (199 frames, 8.98 km): image-only nadir VO 15.5 % final drift, attitude-aided 0.65 %, 3.2 % with a 2 deg yaw bias. altpnt-integrity rerun with each fitted error model. 5 unit tests pass. EuRoC, ORB-SLAM3, cuVSLAM and KITTI 07 were not run (see README).

nodes.n: Drone Remote ID decoder, track table and TAK output
nodes.s: Passive airspace awareness from broadcast Remote ID (ASTM F3411 / ASD-STAN EN 4709-002). A stdlib decoder for Open Drone ID messages and packs, validated field-for-field against opendroneid-core-c, extracts payloads from Wi-Fi beacon, Wi-Fi NAN and BLE captures, feeds a per-UAS track table with spoofing plausibility flags, and emits a UAS track plus operator point as Cursor-on-Target via PyTAK.
nodes.v: Ran on 2026-11-06 (macOS arm64, Python 3.14.7 and 3.12.14, Apple clang 21). odid.py matched opendroneid-core-c master 849c03a field-for-field (exact float32/double values, raw string bytes) on 500 core-c-encoded messages/packs, 500 random raw messages, 81 unique payloads from the three public opendroneid/wireshark-dissector captures, plus a live 600-vector batch; 5 planted decoder mutations each failed the suite. capture.py decoded 42 NAN+beacon packs, 21 beacon packs with positions and 244 CRC-OK BT5 long-range packs from those captures. rid_to_cot.py sent 256 CoT events through PyTAK 7.6.1 to a local TCP sink (synthetic scenario) and 10 to a UDP sink (real beacon capture). Not verified: any live radio reception, a real TAK server or ATAK rendering, the core-c cmake build or its own odidtest (cmake absent; library compiled directly with cc), Auth message semantics beyond decoding, anomaly thresholds against real spoofing.

nodes.n: Headless SITL in Docker: ArduCopter and PX4 SIH with one compose file
nodes.s: Dockerfiles and a compose file that run ArduCopter 4.6.3 SITL (with a simulated vicon for ExternalNav) and PX4 v1.17.0 SIH quadrotor without Gazebo or a GUI, plus a Python client image with pymavlink and mavsdk-grpc that shares the PX4 network namespace. Built and flown on linux/arm64 (Apple Silicon).
nodes.v: Built and ran on 2026-11-06 with Docker 29.5.2 on Apple Silicon (linux/arm64): both SITL images built, the ArduPilot, PX4 and VIO bridge samples flew against them, and docker compose (v5.7.0, run from the docker:29-cli image) brought both services up and a client container reached both. amd64 not tested.

nodes.n: Stone Soup radar tracking of two UAVs with JPDA and OSPA
nodes.s: Simulates two small UAVs observed by a noisy bearing/range radar with clutter and tracks them with Stone Soup's Extended Kalman filter and JPDA data association. Track quality is scored against ground truth with the OSPA metric, the detect-and-track layer of a counter-UAS airspace picture.
nodes.v: ran radar_jpda_ospa.py with stonesoup 1.9.1, numpy 2.5.4, scipy 1.18.1 on Python 3.12.14 on 2026-11-06: 2 tracks held on 2 truths, OSPA mean 17.0 m / max 53.0 m (c=100 m), identical over 3 runs after fixing set-ordering nondeterminism; output in README. Single seed and scenario, no Monte Carlo; initiators/deleters and live radar input not exercised.

nodes.n: Cooperative localization for a GNSS-denied team: UWB ranging, centralized EKF vs covariance intersection, and a spoofed anchor
nodes.s: A stdlib-only simulation of six vehicles with biased odometry where only two keep GNSS. Inter-agent UWB two-way ranging has dropouts, Markov NLOS episodes and gross outliers; optional camera bearings; a lossy, range-limited mesh with a TDMA slot budget. It compares independent dead reckoning, a centralized 24-state EKF at a fusion centre (multi-hop uplink), a naive decentralized filter that ignores cross-correlation, and decentralized covariance intersection, each with plain or robust (gate + Huber + NLOS-aware) ranging. It reports per-agent error over time, NEES and bytes per second, then spoofs one anchor's GNSS with a slow walk-off and shows how far the error propagates with no check, a per-fix gate, peer range votes and solution separation (centralized sub-filters and a distributed per-anchor filter bank).
nodes.v: ran with python3.14.7 stdlib on 2026-11-06: nominal and spoof scenarios, each range-only and with bearings (seed 1), and 10-seed Monte Carlo for all four; outputs saved in out/ and pasted in README. 20 unittest tests pass; mutations (SS gate disabled, robust weighting disabled) make the detection and robust-ranging tests fail. Synthetic data only: NLOS, comms and odometry models are stated assumptions, no UWB dataset or hardware was used, and none of the related repos was run.

nodes.n: Cooperative localization on real UWB: MILUV drones through the swarm-coop filters
nodes.s: Runs the unmodified filters of swarm-coop-localization (dead reckoning, centralized EKF, naive decentralized, covariance intersection; plain vs robust ranging; gate / vote / solution-separation integrity) on real two-way UWB ranges from the MILUV dataset (3 quadcopters, 6 anchors, mocap truth). A stdlib HTTP-range reader pulls only the mocap, uwb_range and height CSVs out of 3-11 GB experiment zips. Two drones get 2-D fixes from multilateration of their own real anchor ranges, the third is denied and uses only real inter-drone ranges (horizontal projection with the height rangefinder) and synthetic odometry. Reports real range error vs the sim's UWB model, per-drone RMSE with real ranges and with the sim's error model on the same geometry, and detection time for a ramp bias on one drone's anchor ranges or on the denied drone's inter-drone ranges, with no-fault controls. Finding: the error core matches the sim (robust sd ~0.10 m) but the real tail stops at 1.9 m where the sim puts 9 % of ranges beyond 5 m, so robust ranging stops mattering; cooperative gain, CI consistency, faulty-anchor propagation and centralized solution separation all reproduce.
nodes.v: Ran 2026-11-06 with /opt/homebrew/bin/python3 3.14.7, stdlib only. fetch_miluv.py fetched the CSVs of default_3_zigzag_0, default_3_random_0 and cirObstacles_3_random_0 by HTTP range (31.4 + 12.6 + 10.6 MB over the wire from 11.1 / 3.2 / 3.2 GB zips). run_real.py stats / nominal / fault / fault --kind peer outputs saved in out/ and quoted in the README (30 runs per table: 3 denied-drone choices x 10 odometry seeds). Truth re-derived from mocap matches the devkit gt_range within 1 cm on 99.91 % of rows. 15 unittest tests pass with data, 7 pass + 8 skip without data; a mutation zeroing the injected fault makes the SS detection test fail. Not verified: real odometry (it is synthetic from mocap), lever-arm or 3-D models, comms, UTIL TDoA data, the MILUV devkit itself (not installed or run).

nodes.n: Heightmap-gradient particle filter on real DEM and 1 m LiDAR (SPRIN-D CTU method) vs TERCOM
nodes.s: Re-implementation of the CTU SPRIN-D winner's localization (arXiv 2510.01348): local heightmap gradients matched to a prior DEM with the unnormalized correlation coefficient, Gaussian-blurred similarity maps weighting a translational particle filter resampled every fixed odometry distance, K-means largest-cluster estimate. Runs 10 km simulated flights with VIO-like drift over three real Copernicus GLO-30 windows (Bavarian Forest hills, Erding where SPRIN-D was flown, Hungarian plain) plus a smoothed-flat control, and compares against a radar-altimeter batch TERCOM baseline. Reports error vs distance, convergence from a 300 m initial offset, flat-terrain failure, a sensor-error sweep and measured CPU time per update. v2 adds a gain-fitted NCC likelihood with a Cramer-Rao information gate (falls back to odometry on featureless terrain: 336 vs 334 m at 10 km where v1 reached 539 m), compass bias as a particle state (8-53 m at 10 km for 0-20 deg bias where the translational filter loses lock above 10 deg), a no-truth confidence record (particle spread, ESS, CRB, NCC significance) checked against true error, and a test on real 1 m airborne LiDAR (Geobasis NRW DOM1/DGM1, dl-de/zero-2.0): the paper's literal binary edges reach 0.6 m median after 4 km at 1 m vs 19.9 m at 30 m reference resolution.
nodes.v: ran 2026-11-06 with CPython 3.13.15 + numpy 2.5.4 / scipy 1.18.1 / rasterio 1.5.2 / matplotlib 3.11.2 on an Apple M2 Max: fetch_dem.py downloaded the three GLO-30 windows over public HTTPS, run_eval.py produced every number and plot in README (results deterministic across two full runs, timings vary with machine load), test_core.py 14 passed and fails when the correlation flip or similarity-map origin is mutated. The flights, odometry and heightmap sensor are simulated; no real UAV, LiDAR or SfM data was used. The paper's own numbers are quoted from the paper, not reproduced. v2 (same date and machine): test_v2.py 8 passed (22 total with test_core.py); run_eval_v2.py re-ran v1 pf_grad and matched out/results.json exactly in all four regions, then produced every v2 table and plot in README; fetch_lidar.py downloaded 32 Geobasis NRW 1 m tiles over public HTTPS; run_lidar.py produced the 1 m vs 30 m table and gave identical error numbers on two runs. v2 gate thresholds were tuned on seeds 100-111 of the same regions. The LiDAR test simulates the onboard map from the same NRW DSM plus noise.

nodes.n: Terrain-relative navigation with a particle filter
nodes.s: A stdlib-only simulation of TERCOM/TRN: an aircraft with a biased INS and a radar altimeter matches its measured terrain profile against a seeded synthetic DEM with a particle filter that also estimates the INS velocity bias. Prints INS-only vs PF error over time, includes a flat-terrain control, and a rasterio loader for Copernicus GLO-30 tiles.
nodes.v: terrain.py and trn_pf.py ran with python3.14.7 stdlib on 2026-11-06, output shown in README; dem_rasterio.py is an unverified sketch: syntax-checked only, requires rasterio (the GLO-30 tile URL returned HTTP 200 on 2026-11-06).

nodes.n: Night / thermal UAV frame to RGB satellite geolocalization with a no-false-fix gate (ALIKED / DISK / SIFT + LightGlue, SGM baseline, Thermal-UAV)
nodes.s: Real nadir DJI M4T thermal frames (Thermal-UAV / SCC-Loc, Apache-2.0 card) matched against the dataset's 0.3 m RGB satellite GeoTIFF, by condition: city and village, day and night, day and night fog. Compares ALIKED, DISK and SIFT with LightGlue (license-clean) under three modality-bridging preprocessings (raw, CLAHE, gradient magnitude), fits a 4-DOF similarity and gates fixes on inliers, inlier ratio, scale, rotation and search radius. Reports fix rate, error, false-fix count and M2 runtime on CPU and MPS, checks the gate on held-out validation-split flights, and runs the IROS 2023 SGM thermal-to-satellite retrieval network (MIT code, unlicensed research-only weights) as an out-of-domain baseline. fetch_data.py pulls a 180-frame subset out of the 19.9 GB ZIP with HTTP range requests.
nodes.v: Ran 2026-11-06 on Apple M2 Max (torch 2.15.0, LightGlue git 5a650c4, OpenCV 5.0.0, Python 3.12.14): fetch_data.py pulled 180 Thermal-UAV frames (9 flights) and cropped the 0.3 m ref.tif (~2.8 GB transfer); run_eval.py on MPS, 120 frames from 6 flights (111 on the map), revised gate: ALIKED/grad 18/111 fixes (median 2.6 m), ALIKED/raw 16/111 (3.3 m), DISK/grad 15/111, SIFT 1/111; village-night best with ALIKED/grad 9/20, village-night-fog 0/14 for every method; 0 false fixes in 1080 attempts (84 accepted), and 0 in 540 attempts (37 accepted) on 3 held-out validation-split flights. The revised gate was chosen after the first run (a-priori gate: 32 accepted, 0 false). SGM retrieval (research-only weights): top-1 within 20 m on 26-29/111, 182 of 238 ungated fixes false. Median s/frame CPU vs MPS: ALIKED 1.26 / 0.18, DISK 2.42 / 0.29, SIFT 0.21 / 0.30. Tests: 11 pass in the venv; plain python3 9 pass, 2 skip. Boson-nighttime (gated, NC, 74 GB), STHN/UASTHN fine stages, MINIMA and RoMa were not run.

nodes.n: GNSS-disciplined clock holdover per oscillator grade, and a slow time-walk spoof
nodes.s: A stdlib-only simulation of a GNSS-disciplined oscillator (type-2 PLL on a noisy 1PPS) for TCXO, OCXO, rubidium and chip-scale atomic clock grades, with ADEV, aging and temperature figures taken from Vig's oscillator comparison table and the Microchip SA65 datasheet. It reports time error after 1 min to 24 h of GNSS outage (Monte Carlo median and 95th percentile, next to an analytic estimate), then walks GNSS time off slowly and compares an internal steering-plausibility monitor with a cross-check against a second time source, including a guard that drops into holdover on alarm and no-spoof control runs.
nodes.v: ran with python3.14.7 stdlib on 2026-11-06 (default arguments, about 5 s); output pasted verbatim in README. 9 unittest tests pass, including an ADEV check of the noise model, a no-spoof negative control and a planted blind-detector control that proves the cross-source alarm can fail. Oscillator parameters are datasheet/table values; PPS noise, second-source noise/asymmetry, temperature fraction and detector thresholds are stated assumptions. No hardware or real GNSS data was used, and none of the related repos was run.

nodes.n: USV own-ship navigation under GNSS spoofing: radar-to-chart fixes and an integrity monitor in the Oresund
nodes.s: A simulated USV runs a 19.6 km transit over real geography (Lillgrund => Drogden channel => Copenhagen approach) built from OpenStreetMap coastline, Oresund bridge, wind turbines and seamarks, with 75 min of real Danish Maritime Authority AIS traffic as radar targets. Compass + bottom-track speed log dead reckoning, a 720-azimuth marine radar ray-cast with clutter, incidence-dependent detection and ship occlusion, likelihood-field + point-to-line ICP matching of returns to the chart (with degenerate, ambiguous and few-return checks), a 4-state EKF that also calibrates compass bias from matched heading, and a monitor (solution separation + 30 s GNSS-vs-radar/DR mean test, exclusion only when the GNSS-free filter has recent radar fixes). Over 5 seeds a slow GNSS drag (0.003 m/s^2 to 0.6 m/s) is excluded 125-131 s after onset near the coast at a 23-26 m offset (max error 10-25 m vs 1391-1395 m for GNSS+DR and for a single filter with radar but only innovation gates); onset in open water is caught at 202-250 s (max 71-102 m); a 1.5 km radar range makes it fail (175-1024 m). Zero false alarms in 25 runs. Writes navdash/1 JSONL for templates/demo-dashboard and own-ship CoT via the mavlink-to-tak-cot builder; README maps the pieces onto OpenCPN/radar_pi, Signal K, colav-simulator and MOOS-IvP.
nodes.v: Ran 2026-11-06 on macOS with python 3.14.7 stdlib: 15 unit tests pass and three negative controls (detection off, degeneracy check off, isolation rule off) each make the targeted test fail; run.py for 5 scenarios x 4 configurations x 5 seeds, numbers in the README come from example_output/summary_5seeds.*; plot.py with matplotlib 3.11.2 (python 3.13.15); example_output/spoof-coastal loaded in templates/demo-dashboard in headless Chrome (metrics panel read). Fixtures built from Overpass (OSM) and a locally downloaded DMA AIS file for 2026-10-20. Not done: real radar data, S-57 ENC input, CoT in a TAK client, running any of the linked maritime stacks. Sensors, radar and attacks are simulated; the simulated world equals the OSM chart apart from buoy offsets, so radar fix errors are optimistic.

nodes.n: VIO to MAVLink bridge with ENU/FLU to NED/FRD conversion
nodes.s: Sends an external pose source (VIO topic or CSV log) to PX4 EKF2 or ArduPilot EKF3 as VISION_POSITION_ESTIMATE or ODOMETRY for GPS-denied position hold. The frame conversion (ENU/FLU to NED/FRD, world to body velocity, MAVLink covariance layout) is a stdlib module with unit tests, and the pymavlink sender plus small set_params / watch_ekf helpers sit on top.
nodes.v: Ran on 2026-11-06: frames.py tests (8 OK) and --dry-run on python3.14.7; the pymavlink ODOMETRY path ran against ArduCopter 4.6.3 SITL (EKF3 'is using external nav data', flags 0x033f) and PX4 v1.17.0 SIH (estimator_status_flags cs_ev_pos/cs_ev_hgt/cs_ev_yaw/cs_ev_vel True), both in Docker from samples/sitl-docker with pymavlink 2.4.50. Only a stationary pose was streamed; no flight on vision was tested. --msg vpe not run.

nodes.n: Drone frame to orthophoto geolocalization with LightGlue
nodes.s: Matches a nadir drone frame against a georeferenced satellite or orthophoto tile with SuperPoint + LightGlue, fits a MAGSAC homography with OpenCV, and maps the frame centre through the GeoTIFF geotransform to lat/lon. The geometry (affine geotransform, homography mapping, WGS84 UTM, haversine) is a stdlib module with unit tests; the pipeline points at UAV-VisLoc, VPAIR and University-1652 for imagery and at hloc / AnyLoc for retrieval over large maps.
nodes.v: geo_math.py and 12 unit tests ran with python3.14.7 stdlib on 2026-11-06. geolocalize.py ran on 2026-11-06 with torch 2.15.0 (CPU), LightGlue git 5a650c4, opencv-python 5.0.0.93, rasterio 1.5.2 on Python 3.12.14 against synthetic pairs cut from one public OpenAerialMap orthophoto (Tbilisi, CC-BY 4.0): 0.04-0.21 m error for yaw 0/60/135 deg, tilt and 60-150 m priors; 30.7 m error with 162 inliers when 40% of the frame was nodata at the ortho edge; a frame from a different city gave no fix (5 inliers). Frame and map come from the same survey, so this is a pipeline/geometry check, not a cross-season or real-UAV result; UAV-VisLoc/VPAIR/University-1652 were not run.

nodes.n: Large-area visual place recognition for lost-GNSS recovery (DINOv2 GeM / VLAD over a 49 km2 NAIP tile DB, chained to LightGlue fine matching)
nodes.s: The coarse first stage that geoloc-license-clean lacks: no position prior, unknown heading. Builds a geo-referenced tile DB over 49 km2 of public-domain NAIP (Planetary Computer, 5 vintages 2015-2023) at 250 m and 100 m tile sizes, 8 rotations. Global descriptors from DINOv2 ViT-S/14 (Apache-2.0): CLS, GeM, AnyLoc-style hard VLAD (own implementation), plus a classic rotation-invariant ring-histogram baseline. Compares four rotation strategies (none, query TTA, rotation-augmented DB, rotation-averaged invariant descriptor). Reports recall@1/5/10 within 50/100/250 m, latency and index size per map-vintage gap, then chains top-5 retrieval into ALIKED+LightGlue fine matching with the inlier gate and compares with fine matching given a known prior. Real CC0 eBee frames (2016) are also run.
nodes.v: Ran 2026-11-06 on Apple M2 Max (DINOv2 ViT-S/14 on MPS, LightGlue on CPU, torch 2.15.0, Python 3.12.14): download_data.py fetched 49 km2 of NAIP 2015/2017/2019/2021/2023 from Planetary Computer, 23 CC0 eBee frames and 3DEP heights; run_vpr.py built 250 m and 100 m tile DBs (18.5k / 19.3k tiles x 8 rotations, ~9 min each) and scored 150 synthetic queries per source year: same imagery R@1 within 50 m 0.77 and R@10 within 100 m 0.98 (gem/invariant8, 250 m tiles), 2-8 year vintage gap 0.18-0.29 / 0.48-0.73; rotation-averaged GeM matched or beat an 8x rotation-augmented DB at 1/8 the index size; classic ring histogram R@10 within 250 m <= 0.13. Real eBee frames vs 2023 DB: cls/invariant8 R@1 within 50 m 0.70-0.74 (23 frames in one park). run_chain.py (VPR top-5 => ALIKED+LightGlue, 25-inlier gate): synthetic 20/20 fixes (same imagery, 0.22 m median), 8/20 and 3/20 at 6 and 4 year gaps vs 20/20 and 12/20 with a known prior; real eBee 0/23 with 100 m windows, 1/23 (20 m) with 50 m windows; no wrong fix accepted. Tests: 23 unittest cases pass in the venv; with plain python3 12 pass and 11 skip (numpy/OpenCV/torch absent).

nodes.s: What each page under docs/ is for and the order to read them in. Every page listed here is also a guide node in the index, so python3 tools/query.py search "<problem statement ", the MCP server and the web UI in site/ return them next to repos and samples.
nodes.b: Docs map What each page under  docs/  is for and the order to read them in. Every page listed here is also a  guide  node in the index, so  python3 tools/query.py search "<problem statement " , the MCP server and the web UI in  site/  return them next to repos and samples.   Read order   Before the event (days to weeks) 1. primer/ - nine chapters, one cluster of the hub each, with the EW failure modes. Learn the vocabulary here. 2. learning-paths.md - three study tracks by available time, built from indexed courses, talks and books. 3. hackathon-playbook.md sections 1-2 (what judges reward, problem space map) and section 6 (pre-hackathon prep checklist: datasets on disk, SITL images, template green). 4. landscape/ - what is already sold and funded, and a real past brief with seven solutions (blind-flight-teardown.md). 5. export-control-and-ethics.md - scope limits, not legal advice. Read once before you pick a project.   H+0: the problem statement drops 1. problem-statement-decoder.md - wording table =  1-3 of 26 rows, each with approach, stack, data, starting sample, risk and pitch. 2. day0-runbook.md - the first three hours, until a walking skeleton runs. 3. ../samples/README.md - every sample with status, deps, first command and key measured result (generated from each  sample.json ).   While building - reference-stacks.md - one default and one alternative per capability, plus what to avoid and why. - integration-cards/ - one repo each: install, wiring, gotchas, license. Indexed by     markers from the catalog pages. - dataset-cards/ - checked sizes, formats and licenses. - paper-digests/ - what a paper claims and what the code does. - integrity-monitoring.md - protection levels, solution separation, Stanford diagram. - timing-resilience.md - holdover, time attacks, timing builds. - model-weights-licenses.md - code license vs weights license for learned matchers and place recognition. - hackathon-playbook.md sections 3-5 - project ideas, reference architectures, 48 h plan.   Pitch - evidence-matrix.md - every measured number across samples, with its input type (real / SITL / synthetic). Cite from here.   Maintaining the hub - SCHEMA.md - data model for  data/ . Sample fields ( verified_status ,  deps ,  first_command ,  key_result ,  input ,  group ,  runtime ) are described in ../samples/README.md. - reports/ - hand-written review and fact-check passes (cold-start review, fact checks, search ranking, card vs sample cross-check). The top-level  reports/  folder is different:  reports/quality.md  there is generated by  tools/build.py .

nodes.s: The source of truth is JSON under data/. Everything else (catalog pages, indexes, graph) is generated by tools/build.py. Never hand-edit generated files.
nodes.b: Data schema The source of truth is JSON under  data/ . Everything else (catalog pages, indexes, graph) is generated by  tools/build.py . Never hand-edit generated files.   IDs - Repo:  repo:<owner /<name  lowercased, taken from the canonical GitHub URL (e.g.  repo:px4/px4-autopilot ). Non-GitHub repos (GitLab, Codeberg, Bitbucket):  repo:<host /<owner /<name , e.g.  repo:gitlab.com/gnss-sdr/foo . - Resource:  res:<short-kebab-slug , e.g.  res:groves-pnt-book-2e . Make slugs specific enough to avoid collisions across lanes (prefix with org or author when unsure). - Concept: only ids that exist in  data/concepts.json . Cross-lane links work because repo ids are derived from URLs: you can reference any GitHub repo by id even if another lane indexes it. The builder reports dangling ids.   Repo record  domains : any of  air, ground, maritime, underwater, space, dismounted, multi .  rel  values:  depends_on, integrates_with, alternative_to, fork_of, extends, evaluated_on, same_org .   Resource record Resource  rel  values:  has_code, uses, evaluates, cites, explains, dataset_for, part_of, same_author .   Rules for contributors (human or agent) - Only include items you have verified exist (URL resolves /  gh api repos/<o /<n  succeeds). - Summaries in your own words. No copied README text beyond a short phrase. - No invented numbers. Leave stars/license to  tools/enrich.py . - Navigation, localization, PNT resilience, situational awareness and defensive EW are in scope. Weapon terminal guidance, targeting and offensive payload content are out of scope.

nodes.s: Not legal advice. This page is practical orientation for a hackathon team working on open-source navigation code. It is not legal advice, it is not complete, and rules change. If your project involves controlled hardware, non-public technical data, a defense customer, foreign team members on non-public work, or any RF transmission, ask your organisation's export-control or legal office, or the relevant authority, before you act. Where this page cites regulation text, read the primary source yourself.
nodes.b: Export control and ethics    Not legal advice.  This page is practical orientation for a hackathon team working on   open-source navigation code. It is not legal advice, it is not complete, and rules change.   If your project involves controlled hardware, non-public technical data, a defense   customer, foreign team members on non-public work, or any RF transmission, ask your   organisation's export-control or legal office, or the relevant authority, before you act.   Where this page cites regulation text, read the primary source yourself. The hub's scope is navigation, localization, PNT resilience, autonomy, situational awareness, defensive EW and counter-UAS detection. Weapon terminal guidance, targeting and offensive payloads are out of scope (AGENTS.md). Contents: 1. Export control basics for open-source navigation code 2. What changes the picture 3. GNSS signal simulation and RF transmission 4. Drone flight rules 5. Responsible AI principles 6. Dual-use etiquette for a public repo 7. Checklist   1. Export control basics for open-source navigation code The US has two main regimes. Other countries have their own, and the EU has one regulation for dual-use items.   Regime   Administered by   Covers   Primary source    -------- ----------------- -------- ----------------     EAR  (Export Administration Regulations, 15 CFR 730-774)   Commerce, Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS)   Commercial and dual-use items, software and technology   eCFR Title 15      ITAR  (International Traffic in Arms Regulations, 22 CFR 120-130)   State, Directorate of Defense Trade Controls (DDTC)   Defense articles, technical data and defense services on the US Munitions List   eCFR Title 22      EU dual-use regulation  (EU) 2021/821   National authorities of each member state   Dual-use items, software, technology; Category 7 is navigation and avionics   Index entry     Published information is outside the EAR Under 15 CFR 734.3(b)(3), information and software that is  published  as described in 734.7 is not subject to the EAR (15 CFR 734.3). Section 734.7 says unclassified technology or software is published when it has been made available to the public without restrictions on further dissemination, and lists ways that happens, including "posting on the Internet on sites available to the public" (15 CFR 734.7; index entry: 734.7). Practical reading, consistent with the Linux Foundation's guide (The EAR and Open Source Software): - Code you write and push to a  public  GitHub repo, with no restriction on who may read it, is generally published and outside the EAR. -  Encryption is the exception to know.  Encryption source classified under 5D002 stays subject to the EAR unless it meets 742.15(b), which involves a notification step (15 CFR 734.7(b); EFF explainer). This can matter if your PNT code adds signal or message authentication. Verifying Galileo OSNMA signatures is a different case from shipping your own encryption, but check rather than assume. -  Private repos are not published.  Sharing a private repo with a foreign national can count as an export (a "deemed export" when it happens inside the US) (Linux Foundation guide).   EAR99 Items subject to the EAR that are not listed on the Commerce Control List are designated EAR99 (15 CFR 734.3(c)). Most commercial software and hardware is EAR99. EAR99 is not "uncontrolled": end-use and end-user prohibitions in Part 744 apply to items subject to the EAR, and 744.21 covers certain Russia and Belarus military end uses "for all items subject to the EAR" (15 CFR 744.1). Published code avoids the EAR; a physical box you ship does not.   ITAR public domain is narrower ITAR defines public domain as information "published and generally accessible or available to the public" through listed routes - bookstores, subscriptions, libraries, patents, open conferences, fundamental research at accredited US universities - and, for general public release in any other form, only "after approval by the cognizant U.S. Government department or agency" (22 CFR 120.34). Practical consequence, as university compliance offices put it: an individual cannot simply put ITAR-controlled technical data into the public domain by posting it (Stony Brook guide). For a hackathon this means:  build only from public civil signals and published methods.  If anyone on the team has seen non-public data from a defense programme, keep it out of the repo entirely.   2. What changes the picture The same navigation algorithm can sit in very different control situations. Things that should make you stop and ask:   Change   Why it matters    -------- ----------------     Military GNSS  (M-code, P(Y) beyond the public interface level) or  anti-jam / adaptive antenna  technology   GNSS receiving equipment is controlled under ECCN 7A005 and related entries; a 2018 BIS rule placed adaptive-antenna GNSS receivers under 7A005.b while items otherwise described in 7A005.a remain ITAR (Federal Register, 20 Dec 2018). The Stony Brook guide notes military GNSS items may be ITAR or EAR controlled.      Inertial navigation hardware and navigation equipment    CCL Category 7 covers navigation and avionics, with 7A994 catching other navigation equipment and aircraft INS not controlled elsewhere. Classification depends on performance parameters; check the current CCL, not a summary.      A specific defense end use or customer    Designing or modifying something for a defense article, or helping foreign persons do so, can become a  defense service : "the furnishing of assistance (including training) to foreign persons... in the design, development... of defense articles" (22 CFR 120.32). Integrating your code into a particular military platform is different from publishing a general algorithm.      Non-public technical data  from a sponsor, NDA, or classified context   Not published, so the exclusions above do not apply.      Shipping hardware  (a built prototype, an SDR loaded with your firmware) across borders   Physic

nodes.n: Hackathon playbook: navigation and PNT under GNSS denial
nodes.s: For a team going into a navigation-themed hackathon that may have a military or defense track. Everything here is framed as defensive: keeping position, navigation and timing trustworthy, detecting interference, and giving operators an honest picture. Weapon terminal guidance and targeting are out of scope (see DoDD 3000.09 for where that line sits, and Policy, export control and ethics).
nodes.b: Hackathon playbook: navigation and PNT under GNSS denial For a team going into a navigation-themed hackathon that may have a military or defense track. Everything here is framed as defensive: keeping position, navigation and timing trustworthy, detecting interference, and giving operators an honest picture. Weapon terminal guidance and targeting are out of scope (see DoDD 3000.09 for where that line sits, and Policy, export control and ethics). Version 2, 2026-11-06. New since v1: each project idea links its integration cards (install, gotchas, license traps) and dataset cards (checked sizes); a section on differentiators (1.1); the prep checklist uses the measured pre-download shortlist; known traps (PX4 v1.17.0 vs  main , ArduPilot 4.6 vs 4.7 params,  mavsdk  vs  mavsdk-grpc , non-commercial SuperPoint weights, Oxford RobotCar withdrawn, EuRoC moved and rate-limited) are folded in where they bite. Updated 2026-11-06 (v2.1): every idea's "Start" points at the sample that already builds it; see the quick picker's last column. Companion docs: - reference-stacks.md - "if you only have X, use Y", with a license column. - day0-runbook.md - the first 3 hours after the problem statement drops. - problem-statement-decoder.md - 26 likely statements =  approach, stack, data, sample, risk, pitch. Start here when the statement drops. - samples/README.md - every sample by problem: status, deps, first command, key result. - evidence-matrix.md - every measured number across samples, real vs simulated input. - landscape/ - what vendors already sell and what funders ask for. - templates/ - project skeleton, threat model, demo script, pitch outline, self-assessment. Contents: 1. What judges reward - 1.1 Differentiators judges have not seen 2. Problem space map 3. Project ideas (24-48h) 4. Reference architectures 5. 48h execution plan template 6. Pre-hackathon prep checklist ---   1. What judges reward Pulled from past challenge designs, funder problem statements and post-mortems in the hub. The common thread: a working, measured, honest prototype on a realistic scenario beats a clever slide.   Judges reward   Evidence in the hub   What it means for your demo    --- --- ---    A working prototype on a realistic simulated system   ONR HACKtheMACHINE Unmanned - Navy judges reward working prototypes on realistic simulated systems   Run against PX4 or ArduPilot SITL, real recorded data, or real hardware. Not a notebook with synthetic sine waves.     Measured accuracy, not coverage   DARPA SubT scored accurate localization of reported artifacts; Kelvins SPEC2019 shows how ESA scores a nav competition   Show one number with ground truth: ATE in metres via evo, OSPA via Stone Soup, error vs time during an outage.     Multi-sensor fusion, not one magic sensor   EDF-2024 drone navigation challenge - "multi-sensor fusion, not a single sensor, is the ask"; DARPA ASPN pushes plug-and-play all-source fusion   Architect for sensor dropout and plug-in sources even if you only finish two. Show the filter surviving one source going away.     Integrity and plausibility over raw accuracy   OPSGROUP 2024 report - "is my position plausible?" checks matter more than accuracy; FAA SAFO 24002 - hybrid GPS/INS can also be corrupted by spoofing   Detect and flag before you fuse. A spoofing alarm that fires and a filter that refuses the bad fix is the strongest 30-second demo moment.     Detect, respond, recover vocabulary   DHS Resilient PNT Conformance Framework (four resilience levels), NISTIR 8323 (identify/protect/detect/respond/recover, GNSS as untrusted input)   Put your features on a slide mapped to these words. Judges from government recognise them.     Holdover time as the value metric   DIU Transition of Quantum Sensing - value is reduced drift and longer holdover without GPS   Report "minutes until error exceeds N metres" with and without your aid.     Deployable, testable, dual-use   NATO DIANA challenges, DIANA cohort feature - selection favors deployable, testable dual-use products   Name the civil use (aviation, shipping, timing) next to the defense one. Show it runs on hardware a unit could buy.     Rapid field relevance, frontline users   Brave1-NATO competition, Ukrainian anti-drone hackathon, Kyiv Independent on EW cycles - adaptation cycles measured in weeks   Show reconfigurability: config-driven sources, thresholds, frequency plans. Say how a field user retunes it.     Sim-to-real honesty   Kelvins SPEED+ scored the synthetic-to-hardware gap; Swift used residual models from real data   If you only ran in sim, say so and show what breaks on real data.     Operator workflow and interop   CERBERUS SubT win - field-hardening and operator workflow mattered as much as algorithms; NeBula - reasoning over localization uncertainty improves decisions   Put the output on a map operators already use (TAK via CoT). Show uncertainty, not just a dot.     Lightweight onboard beats heavy   MAVLab AlphaPilot win, A2RL 2025 - university labs beat well-funded teams   Measure latency and compute. A CPU-real-time pipeline is a feature.     Governable, traceable AI   DoD AI principles, NATO AI principles - judges ask how an AI component can be disengaged   Any learned or LLM component needs a log, a confidence, and an off switch with a safe fallback.     Compliance awareness   Stony Brook ITAR/EAR guide, EAR and open source, EU 2021/821   Stay on public civil signals and published methods. Never radiate GNSS signals; cabled or shielded only. One slide line on this pre-empts the question.     Skepticism toward unverified claims   Vermeer optical navigation report - vendor claims not independently tested; RUSI Meatgrinder - loss figures are contested   Cite numbers with their caveat. Overclaiming in front of practitioners loses points.   Pitch framing sources: CSIS Space Threat Assessment 2025, EASA SIB 2022-02, EASA/IATA plan 2025, UK PNT growth response, GAO-21-320SP. Recent hackathon framing: EUDIS Defence Hackathon 2025, DASA RF

nodes.n: Integrity monitoring for navigation and alt-PNT
nodes.s: After this page you can explain what a protection level is and why it is different from an accuracy number, run a solution-separation monitor over several alt-PNT sources, and show judges a Stanford diagram that proves your navigator does not lie silently.
nodes.b: Integrity monitoring for navigation and alt-PNT After this page you can explain what a protection level is and why it is different from an accuracy number, run a solution-separation monitor over several alt-PNT sources, and show judges a Stanford diagram that proves your navigator does not lie silently. Working code: samples/altpnt-integrity (stdlib Python, run and tested). Numbers quoted on this page from that sample are its observed output.   1. Why this is a differentiator The GNSS-denied navigation products landscape lists about ten vendors selling camera-to-map visual navigation. Most give no accuracy numbers at all, and none of the sources found there publishes integrity or failure data: how often the system is wrong without warning, how fast it warns, or what bound it guarantees. Aviation GNSS has a 30-year vocabulary for exactly that question. Porting it to visual, terrain and magnetic fixes is open work, and a hackathon team that shows a protection level with a negative control is answering a question the products do not.   2. Vocabulary   Term   Meaning    --- ---    Accuracy   statistics of the position error (PE), e.g. 95th percentile     Integrity   the ability to bound the error and to warn in time when the bound cannot be trusted     Continuity   probability that the service, once started, is not interrupted (by alerts, exclusions)     Availability   fraction of time the service meets all requirements, including PL < AL     Protection level (PL)   a bound the system computes on its own error, at a stated integrity risk; HPL horizontal, VPL vertical     Alert limit (AL)   the largest error the operation tolerates; set by the operation, not by the sensor     Time to alert (TTA)   time from the error exceeding AL (or the fault starting) to the alert reaching the user     Integrity risk   probability that PE   PL without an alert within TTA     P_FA, P_MD   false-alert and missed-detection probabilities that set detection thresholds     MI   misleading information: PE   PL while the system says it is available     HMI   hazardously misleading information: PE   AL while the system says it is available   The core rule: a navigator may be inaccurate, but it must not be inaccurate  and  confident.  PL  = AL  is not a failure; it is the system correctly saying "do not use me for this". The failure is PE   PL without an alert. The GPS SPS Performance Standard is the formal statement of these terms for civil GPS; Navipedia covers RAIM, SBAS and integrity terms. The DHS Resilient PNT Conformance Framework describes receiver behaviour under attack (prevent, respond, recover) but does not define protection levels.   3. RAIM and ARAIM in one page  Residual-based RAIM (chi-square).  With more measurements than unknowns, the least-squares residual vector  r  has  r^T W r ~ chi2(n - m)  when fault-free. Exceeding the threshold for  P_FA  means "some measurement is faulty". The PL is derived from how large a single fault can be while still keeping the test statistic under the threshold (the "slope" of each measurement). MichaelBeechan/RAIM is a MATLAB implementation of classic RAIM FDE.  Solution separation (SS).  Compute the all-in-view solution  x0  and one sub-solution  x_j  per fault hypothesis j (all measurements except subset j). Under no fault, the separation  d_j = x0 - x_j  is zero-mean with covariance  P_j - P0  (for optimal estimators). Test  d_j    T_j = K_fa   sigma_dj . The PL covers both the fault-free case and each hypothesis: Brenner introduced SS for integrated GPS/inertial systems: a bank of sub-filters each excluding one satellite, with the separation from the full filter as the test statistic (Brenner 1996). Joerger, Chan and Pervan compare the two: SS can monitor better in principle because its test statistics are tailored to each fault hypothesis and to the state of interest, but in conventional implementations, for computational reasons, residual-based RAIM ends up with tighter integrity-risk bounds (Joerger et al. 2014, abstract). The SS form transfers directly to Kalman filters, which is why the sample uses it.  ARAIM  generalises RAIM to multiple constellations and dual frequency: each fault mode (single satellite, constellation-wide) has a prior probability from an Integrity Support Message, hypotheses whose prior is below a threshold are not monitored, and the integrity and continuity budgets are allocated across the monitored hypotheses with SS (Blanch et al. 2012; Blanch et al. 2015). MAAST for ARAIM is the Stanford GPS Lab MATLAB tool that evaluates ARAIM availability and PLs over service areas. Two ideas from ARAIM carry over to alt-PNT almost unchanged: 1.  Fault priors decide what you monitor.  You cannot protect against every fault combination. You list fault modes, give each a prior, and monitor the ones whose prior exceeds the integrity budget. 2.  Exclusion needs its own check.  After excluding j, the remaining solution must pass its own test, otherwise a wrong exclusion becomes undetected HMI.   4. Integrity in a Kalman filter -  Innovation (NIS) gating.  For each measurement,  nu^T S^-1 nu ~ chi2(dim z)  under the filter's model. Rejecting above the 99.9 % quantile removes gross outliers. It is the first layer, not a monitor: a slow ramp is absorbed by the filter state, so the innovation stays small. The gnss-ins-ekf-outage sample shows a gate missing spoofing walk-offs at 0.5 m/s and below. -  Gate failure under uncertainty.  When the filter is uncertain (long outage), S is large and a 60 m outlier passes. When the filter is confidently wrong (it absorbed a bias), the gate rejects the  healthy  source. The altpnt-integrity sample shows the second case: after absorbing a map-misregistration bias during a GNSS outage, the gate-only filter rejected the returning, healthy GNSS for 61 consecutive epochs with 30-37 m error and a smaller PL. -  Filter-based integrity risk. nodes.s: Commercial products, funded programmes and 2025-2026 trends in GNSS-denied navigation, so a hackathon team can place its idea against what is already sold or funded.
nodes.b: Landscape: what judges already know Commercial products, funded programmes and 2025-2026 trends in GNSS-denied navigation, so a hackathon team can place its idea against what is already sold or funded.   File   Contents    --- ---    gnss-denied-nav-products.md   ~30 vendors by category: visual, magnetic/quantum, LEO PNT, inertial, anti-jam, simulators. Vendor claims labelled, open alternatives from this index     programs-and-challenges.md   DARPA, DIU, AFRL/MIT, NATO DIANA, EDF, ESA NAVISP, UK DASA, Brave1, EUDIS and other hackathons, with their problem statements     trends-2025-2026.md   Fiber-optic drones, commodity visual nav, LEO PNT launches, quantum flight tests, OSNMA service, national backups     ua-ru-sources-overview.md   Ukrainian and Russian-language sources (separate owner)   Index records:  data/resources/landscape.json  (kinds  product ,  company ,  program , tag  landscape ). Query:  python3 tools/query.py search "landscape magnetic" . Caveats: found by web search on 2026-11-06. Most performance numbers are vendor claims that no independent party has published. Some vendor pages block scripted fetches, so for those only search snippets were read. Nothing here was run or tested.   What is commoditized Judges from industry, funders or the military will treat these as solved or for sale: 1.  Camera-to-satellite-map position fix for small drones.  At least ten vendors (Auterion, Theseus, Twist Robotics, Vermeer, Blue Arrow, Spleenlab, UAVOS, Honeywell, Inertial Labs/Maxar, Helsing). One of them (Theseus) began at a 2024 hackathon. A plain "match the frame to Google satellite tiles" demo is the default entry, not a differentiator. 2.  VIO / visual odometry for drift reduction.  Open source ( repo:rpng/open_vins ,  repo:nvidia-isaac/cuvslam ) and built into PX4/ArduPilot integration paths. 3.  GNSS + tactical IMU + velocity aid in one unit , with jamming/spoofing flags (Honeywell HGuide o480, SBG Ellipse firmware, Safran VersaPNT, Advanced Navigation Boreas). 4.  Receiver-level anti-jam and CRPA modules  (NovAtel GAJT, Septentrio AIM+, infiniDome). 5.  Lab GNSS jamming/spoofing simulation  (Spirent, Safran Skydel). 6.  Authenticated nav data : Galileo OSNMA is a free operational service since July 2025.   Where a hackathon team can still add something Ordered by how reachable they are in 24-48 h with the open tools in this index. 1.  Integrity, not accuracy.  No vendor publishes how its visual or magnetic fix fails. A monitor that flags a wrong visual match or a spoofed GNSS fix before the filter accepts it, with a measured false-alarm/missed-detection rate on recorded data, matches the DASA ask ("AI for spoofing detection and multi-source fusion") and is rare in demos. Building blocks:  repo:gnss-sdr/gnss-sdr ,  repo:algafix/osnma ,  repo:s7am1na/gnss-spoofing-dataset ,  repo:cra-ros-pkg/robot_localization ,  repo:borglab/gtsam . 2.  Honest numbers on open data.  Vendors quote RNP levels and "x times better than INS". Showing error vs distance on a public benchmark ( repo:uav-avl/benchmark ,  res:magnav-challenge-site ,  repo:hmf21/aerialvl ) with failure cases is something judges cannot get from a brochure. 3.  The hard conditions vendors skip in marketing:  night/thermal imagery ( repo:arplaboratory/satellite-thermal-geo-localization ), low altitude, snow/season change, water and featureless fields, map staleness. Pick one and measure it. 4.  Fusion of cheap heterogeneous sources  under a small-UAS budget: visual fix + baro + IMU + Starlink/Iridium Doppler or radio beacons, with a switch-over policy. Every problem statement (DASA, EDF 2024, Brave1/NATO) says "multi-sensor", but most products sell one modality. 5.  Drop-in integration path.  Feed the estimate to PX4/ArduPilot as an external position or as a substitute GNSS message ( repo:thien94/vision_to_mavros ,  repo:mavlink/mavros ) and show it in SITL. Funders ask for "plug-in replacement for COTS"; a working SITL loop beats slides. 6.  Detect-and-warn for others.  A crowd or fleet-level GNSS interference map from drone or phone logs ( repo:univaasadigieco/vaara ,  repo:felixott94/fraunhoferiis_jammertest2025 ) fits the UK GNSS-warning and Jammertest themes and needs no special hardware.   What to avoid - Claiming accuracy you did not measure; judges know vendor numbers are unverified and will ask how you measured yours. - Anything that depends on quantum sensors, FOG IMUs or LEO PNT signals you cannot access. Use the software problem with public data instead. - Live GNSS signal transmission. Simulation goes into a cable or shielded box only; see  docs/export-control-and-ethics.md . - Pitches framed around targeting or terminal guidance: out of scope for this index and for most dual-use funding lines (Brave1/NATO joint funding is non-lethal only).

nodes.n: "Polyot vslepuyu" (Blind flight) 2026: problem teardown and seven public solutions
nodes.s: The closest real precedent we have for a navigation hackathon brief: a 48-hour case (26-28 June 2026, Krasnodar, track "Robotics and sensing") where teams had to find position, ground speed and heading of an aircraft from a radar altimeter and a DEM, with no GNSS and no IMU.
nodes.b: "Polyot vslepuyu" (Blind flight) 2026: problem teardown and seven public solutions The closest real precedent we have for a navigation hackathon brief: a 48-hour case (26-28 June 2026, Krasnodar, track "Robotics and sensing") where teams had to find position, ground speed and heading of an aircraft from a radar altimeter and a DEM, with no GNSS and no IMU.  How this was built.  READMEs, two organiser PDFs and selected source files were read as text through the GitHub API on 2026-11-06. Nothing was cloned or run. Every accuracy number below is the team's own claim unless it says "bench", which means it comes from our own harness in samples/blind-flight-bench. The bench re-implements two team approaches from their README text only (no code copied).   1. Reconstructed problem statement   Source documents The organiser PDFs are committed in the GORIZONT repo root:  Описание первичное.pdf  (short version, the same text as the event page) and  Расширенное описание.pdf  (extended brief, two pages). The event page itself ( res:iqarium-polet-vslepuyu-hackathon-2026 ) names no sensors.   Story (both PDFs) A commercial operator runs light unmanned and optionally piloted aircraft delivering cargo to taiga villages, geology camps, Arctic weather stations and mountain bases, over featureless taiga, tundra, steppe and plateaus. GNSS fails there: poor satellite geometry at high latitude, narrow sky in gorges, unintentional or deliberate jamming/spoofing near industrial sites, heavy cloud and geomagnetic storms. The aircraft must still know position, speed and direction, and be able to correct its course.   Task (extended PDF, translated) Build, in 48 hours, an algorithm that, in real time or post-flight, determines from a simple radar altimeter and a digital terrain map: - the current velocity vector: where the aircraft flies and how fast; - an exact map position (x, y), so the course can be corrected.  Inputs    Input   What the brief says    --- ---    DEM   From open sources: Copernicus GLO-30, SRTM, ALOS AW3D30     Radar altimeter   Teams generate it themselves. NMEA-0183 v3, e.g.  $GPGGA,123519.111,,,,,,,,545.4,M,46.9,M,, 47  where  545.4  is the height in metres. Rate 1-10 Hz     Barometric altitude   1500 m, "absolute flight altitude above sea level", constant   Note the format abuse: the radar height sits in the GGA  MSL altitude  field (field 9), and every position field is empty. A parser that validates GGA fix quality rejects every line.  Required  1. Convert radar heights into a profile of absolute terrain heights along the track (1500 - AGL). 2. Correlation: build reference profiles in all directions from an arbitrary start point in the map centre, azimuth 0-360 deg in 1 deg steps; find the angle and offset with the maximum correlation coefficient. 3. Motion vector: speed in m/s, track angle / azimuth, ground speed. 4. Visualisation: heatmap of correlation coefficients over all directions; the found trajectory on the height map.  Optional:  Kalman filter for noise, self-assessment of accuracy, adaptation to flat terrain, run-time optimisation for a low-power onboard computer, "other improvements".  Judging:  "teams must implement a working algorithm that solves positioning". Business scenarios must be strictly civilian and describe the aircraft, hardware and software. Weights and criteria were not published (event page, per the index record).   Organiser clarifications recorded in team READMEs From KROT ( rub1kub/where-are-we-barista , section "Что уточнили у технического эксперта"): - the judged object is the positioning algorithm from radar altimeter + height map; - no additional sensors: no IMU, camera, FPV, GNSS track or external truth trajectory as input; - flight level is constant 1500 m MSL; - on the final day the organisers hand out a validation altimeter log to run together with a map; - by the third checkpoint the organisers switched to a new input format: a TXT file with one radar height (metres AGL) per line, a start point  x,y , a heading in degrees from north, the initial speed, the altimeter rate, and a GeoTIFF map patch; expected output is local and global trajectory coordinates plus a visualisation; - bonus for compute speed, lower load and robustness to altimeter noise and outliers. KROT's local example of that format ( examples/route_1.txt ): start pixel 2396/1000, azimuth 294 deg, 15 m/s, 10 Hz. KROT's sample of the map it received spans 55-56 N, 37-38 E (Moscow region lowland, heights 109.5-273.6 m in its 420x420 resample). From Gagarin: a "fourth checkpoint" module takes a DEM file, a TXT of heights, a start point and flight parameters. From GORIZONT: their test inputs are  heights_m.txt  (one height per line), a packed DEM over Siberian taiga at about 61.5 N, 89.1 E, start pixel (422, 297) and an initial heading of 95 deg; they also show one run on "real data provided by specialists" (a photo dated 2026-07-14, no error numbers).   What the evaluation actually became The PDF asks for a global search from the map centre. By checkpoint 3 the organisers supplied the start point, heading and speed, so the scored problem turned into  tracking from a known start , with heading and speed only as initial hints. A team that over-invested in the 360-degree global search solved the PDF, not the checkpoint.   2. Teams Seven public repos are indexed. Six are hackathon entries;  radagastttt/terrain-relative-navigation  is a later personal project on the same idea. Commit counts and creation dates are from the GitHub API on 2026-11-06.   GORIZONT -  repo:t1gr20an06-k/hackathon-blind-flight  16 commits, created 2026-06-27. Python, one 71 KB script  Radiometr_v2/tercom_final.py  plus data generators and drafts. -  Pipeline (README).  Median + low-pass filter on the radar channel, a Kalman filter on baro.  Bootstrap:  from the last GNSS point, hundreds of (azimuth x speed) hypotheses plus small start offsets (radius 8 px, grid 4 px), scored by correlation over a 200-sample window; candi

nodes.s: Each item: what changed, the source, and what it means for a navigation hackathon project. Scope is navigation only; weapon autonomy and terminal guidance debates are out of scope.
nodes.b: Navigation trends 2025-2026 Each item: what changed, the source, and what it means for a navigation hackathon project. Scope is navigation only; weapon autonomy and terminal guidance debates are out of scope.   1. Fiber-optic drones reduce RF reliance, not navigation need - Fiber-optic FPV drones take control and video over a cable and cannot be radio-jammed; both sides fielded them at scale in 2025 (Lowy Institute, Jun 2025); Russian fiber drones reached Kramatorsk (Oct 2025) and Kharkiv (Euromaidan Press, Kyiv Independent). Range is cable-limited and spools leave tell-tale cables (TWZ). - Implication: fiber solves the short-range, operator-in-the-loop case by keeping a human pilot on video. Longer-range, low-altitude and autonomous segments still need onboard navigation, and jamming of GNSS stays the norm ( res:ngrn-ukraine-deftech-2025 ). It also shifts some C-UAS detection away from RF sensing toward EO/acoustic.   2. Cheap visual navigation modules became a commodity - Several vendors sell camera-to-map modules for small UAS: Twist Robotics OSCAR (Jan 2026), Vermeer, Blue Arrow in Ukraine; Theseus, UAVOS NavAI, Spleenlab, Auterion Visual Navigation elsewhere (see products). Theseus started at a February 2024 hackathon (Aviation Week). - IEEE Spectrum (2025) reports onboard optical navigation as the Ukrainian answer to jamming ( res:ieee-spectrum-ukraine-drones-ew-2025 ). - Implication: "drone matches camera to satellite map" is no longer novel to judges. Novelty moves to robustness (night/IR, seasonal change, low altitude, featureless terrain), integrity (knowing when the match is wrong) and measured error on open data.   3. LEO PNT moved from papers to launches - Xona Pulsar-0 launched mid-2025; FCC conditional approval for the constellation (SmallSat News). - TrustPoint launched its third C-band demo satellite in June 2025 (Business Wire). - Iridium PNT ASIC unveiled Oct 2025, commercially available Jul 2026 (GPS World). - Implication: dedicated LEO PNT service is not available to a hackathon team. Starlink/Iridium signals-of-opportunity work ( repo:przemyslawpiekarski/starlink-leo-pnt ,  res:kassas-starlink-navigation ) is the reachable version and needs SDR hardware plus recorded data.   4. Quantum navigation flight tests multiplied (claims still vendor-reported) - UK flew an optical atomic clock and cold-atom sensor on an RJ100 in May 2024 (gov.uk). - Q-CTRL reported quantum MagNav flight results in April 2025 against an INS (Quantum Insider). - SandboxAQ reported 150+ flight hours with Acubed in 2025 and a drone test in Sep 2026 without error figures (Quantum Insider). - DIU TQS (Mar 2025) and DARPA RoQS (Phase 1 Aug 2025) fund field-ready quantum sensors (DIU, DARPA). - Implication: the sensors are out of reach, but the software problem (map matching, aircraft noise compensation, filter integration) is open, with public data ( res:magnav-challenge-site ).   5. Galileo OSNMA became an operational service - The European Commission declared OSNMA Initial Service on 24 July 2025 (EUSPA); EU smart tachographs in new trucks and buses must use it from December 2025 (GSC one-year note). - Implication: authenticated Galileo navigation data is free and live. Open decoders exist ( repo:algafix/osnma ,  repo:daniestevez/galileo-osnma ). OSNMA authenticates the nav message, not the signal timing, so it does not stop meaconing/replay alone; pairing it with consistency checks is a credible small project.   6. Terrestrial and timing backups got national budgets - UK announced ~GBP 155M for a timing centre, eLoran and GNSS warning in Nov 2025 (RNT Foundation). - Implication: "detect and warn" is a funded government need in its own right, separate from on-vehicle alt-nav.   7. GNSS-denied navigation is a standing hackathon challenge - EUDIS 5th edition (Oct 2026) made GNSS-denied navigation one of two common challenges across eight sites (EC DEFIS). - Implication: judges will have seen many attempts. See README for positioning.
