nodes.s: Lane ua-ru-sources: 38 resources and 12 repos, all tagged lang:uk or lang:ru. Every URL resolved at collection time (Nov 2026). Every repo was checked with gh api repos/<o /<n. Summaries come from the pages, PDFs and READMEs. Nothing was installed or run. Vendor and author performance numbers are passed on as claims. Strike and terminal-guidance content was skipped. One hit about a strike-oriented navigation product was dropped for that reason.
nodes.b: Ukrainian- and Russian-language sources: what they add Lane  ua-ru-sources : 38 resources and 12 repos, all tagged  lang:uk  or  lang:ru . Every URL resolved at collection time (Nov 2026). Every repo was checked with  gh api repos/<o /<n . Summaries come from the pages, PDFs and READMEs. Nothing was installed or run. Vendor and author performance numbers are passed on as claims. Strike and terminal-guidance content was skipped. One hit about a strike-oriented navigation product was dropped for that reason.   What this material teaches that English sources mostly don't  1. EW is layered. GNSS is one target among several.  English material usually treats "GPS-denied" as the whole problem. The Ukrainian explainers split it into the control uplink, the video downlink and GNSS. They also say radio reconnaissance has to come before any jamming (DOU on EW). For a navigation team, that means losing GNSS usually comes together with losing the link. Most designs in this set assume both: Vyriy beacons work "without GPS or a link", and the SPbU return-home project states the same requirement.  2. The anti-jam arms race is public and specific.  Ukrainian reporting gives CRPA element counts going from 4 to 16, 24 and 32 (Harxon 32-element, Shahed breakdown). It also shows a state test lab for domestic anti-jam antennas (Brave1 CRPA lab). The defensive conclusion repeats across sources: once threats carry CRPA plus INS plus position-jump filters, GNSS jamming and spoofing lose much of their effect. Counter-UAS then moves to detection and interceptors.  3. Visual positioning is a fielded product class.  OSCAR is described as feeding map-matched coordinates to the autopilot, with a vendor claim of about 20 m accuracy. That figure is a realistic bar for a hackathon VPS. The academic side shows the structure underneath: tile the GeoTIFF, pre-index keypoints, search only near the last fix, and define what to do when no fix comes (KMA thesis). The thesis also gives a rare honest cost trade-off: SuperPoint+SuperGlue found more matches but ran about 25x slower than ORB.  4. Route choice counts as a resilience lever.  Two Russian/Belarusian papers plan routes over feature-rich terrain so the visual fix doesn't drop out (Rulko, Konovalov). English VPS work rarely couples the planner to the matcher like this.  5. Terrestrial substitutes for GNSS.  Ground beacon ranging is in use in Ukraine (Vyriy), with no numbers published. A Russian MIPT diploma gives an open, inspectable version: LoRa two-way ranging plus an INS error-state EKF and MSCKF (Roosmax/Diploma). Urban rangefinder-to-OpenStreetMap matching is a third, cheap variant (DOU interview).  6. Practitioners modify ArduPilot instead of replacing it.  The KPI paper describes ArduPilot changes for link frequency agility alongside INS backup (KPI). The Lviv paper adds deterministic switching between navigation sources and a mixed fiber/radio link (Lviv Polytechnic). A community Ukrainian translation of the ArduPilot docs exists (ardupilot_ua).  7. Civilians see spoofing too.  Spoofing spills into everyday life, and the signatures are simple: tracks that teleport to a fixed far-away point, and impossible speeds. fit-gps-spoof-fix turns these into detection rules. Novaya Gazeta Europe covers the same effects in European civil aviation.  8. Hackathon problem statements are concrete.  Ukrainian state and cluster hackathons publish their tracks: - Jammer Hackathon: drone detection and tracking. Its winners were mostly detection, direction finding and decision support. - Onslaught of Machines: advanced navigation, resilient comms, coordination of unmanned systems. - EDTH Munich: underwater navigation, counter-UAS vision, radio reconnaissance. Brave1 says it wants components that integrate fast, not finished systems. On the Russian side, the 2026 "Полёт вслепую" (Blind flight) hackathon posed TERCOM: DEM plus radar altimeter in NMEA. Two public solutions exist (GORIZONT, FlyingBlind). KosmoHackathon 2026 posed GNSS-shadow ground navigation (safe-route). If the hackathon brief turns out to be TERCOM-like, these are the closest worked examples.   Russian-language foundations worth knowing - Receiver internals and interference: Klimenko on Habr, MCU GPS SDR, early spoofing overview. - Ground truth on a budget: ZED-F9P RTK, RTKLIB post-processing. - Indoor GNSS-free stack, Russian docs first: Clover with its optical flow and ArUco map pages. This is the quickest "external pose =  PX4 EKF" template here. Also the CopterHack contest. - Return-home without GNSS: rope-ladder (Habr), Bee-Nav translation. - Institutional research: GosNIIAS optical odometry, absolute VI-nav preprint, BSUIR anti-spoofing (metadata only).   Ukrainian academic snapshot These are short, applied papers. They usually set a target spec and report self-measured results on unpublished data: - Zaporizhzhia VO: targets +/-5 m at 10 Hz. - Khmelnytskyi: compares LK, Farneback and RAFT optical flow. - National Guard Academy survey. Use them for problem framing and requirement numbers, not as benchmarks.   Caveats - Much of the Ukrainian material is news or interviews that pass on vendor claims. No independent test data was found for OSCAR, Vyriy or Osiris. Osiris was left out because only an English-language report was found. - Habr blocked automated reads for one article (rope-ladder), so its author and date aren't verified. - Most repos here are small, recent and low-star. They're reference implementations of a problem statement, not libraries. - Telegram channels and YouTube talks weren't captured. Searches didn't surface stable, citable pages for them.   Round 2 (lane  ua-ru-round2 ) 30 resources and 22 repos, all tagged  lang:uk  or  lang:ru . Same rules as round 1: every repo checked with  gh api , every URL fetched or seen in a search result, vendor numbers passed on as claims, strike-oriented items skipped (Osiris on Defense Express and the Ruta navigation story were dropped for that reason). nodes.s: Three study tracks built from the courses, talks, books and docs in this index. Pick one by how much time you have before the hackathon.
nodes.b: Learning paths Three study tracks built from the courses, talks, books and docs in this index. Pick one by how much time you have before the hackathon.  About the times.  A time marked  (source)  is stated by the resource itself or by its index record. Every other time is a  planning estimate  - our budget for the slice you need, not the length of the full course. Adjust to your pace. Background chapters live in the navigation primer. Read export control and ethics before any work with RF, flight or defense end uses, whichever track you pick.   Track 1: one-day crash course (the day before) Goal: every teammate can explain GNSS failure modes, a Kalman filter and the dead-reckon-plus-fix pattern, and has run one tool. Split the team by role after the morning block.   Morning, everyone (about 4 hours, planning estimate)       Resource   Time   Why    --- ---------- ------ -----    1   How to fool a GPS (TEDx, Humphreys)   short talk   The threat in plain words     2   ION Online Tutorial: Basics of Satellite Navigation   45 min   Pseudoranges, clocks, error sources     3   SKYbrary: GNSS jamming and spoofing   20 min   What interference does to real systems     4   Understanding Sensor Fusion and Tracking (MATLAB Tech Talks)   10-15 min per video  (source) ; watch the intro and GPS+IMU episodes   Fusion intuition     5   Udacity AI for Robotics, particle filter lesson   1 hour  (source)    The estimator behind most map matching     6   Primer chapter 1   30 min   Frames, integrity, assured PNT vocabulary     Afternoon, by role (about 4 hours, planning estimate) -  Estimation lead:  Kalman and Bayesian Filters in Python, chapters on the multivariate KF and EKF; then the GTSAM tutorial ("best first hour with GTSAM" per its record). Run  samples/gnss-ins-ekf-outage . -  GNSS / EW lead:  ION webinar: jamming and spoofing on Android (hour-long ION webinar format  (source) ), the Android raw GNSS guide, then log a few minutes with GnssLogger and load it in gnss_lib_py. -  Vision lead:  Scaramuzza VO tutorial, Part I, then run LightGlue on one drone frame and one satellite tile ( samples/visual-geolocalization-lightglue ). -  Vehicle / integration lead:  PX4 simulation docs or ArduPilot SITL to a flying SITL vehicle, then ArduPilot Non-GPS navigation. -  SA / C2 lead:  CoT developer guide and PyTAK docs; run  samples/mavlink-to-tak-cot . -  Pitch lead:  NIST IR 8323r1 summary, DHS conformance framework, and NATO DIANA challenge statements for vocabulary.  Done when:  each role has one tool running on sample data and can state the main failure mode of their component.   Track 2: one week Goal: build a small end-to-end GNSS-denied navigation demo yourself before the event. About 2 to 3 hours per day (planning estimate).   Day   Theme   Resources   Hands-on    ----- ------- ----------- ----------    1   GNSS   Stanford GPS MOOC (selected lectures), Navipedia, primer ch. 2   Least-squares SPP on a RINEX or Android log (georinex, gnss_lib_py)     2   Filtering   Labbe KF/EKF/UKF chapters, kalmanfilter.net, Stachniss Mobile Robotics online training (Bayes filter, EKF, particle filter blocks)   Write a 2D EKF from scratch with FilterPy as reference     3   INS and GNSS/INS   Sola, quaternion kinematics for the ESKF, Kalibr IMU noise model, primer ch. 3   Run KF-GINS, mask GNSS, plot drift     4   Interference   White paper: protecting GNSS, ION webinar Rothmaier, ION webinar Hendeby (hour-long format  (source) )   Detector on TEXBAT or GPS-SDR-SIM  files  through GNSS-SDR; or ADS-B NIC/NACp map from readsb     5   Visual odometry   Scaramuzza VO tutorial I and II, VIN concise review   OpenVINS simulator or EuRoC; score with evo     6   Absolute alt-PNT   Couturier review, WildNav paper, MagNav.jl docs, primer ch. 5    samples/terrain-relative-nav-pf  or WildNav on a few frames     7   Integration   PX4 EKF2 guide or ArduPilot GPS/non-GPS transitions, MAVLink common messages   Feed your day-5 or day-6 output into SITL over MAVLink ( samples/vio-to-mavlink-bridge ); run the outage test from primer ch. 9    Done when:  you have a plot of position error vs time through a GNSS outage, with and without your extra source.   Track 3: one month, deep Goal: real understanding of estimation, GNSS receivers and one perception modality, enough to contribute to the open projects in this index. About 8 to 10 hours per week (planning estimate). Each week picks a slice of a longer course; the full courses are much longer.   Week 1: estimation foundations - Chalmers Sensor Fusion and Non-linear Filtering (edX) - self-paced; do the KF, EKF/UKF and particle filter modules with assignments. - Coursera State Estimation and Localization for Self-Driving Cars - the final ES-EKF fusing IMU, GNSS and LiDAR is a ready template. - micro Lie theory with manif. - Reference: Barfoot, State Estimation for Robotics chapters on nonlinear estimation and matrix Lie groups.   Week 2: GNSS in depth - ESA GNSS Data Processing Vol. I with Vol. II labs - SPP through PPP on real RINEX. - Borre, Software-Defined GPS and Galileo Receiver with SoftGNSS - acquisition and tracking loops. - GNSS-SDR tutorials; then OSNMA receiver guidelines with OSNMAlib. - Psiaki and Humphreys, GNSS spoofing and detection. - Optional paid: ION GNSS+ tutorials, half-day courses  (source) .   Week 3: one perception modality Choose one: -  Vision:  Vision Algorithms for Mobile Robotics (UZH/ETH) exercises to a mini VO pipeline; 14 Lectures on Visual SLAM; OpenVINS docs. -  SLAM / LiDAR:  Robot Mapping course (full semester recording  (source) ; take the graph-SLAM lectures) with exercises (described as a template for a 1-day SLAM crash course  (source) ); LiDAR odometry survey; run KISS-ICP and FAST-LIO. -  Aerial image-to-map:  Photogrammetry I and II (two-semester course  (source) ; take camera models, orientation and bundle adjustment); hloc paper; CVPR image matching workshop. -  Quadrotor navigation end to end:  MIT 16.485 VNAV labs.   Week 4: factor graphs, alt-P

nodes.s: Learned models in navigation pipelines carry three separate sets of terms:
nodes.b: Model weights licenses: code vs weights vs training data Learned models in navigation pipelines carry three separate sets of terms: 1.  Code license  - the repo LICENSE file. 2.  Weights license  - often the same, sometimes not (Depth-Anything-V2, DINOv2 sub-models, SuperPoint inside LightGlue). 3.  Training-data terms  - datasets such as ScanNet are "non-commercial research" only. Whether those terms bind  weights trained on them  is legally unsettled. Some authors pass them on explicitly (MASt3R's  CHECKPOINTS_NOTICE ), most say nothing. This page records what each source actually says. It is engineering triage, not legal advice. "Read" means the license text or README section was fetched on 2026-11-06 via  gh api  or WebFetch. "Paper" means the claim comes from the paper as I remember it, not from a document fetched for this page. Treat those as unverified.   Verdict key -  yes  - the stated terms allow it with normal attribution and notice. -  copyleft  - allowed, but your combined work must ship under the same license (GPL or AGPL) with source, including network use for AGPL. -  check  - the code and weights are permissive, but training-data terms are non-commercial or unknown. Fine for research and most hackathons. Get a lawyer's read before a product. -  no  - the stated terms forbid it. "Defense" means use by or for a defense customer, which is commercial in most readings. It also carries export-control duties whatever the license says: see export-control-and-ethics.md. The NVIDIA Community License, for one, has an explicit trade-compliance clause. nodes.s: After this chapter you can describe any navigation system as "a state, an uncertainty, a set of measurements and a way to check they agree", and you will know the vocabulary judges use when they ask whether your solution is "assured".
nodes.b: 1. PNT fundamentals After this chapter you can describe any navigation system as "a state, an uncertainty, a set of measurements and a way to check they agree", and you will know the vocabulary judges use when they ask whether your solution is "assured". Next: GNSS and its threats   Primer index   What PNT actually is PNT means three related outputs: -  Position  - where you are, in some coordinate frame. -  Navigation  - position over time plus velocity and attitude (which way you face), so you can steer. -  Timing  - a shared clock. GNSS is the world's main time source as well as its main position source, which is why a jammer can upset telecom and power grids, not just vehicles (ION webinar on timing-first PNT). As a software engineer, think of a navigation system as a state estimator: Sensors come in two flavours, and nearly every design in this hub mixes both:   Kind   Examples   Strength   Weakness    ------ ---------- ---------- ----------     Relative / dead reckoning    IMU, wheel odometry, visual odometry, LiDAR odometry, DVL   Smooth, high rate, hard to jam   Error grows without bound over time or distance      Absolute fixes    GNSS, image-to-map matching, terrain matching, magnetic anomaly, star tracker, radio beacons   Error does not grow with time   Intermittent, can be denied, spoofed or ambiguous   The core pattern of resilient navigation is:  dead-reckon between absolute fixes, and check every fix before you trust it.  Chapters 3 and 4 cover the dead-reckoning side, chapters 2 and 5 the absolute side.   Coordinate frames (the number one source of hackathon bugs) You will meet these frames constantly (chapter 7 covers the tooling): -  Geodetic (lat, lon, height)  on an ellipsoid, usually WGS84. Height can be above the ellipsoid or above the geoid (roughly mean sea level); GNSS gives ellipsoidal height, DEMs usually give orthometric height. Mixing them is a classic error (GeographicLib docs). -  ECEF  - Earth-centred, Earth-fixed Cartesian. What GNSS solvers compute in. -  Local tangent planes: ENU or NED  - east-north-up (ROS convention) or north-east-down (aerospace and PX4/ArduPilot convention). Feeding ENU into an NED consumer silently flips axes (PX4 external position docs). -  Body frame  - attached to the vehicle; IMU and cameras measure here, each with its own mounting offset (extrinsics). Rule: write down the frame of every variable, and convert with a library (pymap3d, pyproj), never by hand.   Uncertainty, consistency and integrity -  Accuracy  - how close your estimate is to truth. -  Covariance  - how close your filter  thinks  it is. A filter whose covariance is much smaller than its real error is  overconfident  and will reject good measurements. -  Integrity  - the ability to detect that the solution is wrong and warn in time. In aviation this is formalised as RAIM (receiver autonomous integrity monitoring): use redundant measurements to test for a faulty one and exclude it (Navipedia has good RAIM pages; Groves covers fault detection). The key operational lesson from real spoofing incidents is that  integrity beats accuracy : crews and systems were hurt most by positions that looked plausible but were wrong, and some avionics stayed degraded after GNSS returned (OPSGROUP spoofing report). For a hackathon this means an "is my position plausible?" monitor is often a better demo than a slightly more accurate filter. The basic consistency test, used everywhere from RAIM to EKF innovation gates: PX4 and ArduPilot both expose these innovation tests as tuning parameters (PX4 EKF2 guide, ArduPilot EKF overview).   Assured PNT: the vocabulary Defense and critical-infrastructure documents use a shared framing you should reuse in your pitch: -  Prevent / respond / recover.  The DHS Resilient PNT Conformance Framework grades equipment on four levels from basic recovery up to full threat tolerance. -  Identify / protect / detect / respond / recover.  NIST maps the Cybersecurity Framework onto PNT users and treats GNSS as an untrusted external input (NIST IR 8323r1). -  Source diversity, integrity checking, holdover.  The architectural patterns in the DHS reference architecture. -  Complementary PNT.  No single technology fully backs up GPS (DOT demonstration report; the JRC A-PNT assessment recommends a system-of-systems approach). -  DoD view:  keep GPS at the core and add complements, with integration and testing as the recurring challenge (GAO-21-320SP). For a contrarian counterweight to "GPS loss is catastrophic", read RAND RR-2970.   Timing in one paragraph A receiver's clock offset is a state like any other: GNSS solves for it alongside position (chapter 2). Without GNSS, time drifts at the rate of your local oscillator. Holdover - keeping usable time without GNSS - is what better clocks buy you; DARPA's ROCkN programme targets portable optical clocks for exactly this. In a hackathon, timing shows up as: timestamp alignment between sensors (a common VIO failure), PPS discipline via gpsd, and spoofers that push time rather than position (TEXBAT includes time-push scenarios, see chapter 2).   Failure modes under EW   Threat   What it does   What the system sees    -------- -------------- ----------------------     Jamming    Raises the noise floor in the GNSS band   Loss of fix, C/N0 drop, AGC change. Annoying but obvious.      Spoofing    Transmits counterfeit GNSS signals   A confident, wrong position or time. Hard to see. Regulators treat it as the higher-risk threat (EASA SIB).      Meaconing    Rebroadcasts real signals with delay   Consistent but shifted solution; defeats data authentication alone (OSNMA receiver guidelines).      Link jamming    Denies C2 / telemetry radio   Vehicle must navigate and decide on its own (IEEE Spectrum on Ukraine).      Contaminated fusion    Spoofed GNSS pulls a GNSS/INS filter along   Hybrid solutions can also be corrupted (FAA SAFO 24002).   The environment you are designing for: reporting from the war in Ukraine describes

nodes.s: After this chapter you can explain how a receiver turns satellite signals into a position, read raw receiver output, pick between SPP, RTK and PPP, and build a jamming or spoofing detector that runs on recorded data.
nodes.b: 2. GNSS and its threats After this chapter you can explain how a receiver turns satellite signals into a position, read raw receiver output, pick between SPP, RTK and PPP, and build a jamming or spoofing detector that runs on recorded data. Prev: PNT fundamentals   Next: Inertial and fusion   Primer index   How GNSS works Each satellite broadcasts a spreading code plus a navigation message (orbit and clock parameters). The receiver correlates the incoming signal against local code replicas to measure  when  the signal left the satellite, and so the apparent range: -  r_user  (3 unknowns) and  dt_user , the receiver clock offset (1 unknown), are what you solve for. Four satellites is the minimum; more give redundancy for integrity checks. -  dt_sat , orbits: from the broadcast message (defined bit-for-bit in IS-GPS-200 and the Galileo OS SIS ICD). -  I ,  T : ionospheric and tropospheric delays, modelled or removed with dual frequency. -  e : noise and multipath. Solve with iterative least squares (Gauss-Newton): linearise around a guess, solve for the correction, repeat. The geometry of the satellites in view scales measurement error into position error (DOP). A full derivation with labs is in ESA GNSS Data Processing Vol. I. The receiver pipeline, which Borre's book walks through in MATLAB and GNSS-SDR implements in C++:   Precision modes   Mode   Idea   What the sources say   Hackathon cost    ------ ------ ----------------------- ----------------     SPP  (single point)   Broadcast orbits and clocks, one receiver   The baseline every phone does   Free      DGNSS / RTK    A nearby base station sends corrections; RTK also resolves carrier-phase integer ambiguities   Centimetre-level from low-cost u-blox receivers with RTKLIB demo5 (rtklibexplorer)   Base station or NTRIP caster, RTCM parsing      PPP    Precise orbits and clocks from a global network, one receiver   Galileo HAS broadcasts free PPP corrections for decimetre-level PPP (HAS ICD); IGS products are free (IGS)   Long convergence; post-processing is easier   Corrections travel as RTCM 3 messages over NTRIP (HTTP streaming) (Navipedia RTK standards, BKG NTRIP). Receiver output is usually NMEA 0183 text (NMEA Revealed) or a binary vendor protocol such as u-blox UBX. Phones are real GNSS sensors: Android exposes raw pseudoranges, carrier phase, C/N0 and AGC (Android raw GNSS guide). Google's Smartphone Decimeter Challenge set decimeter-level smartphone positioning as its target, and winning solutions used factor graphs and carrier phase (GSDC 2023).   Threats   Jamming A jammer adds power in the GNSS band until tracking loops lose lock. It is easy to detect: C/N0 drops across all satellites at once and the front-end AGC changes. u-blox receivers expose jamming indicators (MON-RF) that apps can read (u-blox explainer). At the wide-area level, aircraft report degraded navigation integrity (NIC/NACp) in ADS-B, which GPSJam and the Flightradar24 map aggregate. Both caution that empty cells mean no data, not no jamming.   Spoofing A spoofer transmits counterfeit signals. A sophisticated one first aligns with the real signals, then drags the victim's solution away smoothly (Humphreys 2008). The barrier to crude spoofing is low: open-source tools and cheap SDRs fooled phones and a consumer drone (DEF CON 23 talk). In service, spoofing has hit airliners (OPSGROUP), ships (C4ADS, Windward 2025) and, through defensive spoofing, civilian phones in Ukraine (The Record).   Defenses, layered The survey literature agrees that several weak tests combined beat any single test (Psiaki and Humphreys 2016):   Layer   Check   Data you need    ------- ------- ---------------    Receiver signal   C/N0 too uniform or too high, AGC jump, correlation peak distortion   Raw measurements, IQ for the last one     Measurement consistency   RAIM residuals, pseudorange vs Doppler vs carrier consistency, clock jumps   Raw observables     Multi-constellation / multi-band   Spoofing many signals consistently is harder   Multi-GNSS receiver (u-blox)     Cross-sensor   GNSS position vs INS/VIO prediction, innovation gating   A fusion filter (chapter 3)     Spatial   Angle-of-arrival: all spoofed signals arrive from one direction   Antenna array or motion (Rothmaier webinar), or several receivers (Hendeby webinar)     Cryptographic   Galileo OSNMA authenticates navigation data   E1-B I/NAV bits, public key, loose time sync (OSNMA ICD)   OSNMA caveats you should state in a pitch: it authenticates the  navigation data , not the ranging signal, so it does not by itself stop replay or meaconing, and its security depends on the receiver's time-sync assumption (OSNMA receiver guidelines). Hardware defenses such as CRPA null-steering antennas (NovAtel GAJT-410ML) and in-receiver mitigation (Septentrio AIM+) exist; treat vendor performance claims as claims.   Failure modes under EW (summary) -  Jammed:  no fix. Your system must notice quickly and switch to dead reckoning and alternative fixes (chapters 3 to 5). -  Spoofed:  a fix that looks fine. Never let GNSS reset your filter without a consistency check; hybrid GNSS/INS can be dragged too (FAA SAFO 24002). -  After the event:  some systems retain corrupted state after GNSS returns (OPSGROUP). Plan the re-acquisition path, not only the loss path. -  Time:  spoofing can push time instead of position; anything downstream that trusts GNSS time inherits the error.   Working safely with interference data Do not transmit. Generate signals to  files  and feed them to a software receiver, or use recorded datasets (TEXBAT, Jammertest community recordings). The legal reasons are in Export control and ethics.   Learn it 1. Stanford GPS MOOC - pseudoranges and receiver basics. 2. Navipedia and Navipedia OSNMA - quick lookups. 3. White paper: Protecting GNSS against intentional interference - threat and countermeasure taxonomy. 4. ION webinar: Detecting jamming and spoofing on Android - phones as sensors. 5. ESA GNSS Data Processing Vol

nodes.s: After this chapter you can explain why an IMU drifts, write the predict/update loop of a Kalman filter, choose between a filter and a factor graph, and configure an off-the-shelf estimator to survive a GNSS outage.
nodes.b: 3. Inertial navigation and sensor fusion After this chapter you can explain why an IMU drifts, write the predict/update loop of a Kalman filter, choose between a filter and a factor graph, and configure an off-the-shelf estimator to survive a GNSS outage. Prev: GNSS and its threats   Next: Vision, LiDAR and radar odometry   Primer index   Inertial navigation An IMU measures specific force (accelerometers) and angular rate (gyroscopes) in the body frame. Strapdown mechanisation integrates them: It needs no external signal, so it cannot be jammed. The price is drift: a small gyro bias tilts the attitude estimate, which leaks gravity into the horizontal acceleration, which is integrated twice into position error. Error growth depends on sensor grade, so pick numbers from your own IMU, not from a slide. The standard way to characterise an IMU is an  Allan variance  plot from a long static log, giving white-noise density and bias random walk (Kalibr IMU noise model; tool: allan_variance_ros). Record that log before the event. Deep references: Titterton and Weston for INS physics, Groves for integration. For "what if" plots of tactical vs MEMS drift, pyins and gnss-ins-sim simulate IMUs of chosen grade. Attitude-only filters (AHRS) such as Madgwick or Mahony fuse gyro, accelerometer and magnetometer into orientation cheaply (Madgwick report, ahrs, x-io Fusion).   The Kalman filter in five lines -  Q  (process noise) says how much you distrust your motion model (the IMU);  R  says how much you distrust each measurement. Tuning is mostly about these two. -  EKF : linearise  f  and  h  with Jacobians.  UKF : propagate sigma points instead. -  Error-state KF (ESKF) : run the IMU mechanisation as the nominal state and filter only the small error, then reset. This is how most INS/GNSS filters are written (Sola, quaternion kinematics for the ESKF). - Rotations are not vectors. Use Lie-group plus/minus operators to add errors to attitude (micro Lie theory, manif). The  invariant EKF  defines error on the group itself and stays consistent under large initial errors (Barrau and Bonnabel).   GNSS/INS coupling   Coupling   What GNSS gives the filter   Trade-off    ---------- ---------------------------- -----------     Loose    Position/velocity fixes   Simple; needs a full fix (4+ satellites)      Tight    Raw pseudoranges/Doppler   Uses partial constellations; per-satellite outlier rejection      Deep / ultra-tight    INS aids receiver tracking loops   Better under jamming; requires receiver access   Groves explains all three. For a hackathon, start loose (KF-GINS), mask GNSS epochs to simulate an outage, and plot drift.   Filters vs factor graphs A  factor graph  writes the whole problem as a sparse nonlinear least-squares over a window (or all) of past states, with one factor per measurement. Benefits: you can relinearise, add delayed or out-of-order measurements, and add or drop sensors without rewriting the filter (Dellaert and Kaess). iSAM2 makes this incremental (paper); IMU preintegration summarises many IMU samples into one factor between keyframes (Forster et al.). GTSAM implements all of this with Python bindings. Rule of thumb: an EKF is the fastest thing to get working in 48 hours; a factor graph pays off once you have three or more sensors or intermittent absolute fixes.   All-source and plug-and-play fusion DARPA's ASPN programme set the goal that later GNSS-denied architectures inherit: navigation software that accepts arbitrary combinations of sensors and reconfigures quickly (ANS/ASPN, DARPA briefing). AFIT work runs multiple filters in parallel and monitors integrity to isolate a faulty or spoofed input (Gipson webinar). Autopilots do a light version of this: ArduPilot runs one EKF core per IMU and switches lanes on inconsistency (EKF overview).   Learned inertial odometry Networks can regress displacement or noise covariance from raw IMU windows and feed a classical filter: AI-IMU for cars (paper, code), TLIO and RoNIN for pedestrians (chapter 8), AirIO for drones (paper). These reduce drift on data like their training set; test on your own motion profile before claiming anything.   Failure modes under EW -  Spoofed GNSS drags the filter.  A slow spoofer stays inside the innovation gate. Defend with tighter gates during suspicion, cross-checks against other sources (chapters 4 and 5), and never let GNSS hard-reset the state. FAA notes hybrid GPS/inertial solutions can also be corrupted (SAFO 24002). -  Jammed GNSS:  pure inertial drift. The value of better inertial sensors is longer holdover, which is how DIU frames quantum inertial sensing (DIU solicitation). -  Overconfidence:  a filter with too-small  Q  rejects the true fix after an outage. Watch the normalised innovation squared. -  Magnetometer interference:  heading from a magnetometer is corrupted by motors and current; ArduPilot/PX4 allow other yaw sources (ArduPilot EKF source selection). -  Timestamp misalignment and wrong extrinsics  look like sensor faults. Calibrate first.   Learn it 1. Kalman and Bayesian Filters in Python (Labbe) - intuition-first notebooks. 2. kalmanfilter.net tutorial - numeric examples by hand. 3. Understanding Sensor Fusion and Tracking (MATLAB Tech Talks) - 10-15 minute videos; the GPS+IMU episode maps to a nav filter. 4. Udacity AI for Robotics - localization filters in Python. 5. Stachniss Mobile Robotics online training - Bayes filter to EKF to particle filter. 6. Coursera: State Estimation and Localization for Self-Driving Cars - ends in an IMU/GNSS/LiDAR ES-EKF. 7. Sola, quaternion kinematics for the ESKF and micro Lie theory. 8. Chalmers sensor fusion and nonlinear filtering (edX). 9. GTSAM tutorial then Factor graphs for robot perception. 10. Forster IMU preintegration, iSAM2, invariant EKF. 11. Groves, Barfoot, State Estimation for Robotics, Titterton and Weston.   Build with it - FilterPy - KF/EKF/UKF classes for prototypes (not Lie-group aware). - GTSAM - factor graphs with ImuFactor; ad

nodes.s: After this chapter you can explain how a camera, LiDAR or radar measures motion, what SLAM adds on top of odometry, and which open stack to run on which sensor. These are relative sources: they slow drift, they do not remove it. Absolute fixes are chapter 5.
nodes.b: 4. Vision, LiDAR and radar odometry After this chapter you can explain how a camera, LiDAR or radar measures motion, what SLAM adds on top of odometry, and which open stack to run on which sensor. These are  relative  sources: they slow drift, they do not remove it. Absolute fixes are chapter 5. Prev: Inertial and fusion   Next: Absolute alternative PNT   Primer index   Odometry vs SLAM vs relocalization -  Odometry  - estimate motion between consecutive frames or scans. Drift accumulates. -  SLAM  - also build a map and recognise revisited places ( loop closure ), which pulls accumulated drift back. Modern SLAM is MAP estimation on a factor graph with a front end (data association) and a back end (optimisation) (Cadena et al. survey). -  Relocalization  - estimate pose against a map you built earlier. If that map is georeferenced, this becomes an absolute fix (chapter 5).   Visual and visual-inertial odometry A camera sees features (corners, learned keypoints) that move between frames. From matched features you recover relative pose with two-view geometry and RANSAC, then refine with bundle adjustment (minimise reprojection error over poses and 3D points) (Scaramuzza and Fraundorfer VO tutorial). A single camera cannot see metric scale. Adding an IMU (VIO) recovers scale and gravity direction and bridges fast motion (Huang, VIN concise review). Two estimator families coexist: -  Filter-based (MSCKF)  - OpenVINS, whose docs double as a derivation textbook (OpenVINS docs). -  Sliding-window optimisation  - VINS-Mono, ORB-SLAM3 (adds multi-map Atlas to recover from tracking loss), Kimera. Calibration decides whether VIO works at all: camera intrinsics, camera-IMU extrinsics and time offset (Kalibr wiki). Simplest GNSS-free velocity source on a drone:  optical flow plus a rangefinder  for scale, supported natively by both autopilots (PX4 optical flow, ArduPilot optical flow). Learned and foundation-model approaches (DROID-SLAM, MASt3R-SLAM) are more robust on hard sequences and GPU-heavy. Event cameras offer microsecond latency and high dynamic range, with algorithms redesigned for asynchronous data (event vision survey). Thermal-inertial odometry targets darkness and smoke (ETIO).   LiDAR odometry and SLAM LiDAR gives metric 3D points directly. Odometry registers each scan against the previous scan or a local map, typically with ICP (iterative closest point) variants: - KISS-ICP argues that well-engineered point-to-point ICP is a strong baseline across sensors.  pip install  and go. - FAST-LIO2 fuses raw points with the IMU in an iterated Kalman filter; LIO-SAM uses a factor graph where GNSS factors can be added or dropped. - FAST-LIVO2 adds a camera and stays robust when one modality degrades. Known weakness:  geometric degeneracy  - long tunnels, open fields, flat water - where the scan does not constrain all six degrees of freedom (LiDAR odometry survey).   Radar odometry Radar sees through dust, smoke, fog and darkness. Spinning FMCW radars give 2D scans; 4D mmWave radars add elevation and Doppler (radial velocity per point) but produce sparse, noisy clouds that need radar-specific methods (4D radar survey). CFEAR shows simple filtering working well on spinning radar. Radar is an active emitter, which matters in an EW setting (it can be detected).   Place recognition and feature matching Loop closure and map relocalization need to answer "have I seen this place?": -  Global descriptors (retrieval)  - one vector per image; nearest neighbour search. Foundation-model features generalise across domains without VPR-specific training (AnyLoc, SALAD). -  Local matching  - verify and refine with keypoint matches (LightGlue, lightweight XFeat, dense RoMa). -  Retrieve-then-match  is the scalable pattern (hloc paper). Chapter 5 reuses it for image-to-satellite localization.   Failure modes under EW and in the field These sensors are hard to jam, which is why they matter. Their failure modes are physical: -  Low texture or repetitive scenes  (water, snow, sand, fields) starve VIO of features. -  Lighting:  night, glare, fast exposure changes. Thermal or event cameras help. -  Obscurants:  smoke and dust blind cameras and LiDAR; radar keeps working. -  Degenerate geometry  for LiDAR (above). -  Dynamic scenes:  moving vehicles and people violate the static-world assumption. -  Initialization and scale:  monocular VIO needs motion to initialise (VINS-Mono). -  Active sensors are emitters.  LiDAR and radar can be detected; passive vision cannot. -  Drift never goes to zero  without loop closure or an absolute fix.   Learn it 1. Stachniss YouTube channel, "5 Minutes with Cyrill" - short explainers on ICP, RANSAC, SIFT, factor graphs. 2. Scaramuzza VO tutorial, Parts I and II - best single read on VO design. 3. TUM Visual Navigation for Flying Robots or the lighter AUTONAVx MOOC. 4. Vision Algorithms for Mobile Robotics (UZH/ETH) - exercises end in a working mini VO pipeline. 5. 14 Lectures on Visual SLAM - code-heavy bridge to ORB-SLAM-style systems. 6. Robot Mapping course (Freiburg) with exercises. 7. Cadena et al. SLAM survey and VIN concise review. 8. MIT 16.485 VNAV - ROS 2 labs to a quadrotor VIO stack. 9. LiDAR odometry survey and 4D radar survey. 10. SLAM Handbook - current one-stop reference, including radar chapters.   Build with it - OpenVINS - MSCKF VIO with a built-in simulator. - ORB-SLAM3 (ROS 2 wrapper) - visual/VI SLAM. - VINS-Fusion - VIO with a global-fusion node for GNSS. - RTAB-Map (ROS) - RGB-D/stereo/LiDAR SLAM with map save and relocalization. - Kalibr - camera and camera-IMU calibration. - KISS-ICP and KISS-SLAM - minimal LiDAR odometry and SLAM. - FAST-LIO and LIO-SAM - LiDAR-inertial. - small_gicp - scan-to-map registration for localization prototypes. - RIO and 4DRadarSLAM - radar-inertial odometry and SLAM. - LightGlue, XFeat, hloc, AnyLoc - matching and retrieval. - evo - evaluate any trajectory (chapter 9). Samples in this hub:  samples/vio-to-mavlink-bridge . Related c

nodes.s: After this chapter you can explain the five main ways to get an absolute position without GNSS - image-to-map matching, terrain matching, magnetic anomaly matching, celestial fixes and signals of opportunity - pick the one that fits your platform, and feed its output into a filter as a measurement with honest uncertainty.
nodes.b: 5. Absolute alternative PNT After this chapter you can explain the five main ways to get an absolute position without GNSS - image-to-map matching, terrain matching, magnetic anomaly matching, celestial fixes and signals of opportunity - pick the one that fits your platform, and feed its output into a filter as a measurement with honest uncertainty. Prev: Vision, LiDAR and radar odometry   Next: Autopilots and C2   Primer index   The common pattern: map matching Four of the five techniques share one structure: Because maps have repeated patterns, the match likelihood is often multi-modal, so a  particle filter  or a gated multi-hypothesis search is the usual estimator. Uncertainty matters as much as the fix: work such as UASTHN adds uncertainty estimation precisely so a navigation filter can weight or reject visual fixes (UASTHN).   Visual geo-localization (image-to-map) Match a downward or oblique camera frame against georeferenced satellite or orthophoto tiles. This is the technique most visible in current conflict reporting: Ukrainian drone developers use onboard optical navigation to keep flying after links and GNSS are jammed (IEEE Spectrum, IISS dossier). Vendor performance claims there are not independently tested (Militarnyi report). Pipeline (retrieve-then-match, from chapter 4): 1.  Retrieve  candidate tiles near the predicted position with a global descriptor (AnyLoc, Sample4Geo for cross-view). 2.  Match  keypoints between frame and tile (LightGlue, RoMa for cross-season, MASt3R for extreme viewpoint change). 3.  Estimate  a homography or PnP pose, convert tile pixels to lat/lon. 4.  Gate  against the filter prediction and inlier count. What the papers report about failure: WildNav's failures cluster over low-texture and changed terrain (paper); low-altitude oblique views are much harder than nadir (AnyVisLoc benchmark); altitude changes strongly affect retrieval accuracy (SUES-200). Night operation is possible with thermal-to-RGB matching (thermal geo-localization, STHN). Reference imagery: Sentinel-2 via public STAC APIs needs no key (STAC spec); see chapter 7.   Terrain-relative navigation Measure terrain height under the vehicle (radar or laser altimeter minus barometric altitude), collect a profile along the track, and correlate it with a DEM. This is the TERCOM idea. It works over rough terrain and fails over flat ground and water, where every position looks the same. A free global DEM is the 30 m Copernicus GLO-30 on AWS (Copernicus DEM); remember the geoid vs ellipsoid height difference (GeographicLib). Vision-based terrain-aided localization for aircraft is the camera variant (Navon webinar).   Magnetic anomaly navigation (MagNav) The Earth's crust has a spatially varying magnetic anomaly field, mapped by survey flights. A magnetometer reading compared against the anomaly map gives position. It is passive and cannot be jammed by RF. The hard part is not matching but  compensation : the aircraft's own magnetic field swamps the signal. The scalar reading mixes core field, crustal anomaly and platform field; Tolles-Lawson is the classical compensation baseline, and physics plus ML beat either alone in the AFRL/MIT challenge (challenge paper, challenge site). The method's flight-test basis is AFIT's dissertation work (Canciani 2016). A 2025 field-trial paper reports quantum-magnetometer MagNav outperforming a strategic-grade INS in airborne and ground trials (Q-CTRL 2025); DARPA's RoQS targets platform noise as the barrier (RoQS). Map coverage and resolution limit where it works.   Celestial navigation A camera that sees stars plus a catalogue gives attitude (a star tracker solves "lost-in-space" identification, tetra3 docs). Position additionally needs an accurate local vertical and time. Daytime and low-altitude use is limited by sky brightness and clouds. Sky polarization offers a heading reference under clear sky (OpenSky polarization simulator). GAO lists celestial among DoD's alternative PNT families (GAO-21-320SP).   Signals of opportunity (SoOP) and radio ranging Use signals never designed for navigation: LEO broadband constellations, cellular LTE/5G, broadcast, or your own beacons. -  LEO Doppler.  A LEO satellite moves fast, so its Doppler shift encodes geometry, as the old TRANSIT system used. With many satellites in view, Doppler-only positioning is geometrically viable (Psiaki, TRANSIT on steroids). -  Starlink without cooperation.  Researchers track Starlink downlinks without operator support (Kassas first results), partly by reverse-engineering the OFDM signal structure (Humphreys 2023). Carrier-phase positioning results are reported at metre level with known altitude (Kassas 2022). Ephemeris error is a dominant limitation. -  Cellular  signals are viable in cities (LTE receiver webinar). -  Terrestrial backups : eLoran fails differently from GNSS, which is its value (DOT demonstration); R-Mode in the jammed Baltic (39C3 talk). -  Own beacons : UWB anchors indoors (Loco Positioning, where anchor geometry dominates accuracy) or LoRa ranging for GPS-denied return-to-home (Hyams).   Failure modes under EW   Technique   Jam/spoof exposure   Main physical failure    ----------- ------------------- -----------------------    Visual geo-localization   Passive, no RF   Low texture, changed terrain, clouds, night (without thermal), oblique views, stale maps     Terrain matching   Altimeter is an emitter   Flat terrain and water; DEM resolution and datum errors     MagNav   Passive   Platform interference; map coverage     Celestial   Passive   Cloud, daylight, needs accurate vertical and time     SoOP / beacons   RF: can be jammed or spoofed like any radio; receivers do not authenticate   Unknown signal structure, ephemeris and clock errors, geometry   Any absolute fix can be wrong. Treat each as a measurement with a covariance, gate it, and keep dead reckoning running underneath.   Learn it 1. GAO-21-320SP - the families and their maturity. 2. Review on deep learn

nodes.s: After this chapter you can run PX4 or ArduPilot in simulation, inject your own position source over MAVLink, configure the estimator to switch away from GNSS, and push your vehicle's position and detections onto a TAK common operating picture.
nodes.b: 6. Autopilots and C2 After this chapter you can run PX4 or ArduPilot in simulation, inject your own position source over MAVLink, configure the estimator to switch away from GNSS, and push your vehicle's position and detections onto a TAK common operating picture. Prev: Absolute alternative PNT   Next: Maps, geodesy and planning   Primer index   The two open autopilots -  PX4  - Dronecode flight stack on NuttX with a uORB pub/sub bus. Its estimator is EKF2, which fuses IMU, GNSS, baro, magnetometer, optical flow, external vision and range (EKF2 guide). -  ArduPilot  - Copter, Plane, Rover (incl. boats) and Sub. Its estimator is EKF3, with one core per IMU and automatic lane switching (EKF overview). Both run in software-in-the-loop (SITL) with Gazebo, which is where you should spend the whole hackathon unless you have flight approval (PX4 simulation, ArduPilot SITL). Typical architecture for an alt-nav build:   Getting your position into the autopilot MAVLink is the lightweight binary protocol between autopilots, ground stations and companion computers (MAVLink guide). The hooks for alternative PNT are in the common message set (common.xml reference):   Message   Use    --------- -----     VISION_POSITION_ESTIMATE    Pose from VIO/SLAM in a local frame      ODOMETRY    Full pose and velocity with covariance (preferred)      VISION_SPEED_ESTIMATE    Velocity only      GPS_INPUT    Present your fix as if it were a GNSS receiver (e.g. absolute map-matching output)   ArduPilot documents the accepted messages and frames (non-GPS position via MAVLink); PX4 documents EKF2_EV_  parameters and ENU vs NED handling (external position). Frame transforms are the usual failure point (ArduPilot ROS VIO tutorial).   Switching sources when GNSS goes bad -  ArduPilot EKF3  supports up to three source sets ( EK3_SRCn_ ) with per-axis choice of position, velocity and yaw source, switchable in flight by RC switch, Lua script or MAVLink (source selection, GPS / non-GPS transitions). A Lua script that watches GNSS health and your detector, then switches sets, is a solid hackathon deliverable. -  PX4 EKF2  uses innovation tests to reject inconsistent aiding and documents aiding modes; recent summit talks cover non-GNSS aiding and "reset by fusion" (EKF2 tuning guide, Riseborough 2020, PX4 Developer Summit). - Full menu of ArduPilot GPS-free sources: optical flow, beacons, wheel encoders, VIO, motion capture, external nav (Non-GPS navigation).   C2 links and their security -  MAVLink 2 signing  adds a SHA-256 based signature and timestamp to resist injection and replay. It authenticates, it does not encrypt, and key distribution is up to you (MAVLink 2 signing). -  Mission protocol  uploads waypoints, geofences and rally points (mission protocol). -  NATO interoperability : STANAG 4586 defines five levels of interoperability from receiving payload data up to full flight control (STANAG 4586 overview). -  Cyber-resilience of autopilots  is treated as part of autonomy in Navy challenges (HACKtheMACHINE).   Situational awareness: CoT and TAK Cursor on Target (CoT) is a small XML event schema: what (a hierarchical  type  string derived from military symbology), where (point with error estimates), when (CoT NDIA briefing, MITRE CoT guide). TAK (ATAK, WinTAK, TAK Server) carries CoT as XML or protobuf over UDP multicast (mesh) or TCP/TLS (streaming) (TAK protocol). Pick type codes from cot-types; render symbols per MIL-STD-2525 / APP-6. Register on TAK.gov early; SDK downloads are behind an account. A useful honesty point for any SA display: CoT points carry circular and linear error fields. Fill them from your filter covariance instead of leaving defaults, so an operator can see when your position is degraded.   Defensive counter-UAS detection Within this hub's scope: detecting and tracking drones, not defeating them. -  Cooperative:  Remote ID broadcasts drone and control-station position under ASTM F3411 (FAA Remote ID, MAVLink Open Drone ID). -  Protocol analysis:  DJI DroneID was shown to be unencrypted and decodable with an SDR (NDSS 2023). -  Vision/thermal tracking:  Anti-UAV benchmark. -  Track fusion:  Stone Soup for multi-target tracking with defensible metrics.   Failure modes under EW -  Link loss:  the vehicle must have a sane onboard behaviour (hold, return on dead reckoning, land). Do not assume the GCS can intervene. -  GNSS failsafe triggers on spoofed-but-healthy-looking data:  failsafes key on fix loss, which spoofing does not cause. Add your own plausibility check. -  Source switching transients:  switching EKF source sets can jump the estimate; test it in SITL with a scripted outage. -  Unsigned MAVLink  accepts injected commands from anyone on the link. -  TAK displays  show whatever position they receive; a spoofed vehicle position propagates to every operator.   Learn it 1. PX4 simulation docs or ArduPilot SITL - get a vehicle flying in Gazebo. 2. MAVLink developer guide and common messages. 3. ArduPilot Non-GPS navigation and GPS / Non-GPS transitions. 4. PX4 EKF2 guide and PX4 VIO. 5. MAVLink 2 signing. 6. CoT developer guide, TAK protocol, PyTAK docs. 7. Riseborough PX4 state estimation 2020 and ArduPilot DevCon 2024 - estimator design from the authors. 8. STANAG 4586 overview for NATO framing.   Build with it - PX4 with px4_ros_com / px4_msgs. - ArduPilot with ardupilot_gazebo and ardupilot_ros. - MAVSDK-Python and pymavlink - script the vehicle and send position messages. - vision_to_mavros - external pose to MAVLink. - mavlink-router - fan telemetry out to several consumers. - QGroundControl and Mission Planner - ground stations. - PyTAK, takproto, OpenTAKServer, FreeTAKServer - TAK side. - milsymbol - MIL-STD-2525 / APP-6 symbols in JS. - Open Drone ID receiver (Android) and opendroneid-core-c - Remote ID. - Stone Soup - tracking and data association. Samples in this hub:  samples/mavlink-to-tak-cot ,  samples/vio-to-mavlink-bridge ,  samples/stone-soup-tracking . Related concepts: auto

nodes.s: After this chapter you can convert between the coordinate systems your tools disagree on, fetch free imagery and elevation data for a region, display it, and plan a path or a multi-vehicle mission over it.
nodes.b: 7. Maps, geodesy and planning After this chapter you can convert between the coordinate systems your tools disagree on, fetch free imagery and elevation data for a region, display it, and plan a path or a multi-vehicle mission over it. Prev: Autopilots and C2   Next: Maritime, underwater and ground   Primer index   Geodesy you actually need -  Datum and ellipsoid.  GNSS works in WGS84 (in practice an ITRF realisation). Other datasets may use national datums; PROJ handles datum transforms, including time-dependent ones, given its grid files (PROJ). -  Heights.  Ellipsoidal height (GNSS) vs orthometric height (DEMs, maps). The difference is the geoid undulation, and it matters whenever you compare GNSS altitude with terrain (GeographicLib docs). Barometric altitude is a third reference with its own drift. -  Projections.  UTM gives metric x/y in zones; local ENU/NED is best for a filter (chapter 1). Do math in a local metric frame, store and exchange in lat/lon. -  Military grid.  MGRS strings are what operators read and type (mgrs); mind the precision argument. -  Geodesics.  Distance and bearing on the ellipsoid, not on a sphere, for anything beyond a few kilometres (GeographicLib).   Data you can get without an account -  Elevation:  Copernicus GLO-30/GLO-90 DEM as cloud-optimised GeoTIFFs on AWS, sampled directly with rasterio (Copernicus DEM). -  Imagery:  public STAC APIs give key-free access to Sentinel-2 and Copernicus DEM (STAC spec, pystac-client). -  Roads and features:  OpenStreetMap via OSMnx. -  Your own orthophoto:  fly (or simulate), then build one with OpenDroneMap. A fresh map of the area is often the best reference for chapter 5 visual matching. Tooling: GDAL for format conversion (use conda or Docker to avoid binding mismatches), rasterio for Python raster access, QGIS to look at everything.   Displaying it - 2D web maps: Leaflet, MapLibre GL JS, served by Martin for vector tiles. - 3D globe with terrain and time-dynamic tracks: CesiumJS. - Large point/track layers: deck.gl. - Military symbology: milsymbol (chapter 6).   Planning Three levels, from fast to slow:   Level   Question   Typical tools    ------- ---------- ---------------     Mission / task    Which vehicle does what, in which order?   Behaviour trees (BehaviorTree.CPP), PDDL (PlanSys2), auction-style allocation (CBBA), coverage (Fields2Cover)      Global path    Which route through the map?   Graph search (A , Dijkstra) on a grid or road graph (OSRM, Valhalla), sampling planners (OMPL)      Local / trajectory    How to move the next few seconds without hitting things?   Nav2 controllers (Nav2 docs), quadrotor planners (Fast-Planner, EGO-Planner)   Navigation-aware planning is a good defense-hackathon angle: cost a route not only by distance and terrain but by  expected navigation quality  - texture for visual matching, terrain roughness for TERCOM, known interference areas from GPSJam. Reasoning over localization uncertainty improved mission decisions in DARPA SubT (NeBula).   Multi-agent - Swarm planning: EGO-Swarm. - Multi-robot frameworks: Aerostack2 (same mission across autopilots and simulators, paper), Crazyswarm2. - Collaborative SLAM under limited bandwidth: Swarm-SLAM, Kimera-Multi. - Relative localization between agents by UWB ranging needs no anchors, but observability depends on relative motion (Li et al.). - Cooperative ranging reduced drift in UAV-UGV teams underground (Gross webinar).   Failure modes under EW -  Planner trusts a spoofed position:  the path is correct for the wrong place. Feed the planner the covariance and refuse aggressive plans when it is large. -  Geofences  enforced on GNSS position fail with GNSS; enforce on the fused estimate. -  Comms-denied multi-agent:  decentralised allocation (CBBA) and budgeted map sharing (Swarm-SLAM) degrade more gracefully than a central server. -  Map mismatch:  stale imagery, wrong datum or height reference shift every downstream computation silently.   Learn it 1. GeographicLib docs - geodesics, geoid, projections. 2. STAC spec and Copernicus DEM on AWS - data access. 3. Udacity AI for Robotics - search and planning basics. 4. Survey of ROS 2 algorithms by maintainers - what is production-ready. 5. Nav2 docs, Marathon 2 paper, Nav2 GPS tutorial. 6. OMPL site - define state spaces, benchmark planners. 7. Fast-Planner and EGO-Planner papers. 8. Aerostack2, PlanSys2, Fields2Cover.   Build with it - pyproj, pymap3d, GeographicLib, mgrs. - GDAL, rasterio, pystac-client, elevation, OpenDroneMap. - Leaflet, MapLibre, CesiumJS, QGIS. - PythonRobotics - readable planners, e.g. over a rasterised DEM. - Nav2, OMPL, grid_map. - EGO-Swarm, Aerostack2, CBBA, Fields2Cover. - OSRM, Valhalla, OSMnx - road routing. Related concepts: geodesy, GIS and mapping, path planning, mission planning, obstacle avoidance, multi-agent.

nodes.s: After this chapter you know how navigation changes off the drone: what ships broadcast and how spoofing shows up in it, how vehicles navigate underwater where no radio reaches, how ground robots and pedestrians dead-reckon, and which open stacks cover each domain.
nodes.b: 8. Maritime, underwater, ground and dismounted After this chapter you know how navigation changes off the drone: what ships broadcast and how spoofing shows up in it, how vehicles navigate underwater where no radio reaches, how ground robots and pedestrians dead-reckon, and which open stacks cover each domain. Prev: Maps, geodesy and planning   Next: Evaluation and datasets   Primer index   Maritime surface  Data on a ship.  Position, heading, speed and AIS flow between devices as NMEA 0183 sentences (NMEA 0183) or NMEA 2000 PGNs on a CAN bus (NMEA 2000). Neither is authenticated. Signal K wraps marine data as JSON over REST and WebSocket, easy to consume from any language (Signal K spec).  AIS  is a VHF TDMA broadcast where ships report identity, position, course and speed (ITU-R M.1371). It is unauthenticated, so AIS anomalies are the main public signal of GNSS manipulation at sea (Windward 2025). C4ADS used impossible AIS tracks to map thousands of spoofing events around Russia, Crimea and Syria (Above Us Only Stars). A practical hackathon detector: decode AIS with an RTL-SDR, then flag ships whose reported positions jump, cluster on one point, or violate their own speed.  Resilient maritime PNT.  Backups at sea include eLoran and R-Mode, which reuses existing radio beacons and coastal infrastructure and has been tested in the jammed Baltic (39C3 talk, MarRINav webinar). Marine radar plus charts is the traditional independent cross-check.  Autonomy at sea.  Collision regulations (COLREGs) define give-way and stand-on duties; rules 13 to 17 drive most USV avoidance logic, and they are written for human judgement, which makes formalisation hard (COLREGs). MOOS-IvP is the long-running behaviour-based autonomy stack, taught in MIT 2.680 (MIT 2.680, MOOS-IvP docs).   Underwater GNSS does not penetrate water, so an AUV or ROV combines: -  INS + DVL.  A Doppler velocity log measures velocity over the seabed; integrated with attitude, it gives dead reckoning (Water Linked DVL docs). -  Depth sensor  - absolute in one axis. -  Acoustic positioning  (USBL/LBL) from a surface reference that does have GNSS (Water Linked Underwater GPS). -  Sonar odometry / SLAM  against the seabed or structures (sonar-SLAM, DISO). -  Surfacing  for a GNSS fix, which exposes the vehicle. ArduSub feeds external DVL and USBL positions into its EKF via MAVLink (ArduSub docs). Simulate with HoloOcean, which models sonar, DVL, IMU and depth sensors (HoloOcean docs).   Ground vehicles Ground robots have extra constraints a drone lacks: wheels (odometry), contact with the ground (non-holonomic motion, zero-velocity when stopped) and terrain that decides where they can go. -  Fusion:  wheel odometry + IMU + GNSS with robot_localization's EKF and  navsat_transform  is the standard ROS 2 recipe (Nav2 robot_localization guide, Nav2 GPS tutorial). Datum and frame setup trips people up. -  Map-based localization:  NDT scan matching plus EKF in Autoware (Autoware docs). -  Contact-aided estimation  for legged robots adds leg kinematics to an invariant EKF (Hartley et al.). -  Off-road  semantics differ sharply from urban data (RELLIS-3D); traversability can be learned online from pre-trained features (Wild Visual Navigation). -  Urban canyons  degrade GNSS through blockage and multipath (UrbanLoco).   Dismounted and indoor -  Foot-mounted INS  uses the moment the foot is still each step as a zero-velocity update (ZUPT) that resets velocity drift (PyShoe). -  Learned pedestrian inertial odometry  from a phone IMU (RoNIN, TLIO). -  UWB  anchors for indoor positioning (chapter 5).   Space (brief) Space navigation in this hub covers spacecraft pose estimation and star trackers (Kelvins SPEED+, tetra3) and LEO signals (chapter 5). Space-segment security is part of assured PNT (Hack-A-Sat).   Failure modes under EW -  Maritime:  spoofed GNSS propagates into AIS, ECDIS and every NMEA consumer on an unauthenticated bus. Cross-check with radar, compass and log speed. -  AIS itself  can be spoofed or switched off; absence of a track is not absence of a ship. -  Underwater:  RF-based threats barely apply, but surfacing for GNSS and acoustic positioning are exposure points; DVL loses bottom lock over deep water. -  Ground:  wheel slip, GNSS multipath in streets and under trees, and spoofed GNSS dragging  navsat_transform . -  Dismounted:  consumer phones in areas with defensive spoofing get wrong location and time (The Record).   Learn it 1. Signal K spec and ITU-R M.1371 (AIS). 2. C4ADS Above Us Only Stars - spoofing OSINT method. 3. 39C3: Terrestrial navigation in the Baltic. 4. MIT 2.680 marine autonomy and MOOS-IvP docs. 5. COLREGs. 6. ArduSub docs and Water Linked docs. 7. Nav2 GPS tutorial, robot_localization docs, ROSCon UK 2025 state estimation workshop. 8. Coursera Self-Driving Cars specialization and Autoware docs.   Build with it - AIS-catcher and pyais - receive and decode AIS. - Signal K Server and OpenCPN - marine data hub and chartplotter. - ArduPilot (Rover boat / ArduSub) and BlueOS. - MOOS-IvP, VRX, NTNU colav-simulator - surface autonomy and collision avoidance. - Stonefish, HoloOcean ROS, Ping Python, sonar-SLAM - underwater. - robot_localization, Nav2, CARLA, elevation_mapping_cupy - ground. - PyShoe, RoNIN, TLIO - pedestrian. Related concepts: maritime, underwater, ground vehicle, indoor and pedestrian, space.

nodes.s: After this chapter you can pick a dataset or simulator that matches your scenario, compute the trajectory metrics judges and reviewers expect, and design a GNSS-outage or interference test that shows what your system does when it matters.
nodes.b: 9. Evaluation and datasets After this chapter you can pick a dataset or simulator that matches your scenario, compute the trajectory metrics judges and reviewers expect, and design a GNSS-outage or interference test that shows what your system does when it matters. Prev: Maritime, underwater and ground   Primer index   Metrics -  ATE / APE (absolute trajectory/pose error)  - align estimate to ground truth, then RMSE of position differences. Measures global consistency. -  RPE (relative pose error)  - error over fixed sub-trajectory lengths. Measures drift rate independent of where it started. -  Alignment matters.  VIO without absolute fixes is only defined up to a rigid transform (and scale for monocular); align with SE(3) or Sim(3) and say which you used. Systems that claim absolute position (GNSS, map matching) should be scored  without  alignment. -  Drift under outage  - error as a function of time or distance since GNSS was lost. This is the number a resilient-PNT pitch needs. -  Integrity metrics  - for a detector: detection rate, false-alarm rate, time to alarm. For a navigator: how often the true error exceeded the reported uncertainty (consistency). -  Tracking metrics  for SA and C-UAS: OSPA and SIAP in Stone Soup (Stone Soup docs). evo computes APE/RPE with alignment flags and reads most dataset formats directly.   Datasets by scenario   Scenario   Datasets in the index    ---------- ------------------------    First VIO sanity check   EuRoC MAV (small, stereo + IMU)     Long-term VIO drift   TUM VI     Aggressive drone flight   UZH-FPV     Driving, LiDAR/stereo odometry   KITTI odometry, KITTI-360     Urban GNSS degradation   UrbanLoco, UrbanNav, Complex Urban     Aerial LiDAR-visual-inertial-GNSS (incl. raw GNSS)   MARS-LVIG     Smartphone GNSS   GSDC 2023, GSDC 2022     GNSS spoofing (IQ)   TEXBAT     GNSS interference maps   GPSJam, Flightradar24 map     UAV-to-satellite localization   UAV-VisLoc, University-1652, SUES-200, AnyVisLoc     Magnetic navigation   MagNav flight data (Zenodo)     Radar odometry   Oxford Radar RobotCar, MulRan     Long-term place recognition   Oxford RobotCar, NCLT, HeLiPR     Underground / degraded   SubT-MRS, DARPA SubT reference data, Hilti SLAM Challenge     Event cameras   VECtor, DSEC, MVSEC     Synthetic, any weather   TartanAir, Mid-Air     UWB indoor   UTIL     Drone tracking (C-UAS)   Anti-UAV   Check each dataset's licence on its catalog page; several are non-commercial (for example KITTI and Oxford RobotCar per their sites).   Simulators   Need   Simulator    ------ -----------    Autopilot in the loop   PX4 / ArduPilot SITL with Gazebo (PX4, ArduPilot)     Photo-realistic camera   AirSim (end of active development noted in its docs), CARLA, Isaac Sim     IMU/GNSS error models only   gnss-ins-sim     GNSS signal level (to files)   GPS-SDR-SIM, OSNMA-SDR-SIM     Multi-drone RL   gym-pybullet-drones     Maritime / underwater   VRX, HoloOcean     Built-in VIO sim   OpenVINS     Designing a test that shows resilience A judge-friendly experiment, adaptable to almost any project: 1.  Baseline:  run with healthy GNSS, record error vs ground truth. 2.  Outage:  remove GNSS for a defined window (mask epochs in a dataset, or disable the sensor in SITL). Plot error vs time for dead reckoning alone and for your system. 3.  Spoof:  inject a slowly drifting offset into GNSS (in software, on recorded data). Report time to detect and the maximum position error reached before rejection. 4.  Recovery:  restore GNSS; show the system re-accepts it without a jump. 5.  Report honestly:  dataset, alignment, number of runs, and where it failed. For real interference behaviour, read the public Jammertest test catalogue; it describes the scenarios that Norway transmits under controlled conditions. Use it to script realistic software scenarios, not to transmit.   What competitions reward - DARPA SubT scored accurate localization of reported artifacts, not just coverage; robust multi-sensor odometry and operator workflow mattered as much as algorithms (SubT, CERBERUS lessons). - ESA Kelvins scored the sim-to-real gap explicitly (SPEED+). - The MagNav challenge was scored against a professionally compensated reference magnetometer (challenge site). - European and NATO challenges frame GNSS-denied drone navigation as multi-sensor fusion, with evaluation campaigns (EDF 2024 challenge, NATO DIANA challenges).   Failure modes of the evaluation itself - Scoring an absolute-positioning system with Sim(3) alignment hides its real error. - Tuning on the test sequence. - Simulated GNSS outages that start at a convenient moment (e.g. straight flight). - Spoof tests where the "spoofer" jumps instantly; real spoofers drag smoothly (Humphreys 2008). - Reporting one lucky run.   Learn it 1. evo README and TUM RGB-D benchmark (its trajectory format is used widely). 2. EuRoC and KITTI odometry pages - the two most common baselines. 3. Stone Soup docs - tracking metrics. 4. Long-term visual localization benchmark - evaluation under changing conditions. 5. Hilti SLAM Challenge - hard GNSS-denied sequences with accurate truth. 6. Jammertest - real interference scenarios. 7. CERBERUS SubT paper - lessons from a winning field system.   Build with it - evo - APE/RPE. - pykitti, tartanairpy, pyboreas - dataset loaders. - gnss_lib_py - GSDC loaders. - VPR-methods-evaluation and AnyVisLoc benchmark code. - Stone Soup - tracker evaluation. - Gazebo Sim, gnss-ins-sim, GPS-SDR-SIM. Related concepts: datasets and benchmarks, simulation.

nodes.s: A field guide to navigation and PNT (positioning, navigation and timing) for software engineers joining a defense-flavoured hackathon. Each chapter explains one cluster of the hub in plain language, names the ways it fails under electronic warfare (EW), and ends with two lists:
nodes.b: Navigation primer A field guide to navigation and PNT (positioning, navigation and timing) for software engineers joining a defense-flavoured hackathon. Each chapter explains one cluster of the hub in plain language, names the ways it fails under electronic warfare (EW), and ends with two lists: -  Learn it  - resources from this index in reading order, intro =  advanced. -  Build with it  - the repos from this index you are most likely to ship with. Every link points at a generated catalog page ( ../../catalog/... ), which in turn links to the upstream source. Numbers (accuracy, drift, cost) appear only where a cited source states them; otherwise the chapter says what drives the error instead of inventing a figure.   Chapters       Chapter   Read it if you are going to...    --- --------- --------------------------------    1   PNT fundamentals   do anything here. Frames, state, uncertainty, integrity, timing, assured PNT vocabulary.     2   GNSS and its threats   parse receiver data, detect jamming or spoofing, use RTK/PPP, OSNMA.     3   Inertial navigation and sensor fusion   write or tune a Kalman filter or factor graph, fuse GNSS with an IMU.     4   Vision, LiDAR and radar odometry   navigate relative to the surroundings: VIO, SLAM, LiDAR and radar odometry.     5   Absolute alternative PNT   get an absolute fix without GNSS: image-to-map, terrain, magnetic, celestial, signals of opportunity.     6   Autopilots and C2   feed a position into PX4/ArduPilot, talk MAVLink, push tracks to TAK.     7   Maps, geodesy and planning   convert coordinates, load DEMs and imagery, plan paths or missions.     8   Maritime, underwater and ground   work off the drone: ships, AIS, ROVs, DVL, ground robots, dismounted users.     9   Evaluation and datasets   prove your system works: metrics, datasets, simulators, test events.     Suggested order -  Air-domain alt-nav team (most common):  1 =  3 =  2 =  5 =  4 =  6 =  9. -  Interference-monitoring / OSINT team:  1 =  2 =  7 =  6 (TAK part) =  9. -  Ground or maritime robot team:  1 =  3 =  4 =  8 =  7 =  9.   Read alongside - Learning paths - 1-day, 1-week and 1-month study tracks. - Export control and ethics - read before you touch GNSS signal generation, RF transmission, flight tests or defense end uses. - INDEX.md - concept tree and high-fit repos. -  python3 tools/query.py concept concept:<id  - full listing for any concept.   Scope The hub covers navigation, localization, PNT resilience, autonomy, situational awareness, defensive EW and counter-UAS detection. Weapon terminal guidance, targeting and offensive payloads are out of scope, and this primer does not cover them.

Use it in the first 20 minutes of day 0: match the real statement to one to three rows, then score them with the rubric there. Written 2026-11-06. The statements are paraphrases of the kind funders and past hackathons publish (programs and challenges, UA/RU hackathon tracks), not leaked briefs. Dataset sizes come from the dataset cards (checked against the host, not downloaded). Card snippets were read from source, not run. Pitches contain no numbers on purpose: put in the number you measure. Legend: "card" = integration card (install, gotchas, license); "Idea N" = project idea N in the playbook; project-repo = the template skeleton (PoseSource =  NavFilter =  IntegrityMonitor =  Publisher, metrics included). "Start from" lists samples best match first. Status, deps, first command and the key measured number of each are in samples/README.md; the numbers with their input type (real / SITL / synthetic) are in evidence-matrix.md. The "Start from" column was refreshed on 2026-11-06 against all samples in  samples/ . DF only if hardware is named   3, 5     "5 km", "10 km", "route", "mission", + "jammed and spoofed"   Vehicle demo with an integrity layer; one SITL flight plus a Monte Carlo   1, 2, 4, 20     "spoofing", "deception", "trust", "integrity", "assured"   Detect-before-fuse; integrity metrics   4, 7, 19, 20, 23     "timing", "synchronisation", "time server", "critical infrastructure"   Holdover and time-push detection   6, 19     "ship", "USV", "port", "AIS", "maritime"   Maritime integrity or AIS plausibility   7, 8     "underwater", "AUV", "UUV"   No GNSS at all: DVL + acoustic   17     "soldier", "dismounted", "indoors", "underground", "tunnel"   Pedestrian INS + ranging + map   9     "swarm", "team", "cooperative", "relative"   Inter-agent ranging, shared estimate   10, 11     "C2", "common operating picture", "operator", "TAK"   Picture with nav-health and uncertainty   12, 22     "drone detection", "counter-UAS", "airspace awareness"   Passive detection =  tracks =  TAK   13     "UGV", "ground robot", "convoy", "forest", "urban canyon"   LiDAR / wheel odometry, GNSS FDE on re-entry   14, 23     "plug-in", "drop-in", "COTS", "autopilot"   Feed the autopilot a standard message   20     "AI", "LLM", "agent", "assistant"   Deterministic tools + LLM narration + human approval   21, 22     "night", "thermal", "smoke", "weather"   Thermal geolocalization or radar   16, 14     "how long", "endurance", "holdover", "budget"   Holdover calculator with IMU grades   26     The table       Problem statement   Recommended approach   Stack   Datasets   Start from   Main risk   Pitch    --- --- --- --- --- --- --- ---    1   Navigate a small drone 10 km without GNSS   VIO for relative motion + periodic visual fixes against satellite tiles (retrieval =  match =  homography) + a gate that rejects bad matches before the EKF. Idea 18.   OpenVINS card, LightGlue card (ALIKED), AnyLoc card, px4-ros2-interface-lib card, evo card   UAV-VisLoc site 03 2.0 GB, VPAIR sample 0.86 GB, AerialVL   golden-demo (v2: real geoloc replay + integrity), geoloc-license-clean, visual-geolocalization-lightglue, vpr-large-area (retrieval), relative-nav-benchmark (measured VO/VIO drift), altpnt-integrity   Commodity demo: judges have seen satellite matching; seasonal/altitude mismatch   "Every visual fix is checked before the autopilot trusts it, and the error curve over distance is on open data."     2   Bring the drone home after GNSS jamming   Switch EKF to non-GNSS sources on loss; dead reckoning + ranging to two or three home beacons; RTH in SITL. Ideas 9, 13.   ArduPilot card (EKF3 source sets,  SIM_GPS1_  vs  SIM_GPS_ ), pymavlink card, FilterPy card, Crazyflie firmware   UTIL UWB TDoA 1.86 GB, NTU VIRAL eee_03 2.0 GB   golden-demo (detect =  EKF3 source switch), ardupilot-ekf3-source-switch, altpnt-integrity (jam then spoof), sitl-docker   Beacons are RF and can be jammed too   "The aircraft comes back when GNSS goes away - and tells the operator which source it is flying on."     3   Detect and map GNSS jamming over an area   Many cheap sensors (u-blox MON-RF, phone C/N0, ADS-B NIC/NACp) =  hex-cell aggregator with time windows and confidence =  TAK overlay. Ideas 1, 2.   pyubx2 card, readsb card, PyTAK card, OpenTAKServer card, ADSBCOT   Jammertest VAARA 1.57 GB + chunk pair 2.9 GB; OpenSky states (OAuth2)   gnss-interference-monitor (per-node scorer, UBX replay), jammer-sensor-network (many cheap nodes =  map + TAK), osint-jamming-map (ADS-B / Sentinel-1 context layer)   Empty cells mean no data, not no jamming   "A live map of where GNSS cannot be trusted, built from receivers you already own."     4   Detect GNSS spoofing on a vehicle and keep navigating   Detect before fuse: receiver flags + residual / RAIM checks + innovation gate vs INS or odometry; exclude GNSS, coast, re-validate on return.   gnss_lib_py card (FDE), robot_localization card, GTSAM card, ArduPilot card   Jammertest, TEXBAT 8.8 GB subset, GSDC 2.76 GB with injected faults   golden-demo, altpnt-integrity (PL, Stanford diagram), gnss-signal-chain (signal-level spoof, file only), osnma-authentication, gnss-ins-ekf-outage   A slow drag-off is absorbed before the test fires - the template's own run shows it   "
