nodes.n: Timing resilience: the T in PNT
nodes.s: After this page you can explain why a GNSS-denied system loses time before it loses position, estimate how long a given oscillator holds time from its datasheet, name the attacks on GNSS and network time, and pick a 24-48 h build that shows timing resilience with numbers.
nodes.b: Timing resilience: the T in PNT After this page you can explain why a GNSS-denied system loses time before it loses position, estimate how long a given oscillator holds time from its datasheet, name the attacks on GNSS and network time, and pick a 24-48 h build that shows timing resilience with numbers. Working code: samples/timing-holdover (stdlib Python, run and tested). Numbers on this page marked "sample" are that run's observed output; numbers marked "computed" come from the formulas below and the cited oscillator figures.   1. Why timing is its own problem -  GNSS receivers are clocks first.  Every GNSS fix solves for receiver clock bias, and many systems (telecom, power grid phasor units, data centres, broadcast) use GNSS only for time. Jamming takes that time away; spoofing can move it without any position effect on a static site. -  Distributed sensing needs common time.  TDOA localization, multistatic radar and coherent DF arrays turn time error straight into position error: light covers about 0.3 m per nanosecond. A TDOA network whose receivers each hold time from GNSS fails when GNSS is jammed, even if nothing else in the system uses GNSS. -  Faults happen without attackers.  On 26 January 2016 GPS receivers worldwide reported time about 13 microseconds off for hours, traced to faulty UTC correction parameters uploaded during the retirement of SVN 23 (Meinberg note, Inside GNSS). Navigation was fine; only time was wrong. -  Policy says so.  CISA time guidance, the DHS S&T 2025 PNT best practices (stationary timing use case), the NIST PNT profile and the DHS conformance framework all ask for the same three things: know your time sources, have more than one, detect when one is wrong.   2. Vocabulary   Term   Meaning    --- ---    Phase / time error  x(t)    local clock minus reference time, seconds     Fractional frequency  y     dx/dt ; 1e-9 = 1 ppb = 86.4 us per day     Aging  D    slow linear change of  y  with time, quoted per day, month or year     ADEV  sigma_y(tau)    Allan deviation: frequency stability over averaging time  tau  (NIST SP 1065)     TDEV, MTIE   time-domain stability statistics used in telecom specs     Holdover   running on the local oscillator after the reference (GNSS) is lost     GPSDO   GNSS-disciplined oscillator: a loop steers a local oscillator to the receiver's 1PPS     PRTC / ePRTC   telecom names for a GNSS-fed time source and its enhanced, long-holdover version (G.8272, G.8272.1)     Grandmaster, BC, TC   PTP roles: the time source, boundary clock, transparent clock (IEEE 1588-2019)     PHC   PTP hardware clock inside a NIC; linuxptp's  phc2sys  copies it to the system clock     NTS   Network Time Security, authenticated NTP (RFC 8915)     3. Holdover math: from a datasheet to time error After GNSS is lost at  t = 0 , free-running time error grows as -  x0 : time error at the moment of loss (the loop's locked error, a few to tens of ns). -  y0 : residual frequency error the loop left behind. 1e-11 gives 0.86 us per day; 1e-9 gives 3.6 us per hour. A good holdover design spends most of its effort here: long averaging before the loss, and aging-rate estimation. -  D t^2 / 2 : aging. Quadratic, so it dominates long outages. -  e(t) : oscillator noise. A useful order-of-magnitude rule is  e(t)  ~ t   sigma_y(t) . For white frequency noise  sigma_y(t) = sigma_1 / sqrt(t) , so  e(t) ~ sigma_1   sqrt(t) , which is exactly the random-walk phase the sample simulates. For flicker or random-walk FM the growth is faster ( ~t  and  ~t^1.5 ); read the slope of your ADEV plot before extrapolating. - Temperature: a TCXO or OCXO frequency follows temperature. Over a day the temperature term is often bigger than aging for anything below an OCXO. Computed, aging term alone over 24 h, from Vig's oscillator table (Vig) and the SA65 datasheet:   Grade   ADEV at 1 s   Aging    D  (1/s)   Aging error after 1 h   after 24 h   White-FM noise after 24 h    --- --- --- --- --- --- ---    TCXO   1e-9   5e-7 / year   1.6e-14   103 ns   59 us   0.29 us     CSAC (SA65)   3e-10   <9e-10 / month   3.4e-16   2.2 ns   1.3 us   88 ns     OCXO   1e-12   5e-9 / year   1.6e-16   1.0 ns   0.59 us   0.3 ns     Rubidium   3e-12   2e-10 / year   6.3e-18   0.04 ns   24 ns   0.9 ns   Read it with care: Vig's 1 s figure for an OCXO is near its flicker floor, so white-FM extrapolation understates OCXO noise at long  tau ; real units also have retrace after power cycling, warm-up, vibration and temperature terms. Reference points from sources: Meta's open Time Card targets within 1 us over 24 h of holdover with a miniature atomic clock (Meta 2021); the telecom ePRTC is summarized as within 100 ns of UTC over a multi-week holdover with a cesium-class reference (Calnex summary, check the ITU text).  Loop time constant.  GNSS 1PPS noise is white phase noise, ADEV about  sqrt(3)   sigma_pps / tau ; the oscillator is about  sigma_1 / sqrt(tau) . Trust GNSS above the crossover, trust the oscillator below it:  tau_c = (sqrt(3)   sigma_pps / sigma_1)^2 . With 20 ns PPS noise that is about 1200 s for a TCXO and over 13000 s for the SA65 (computed). Long time constants also mean a disciplined clock follows a slow spoof slowly, which is what makes the internal monitor in section 5 possible.   Sample results (samples/timing-holdover, default run) Median  time error  after a GNSS outage, 20 runs per grade, no temperature term:   Grade   1 h   4 h   24 h    --- --- --- ---    TCXO   146 ns   1.67 us   59.6 us     CSAC   19 ns   89 ns   1.27 us     OCXO   2.1 ns   20 ns   0.61 us     Rb   1.5 ns   5.2 ns   44 ns   With a 24 h temperature cycle at 10 % of each spec (an assumption) the 24 h medians become TCXO 3.4 ms, OCXO 6.5 us, CSAC 3.1 us, Rb 2.1 us: the CSAC overtakes the OCXO because its temperature figure is a third of Vig's OCXO figure.   4. Threats to time   Threat   What happens   Reference    --- --- ---    GNSS jamming   receiver loses lock; system enters holdover; error grows per section 3   Jam

Code license and weights license often differ, and several defaults here are non-commercial.   Feature matching (fine registration) - LightGlue - Sparse learned matcher in a few lines of PyTorch. Its default extractor is SuperPoint, whose weights are non-commercial, so use ALIKED or DISK for clean licensing. - hloc - Retrieval =  matching =  PnP against a COLMAP model, with HDF5 handoffs between stages. The  superpoint_  and  superglue  configs pull in non-commercial Magic Leap code. - RoMa - Dense matcher that holds up across season, lighting and sensor changes. Slow and CUDA-oriented, so use it as a verifier. The indoor weights are trained on ScanNet, which is non-commercial. - XFeat - Small detector/descriptor plus LighterGlue that runs in real time on a laptop CPU. Apache-2.0, weights included. The no-GPU option. - LightGlue-ONNX - Exports extractor plus LightGlue to one ONNX graph for ONNX Runtime (CPU, CUDA, TensorRT, OpenVINO) or plain TensorRT. The Jetson deploy path. Licence traps first -  AGPL-3.0:  Ultralytics (code  and  pretrained weights; Enterprise licence otherwise), BoxMOT, and BlueOS (AGPL-3.0-only or a custom BlueOS licence). AGPL applies on network use, so a hosted dashboard counts. Per Ultralytics' own answer in issue  26703, the whole project that includes YOLO must be open, and wrapping YOLO in a separate process does not exempt the rest. TypeFly is Apache-2.0 but depends on ultralytics. -  GPL:  OpenSky API client (GPL-3.0; data under OpenSky terms), pyModeS (GPL-3.0), AIS-catcher (GPL-3.0), Rpanion-server (GPL-3.0), OpenCPN (GPL-2.0+), MOOS-IvP (mixed GPLv3/LGPLv3 plus a commercial option). -  No licence:  QGIS MCP has no LICENSE file. drone-mesh-mapper is MIT but forked from an unlicensed repo. -  Data and docs:  OSM-derived routing and tiles are ODbL (OSMnx, Valhalla, OSRM, TileServer GL; its default styles have a separate CC BY 3.0 design licence). Anti-UAV data has no stated licence. BoxMOT's person-ReID weights come from r

LiDAR / visual odometry and SLAM - LIO-SAM - LiDAR-inertial SLAM on GTSAM with GPS factor and loop closure (ROS 1 and ROS 2 branches). Needs a 9-axis IMU and per-point  time  +  ring . GPS is effectively off by default ( gpsTopic  defaults to  odometry/gpsz ). - RKO-LIO - pip ( rko-lio ) or apt (Humble..Rolling) LiDAR-inertial odometry. Extrinsics are mandatory, and the  <from 2<to  naming is easy to invert. No GNSS input. - KISS-SLAM - offline LiDAR SLAM with loop closure and Nav2-style  map.png/.yaml .  --refuse-scans  is broken in PyPI 0.0.2 ( 59). No Linux aarch64 wheels. - small_gicp - MIT ICP/GICP/VGICP library with aarch64 and macOS arm64 wheels. Library only, no ROS node, and Python defaults to  num_threads=1 . - FAST_LIO_LOCALIZATION - prior-PCD-map relocalization on FAST-LIO via 0.5 Hz Open3D ICP. ROS 1 + Python 2.7 + Open3D 0.9 makes it close to uninstallable today. Needs a rough initial pose. - rtabmap_ros - apt ROS 2 RTAB-Map with localization-only mode and Nav2 outputs. Fast DDS with  qos=0  silently drops large messages. The  -d  arg wipes the map DB on start. - orb_slam3_ros2 - thin ROS 2 wrapper over ORB-SLAM3. Publishes no pose and no TF, only  KeyFrameTraj

docs.b: gnss-ins-sim - integration card One-line: pure-Python generator of reference trajectories plus noisy IMU, GNSS, magnetometer and odometer data from a CSV motion profile, with per-segment GNSS visibility so you can script outages and test your filter against truth.        --- ---    Install   Not on PyPI (pypi.org/pypi/gnss-ins-sim returns 404).  git clone https://github.com/Aceinna/gnss-ins-sim && cd gnss-ins-sim && pip install -e .  ( setup.py : name  gnss-ins-sim , version 2.1, requires  numpy 1.10 ,  matplotlib ). Or just run demos from the repo root.     Runs on   Any OS with Python 3 + numpy/matplotlib. The Aceinna DMU380 INS demo ( demo_aceinna_ins.py ) loads prebuilt Windows  .dll s (x86/x64) from  demo_algorithms/dmu380_sim_lib ;  demo_algorithms/aceinna_ins.py  raises  OSError('Only support windows.')  on any other OS. The README's  demo_aceinna_vg.py  is not in the repo.     Inputs   Motion profile CSV: first row initial lat (deg), lon (deg), alt (m), body velocity (m/s), yaw/pitch/roll (deg); then command rows  type, yaw, pitch, roll, vx, vy, vz, duration, GPS visibility  (5 command types). IMU error model: built-in  'low-accuracy' ,  'mid-accuracy' ,  'high-accuracy'  or a dict (gyro bias deg/h, ARW deg/rt-h, bias instability, correlation s; accel bias m/s^2, VRW m/s/rt-h, ...). Optional vibration model. Or logged data via  demo_gen_data_from_files.py .     Outputs   Named data sets:  ref_pos  (LLA rad,rad,m for  ref_frame=0  NED),  ref_vel ,  ref_att_euler ,  ref

Inputs   Height grid as a NumPy  .npy  2D array (metres) in  data/ , plus a JSON sidecar with  lat_top ,  lon_left ,  lat_bottom ,  lon_right ,  height ,  width  (rows/cols must equal the array shape, checked in  load_terrain_data ). No GeoTIFF/DEM reader: SRTM/Copernicus tiles must be converted to  .npy  + JSON yourself. Measured profile: 1D array of terrain heights, one sample per grid cell along a straight heading.     Outputs   Console: true vs estimated start cell, lat/lon, heading, MSE. docs.b: ArduPilot - integration card One-line: GPL autopilot with a scriptable EKF3 that can switch between GPS, external nav (VIO/mocap), optical flow, beacons and wheel encoders in flight, plus a SITL that can disable, jam or glitch its simulated GPS, so a GNSS-denied demo runs on a laptop.        --- ---    Install    git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/ArduPilot/ardupilot && cd ardupilot && Tools/environment_install/install-prereqs-ubuntu.sh -y && . ~/.profile , then  ./waf configure --board sitl && ./waf copter . Prereq scripts also exist for mac, arch, alpine, openSUSE and Windows ( Tools/environment_install/ ). Stable tags:  Copter-4.6.3 ,  Copter-4.7.2  (latest seen).     Runs on   Linux x86-64/arm64 is the main path. macOS works but see Gotchas. WSL2 is handled by  sim_vehicle.py  (forwards MAVLink to the Windows host). No GPU. docs.b: Satellite-thermal geo-localization (STGL) - integration card One-line: pretrained thermal-query =  satellite-RGB retrieval (SGM) plus a satellite =  synthetic-thermal generator (TGM), with demo scripts that pull weights from Hugging Face - the quickest way to show night-time map matching.        --- ---    Install    git clone https://github.com/arplaboratory/satellite-thermal-geo-localization && cd satellite-thermal-geo-localization && conda env create -f env.yml  (env.yml pins python=3.9, pytorch=1.12.0, torchvision=0.13.0, cudatoolkit=11.3, faiss-gpu, h5py, torchscan=0.1.1). For inference use the  demo  branch:  git checkout demo  (README: aligns with STHN/global_pipeline "for pretrained model compatibility"). Demos also import  huggingface_hub  and  safetensors . No releases.     Runs on   env.yml is Linux + NVIDIA (cudatoolkit 11.3, faiss-gpu). Demo scripts select  "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu" , so inference should work on CPU with a hand-built env (not tried). Training scripts are SLURM  sbatch  files (README: change suffix to  .sh  for bash). No MPS, ONNX or TensorRT path.     Inputs   Thermal query: 8-bit image, contrast-adjusted (factor 3), grayscale =  3 channels, resized to 512x512 ( SGM_demo.py ). Database: 512x512 RGB satellite crops, ImageNet-normalized; demo crops them from a 1536x1536 map with stride 35 px. Training/eval data: HDF5 files ( train/val/test/extended_database.h5 ,  _queries.h5 ) from the Boson-nighttime dataset.     Outputs   SGM

docs.s: Header-only C++ Lie group library (SO2/SE2/SO3/SE3/SE_2(3)/SGal(3)/Rn/Bundle) with analytic right Jacobians and Python bindings, so you can write an on-manifold ESKF or a Ceres factor in an afternoon without deriving Jacobians by hand.
docs.b: manif - integration card Header-only C++ Lie group library (SO2/SE2/SO3/SE3/SE_2(3)/SGal(3)/Rn/Bundle) with analytic right Jacobians and Python bindings, so you can write an on-manifold ESKF or a Ceres factor in an afternoon without deriving Jacobians by hand.        --- ---    Install   C++ (header-only, needs Eigen3):  apt-get install libeigen3-dev , then  git clone https://github.com/artivis/manif.git && cd manif && mkdir build && cd build && cmake .. && make install  ( docs/tutorial/cpp.md ). Python:  conda install -c conda-forge manifpy  (conda-forge 0.0.5, builds for linux-64, linux-aarch64, osx-64, osx-arm64, win-64), or from source  python3 -m pip install "pybind11[global]"  then  python3 -m pip install .  in the clone ( docs/tutorial/python.md ).  manifpy  is not on PyPI  (pypi.org/pypi/manifpy/json returns 404), so  pip install manifpy  fails. Latest tag 0.0.5 (2024-08-11);  CMakeLists.txt  still says  project(manif VERSION 0.0.3)  (closed issue  312).     Runs on   Anything with a C++11 compiler and Eigen3. CMake warns on Eigen < 3.3.8 and on the buggy 3.3.6. No ROS dependency, no GPU. Python bindings via pybind11; MSVC  cl.exe  fails to compile them,  clang-cl  works (open issue  311).     Inputs   Group elements and tangent vectors as Eigen types (C++) or numpy arrays (Python). Tangent order matters: SE3 = (rho, theta), SE_2(3) = (rho, theta, nu), SGal(3) = (rho, nu, theta, s) (README "Tangent spaces"; note the SE_2(3)/SGal(3) order mismatch).     Outputs   Compo

docs.b: PX4 ROS 2 Interface Library - integration card One-line: C++ (partial Python) library for writing PX4 flight modes and navigation inputs as ROS 2 nodes; its  GlobalPositionMeasurementInterface  is the shortest path from a map-matching lat/lon to PX4's EKF2, and external modes let you define "what to do when GNSS is gone" without forking firmware.        --- ---    Install   Clone into a ROS 2 workspace with a matching  px4_msgs :  git clone https://github.com/Auterion/px4-ros2-interface-lib src/px4-ros2-interface-lib  (use branch  release/1.17  for PX4 v1.17,  release/1.16 ,  release/1.18 , or  main  with PX4  main ),  git clone https://github.com/PX4/px4_msgs src/px4_msgs  on the matching branch,  colcon build . docs.b: elevation - integration card One-line: one command ( eio clip --bounds ... ) gets you a clipped, cached 30 m or 90 m global DEM GeoTIFF for an AOI - the map half of terrain-relative navigation.        --- ---    Install    pip install elevation  (latest release v2.0.1, 2026-10-21). Requires GDAL command line tools on PATH ( gdal_translate ,  gdalbuildvrt ,  gdalinfo ,  ogrinfo ); check with  eio selfcheck --verbose .     Runs on   Linux and macOS are the target platforms; Windows "only lightly tested" (README). Python  = 3.11. No GPU. Needs internet on first access to an area.     Inputs   Bounds as  left bottom right top  in WGS84 lon/lat degrees, or  --reference  any GDAL/OGR raster or vector file whose extent is used. Product choice:  MAPZEN  (default),  GLO-30 ,  GLO-90 ,  AW3D30 ,  SRTM1_GEOID ,  SRTM1_ELLIP ,  SRTM3  ( GEDTM30  only in unreleased 2.1.0).     Outputs   A GeoTIFF (default creation options  TILED=YES COMPRESS=DEFLATE ) in the product's native geographic CRS; heights in metres on the product's vertical datum (EGM96, EGM2008, or WGS84 ellipsoid for  SRTM1_ELLIP ). Local tile cache under the user cache dir or  EIO_CACHE_DIR .     Key API / entry points   CLI:  eio [--product P] [--cache_dir D] clip -o out.tif --bounds L B R T [--margin M] [--max_download_tiles N] ,  eio seed ,  eio info ,  eio dataset [ID]  (STAC metadata),  eio clean ,  eio distclean ,  eio selfcheck . Python:  elevation.clip(bounds, output="out.tif", margin="0", product=...,  , cache_dir=No

First set up the Autonomous Exploration Development Environment on the matching branch and download its simulation worlds. No releases or tags. Includes ArUco-marker navigation for GNSS-free indoor flight and a Gazebo + PX4 SITL simulator VM.        --- ---    Install   Preferred: flash the Raspberry Pi image from GitHub Releases (latest stable  v0.25 , 2024-08-08;  v0.26-alpha.1  2024-09-19). The README lists Raspbian Buster, ROS Noetic, mavros and OpenCV. Manual: ROS Noetic catkin workspace,  git clone https://github.com/CopterExpress/clover.git clover  into  src ,  rosdep install -y --from-paths src --ignore-src ,  catkin_make -j1 , then  curl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mavlink/mavros/master/mavros/scripts/install_geographiclib_datasets.sh \  sudo bash  (clover/README.md). Simulation: the  clover_simulation  package (needs  px4  and  sitl_gazebo  in the workspace) or the prebuilt VM from  CopterExpress/clover_vm  (release v1.4, 2023-04-12).     Runs on   Raspberry Pi 4 companion + PX4 flight controller (USB  /dev/px4fmu  by default, via udev rule  99-px4fmu.rules , or set  fcu_url  in  mavros.launch ). Desktop: Ubuntu 20.04 + ROS Noetic for the simulator. ROS 1 only, with no plans for ROS 2 (maintainer in  497).     Inputs   ROS services from your script; PX4 state through mavros; Pi camera ( main_camera.launch ); ArUco marker map file for  aruco_pose  ( aruco.launch ,  map/ ); optional optical flow / rangefinder per the docs.

docs.b: robot_localization - integration card One-line: config-only ROS 2 EKF/UKF that fuses wheel odometry, IMU and GNSS into  odom  and  map  frames, so a ground robot gets a GNSS-anchored pose in an afternoon.        --- ---    Install   ROS 2 binary:  sudo apt install ros-$ROS_DISTRO-robot-localization  (standard ROS package naming; distro branches exist for humble, iron, jazzy, kilted, lyrical, rolling). Source: clone the  <distro -devel  branch into a colcon workspace,  colcon build . Version on  jazzy-devel  package.xml: 3.8.4.     Runs on   Ubuntu with ROS 2 (humble/jazzy/rolling...) or ROS 1 (noetic-devel and older branches). CPU only.     Inputs    nav_msgs/Odometry ,  sensor_msgs/Imu ,  geometry_msgs/PoseWithCovarianceStamped ,  geometry_msgs/TwistWithCovarianceStamped  into  ekf_node / ukf_node  (configured as  odom0 ,  imu0 ,  pose0 ,  twist0 ...).  navsat_transform_node  takes  sensor_msgs/NavSatFix  ( gps/fix ),  sensor_msgs/Imu  ( imu , needs absolute yaw) and  nav_msgs/Odometry  ( odometry/filtered ). Frames per REP-103/105 (ENU,  map / odom / base_link ).     Outputs    odometry/filtered  ( nav_msgs/Odometry ), TF  odom- base_link  or  map- odom ; from navsat:  odometry/gps  (GNSS as Odometry in the world frame), optional  gps/filtered  (NavSatFix), optional  utm  TF.     Key API / entry points   Executables  ekf_node ,  ukf_node ,  navsat_transform_node . Launch files  launch/ekf.launch.py ,  ukf.launch.py ,  navsat_transform.launch.py ,  dual_ekf_navsat_example.la

docs.b: navlie - integration card Pure-Python on-manifold estimation toolkit: define a  State  (vector or any Lie group), a process and a measurement model, and reuse EKF / iterated EKF / UKF / cubature / IMM / Gaussian-sum filters or batch MAP, with numerical Jacobians, IMU kinematics and preintegration, NEES plots and Monte Carlo runs. Fastest way to prototype and sanity-check a custom fusion idea (e.g. IMU + range beacons, IMU + baro + mag) before writing C++.        --- ---    Install   README:  git clone https://github.com/decargroup/navlie && cd navlie && pip install -e . .  setup.py  pulls  pymlg @ git+https://github.com/decargroup/pymlg@main  (Lie group backend), numpy, scipy, matplotlib, joblib, tqdm, seaborn, evo. PyPI has  navlie  0.0.1 (same project, uploaded 2023-07-28), but its metadata omits  pymlg  and  pymlg  is not on PyPI (404), so  pip install navlie  alone leaves  import navlie  broken; install from git.     Runs on   Python, CPU, any OS. CI ( .github/workflows/test_package.yml ) tests Python 3.9 to 3.13; README badge still says 3.8-3.10. Optional ROS 1 message conversion in  navlie/lib/states.py  imports  rospy  only if available.     Inputs   Python objects:  navlie.lib.imu.IMU  inputs (gyro, accel, stamp),  navlie.Measurement(value, stamp, model)  lists, and your own  ProcessModel  /  MeasurementModel  subclasses ( evaluate ,  covariance , optional  jacobian , else finite differences via  jacobian_fd ). docs.b: Stone Soup - integration card One-line: Dstl's modular Python framework for tracking and state estimation (Kalman/EKF/UKF/particle filters, data association, track management, metrics); use it to turn ADS-B, Remote ID or DF bearing detections into tracks on one air picture, with bearing-only and range-bearing measurement models ready to use.        --- ---    Install    pip install stonesoup  (latest release seen v1.9.1, 2026-06-24).  requires-python  = 3.11  in  pyproject.toml .     Runs on   Any OS with Python 3.11+ (numpy/scipy stack). Tutorials and demos run in Jupyter.     Inputs    Detection  objects carrying a  measurement_model ; readers for CSV ( CSVDetectionReader ,  CSVGroundTruthReader ,  CSVTrackReader  in  stonesoup/reader/generic.py ), dicts, pandas, YAML, HDF5, Kafka, video/images, OpenSky Network API ( reader/opensky.py ), AISHub ( reader/aishub.py ). Units are whatever your state vector uses; angle models use radians.     Outputs    Track  objects (state sequences with covariances), metrics (OSPA, SIAP, PCRB), plots ( stonesoup.plotter ), YAML serialisation of whole tracker configs.     Key API / entry points   Models:  stonesoup.models.transition.linear.CombinedLinearGaussianTransitionModel ,  ConstantVelocity ;  stonesoup.models.measurement.nonlinear.Cartesian2DToBearing ,  CartesianToBearingRange ,  CartesianToElevationBearing ,  CartesianToBearingRangeRate ,  CartesianToElevationBearingRange . Filters:  predictor.kalman.ExtendedKalmanPredictor ,  updater

docs.b: jetson-containers - integration card One-line: prebuilt and buildable Docker images for NVIDIA Jetson (PyTorch, TensorRT tooling, OpenCV with CUDA, ROS 1/2, DeepStream, VLMs) matched to your JetPack/L4T version. It saves the day you would otherwise lose compiling CUDA wheels on the device.        --- ---    Install   On the Jetson:  git clone https://github.com/dusty-nv/jetson-containers && bash jetson-containers/install.sh  (README). The script runs  pip3 install -r requirements.txt  with the host pip (installing  python3-pip  through apt if missing) and symlinks  autotag  and  jetson-containers  into  /usr/local/bin  (install.sh). Optional  sudo bash jetson-containers/install.sh --pypi  adds a local devpi + APT cache. You can skip the tools entirely:  sudo docker run --runtime nvidia -it --rm --network=host dustynv/l4t-pytorch:r36.2.0  (README). No PyPI package.     Runs on   NVIDIA Jetson with Docker and the NVIDIA container runtime. The README says only JetPack 6.2 (CUDA 12.6) and JetPack 7 (CUDA 13.x) are "tested and supported". Ubuntu 24.04 containers exist for JP6/JP7. ARM SBSA (GH200/GB200) is also supported. The older stack is on the  legacy  branch. Builds happen on the device and need a lot of disk (see Gotchas).     Inputs   Package names to build or run ( pytorch ,  ros:humble-desktop ,  torch2trt ,  opencv ,  onnxruntime ,  deepstream ,  isaac-ros ...),  CUDA_VERSION ,  LSB_RELEASE  and  ROS_DISTRO  environment variables, host directories mounted into  /data .

docs.s: One-line: the physics + sensor simulator behind PX4 and ArduPilot SITL and Nav2 demos, with IMU, NavSat (GNSS), magnetometer, altimeter, air pressure, cameras and LiDAR, so you can fly or drive a vehicle and cut its GNSS on cue.
docs.b: Gazebo Sim (gz-sim) - integration card One-line: the physics + sensor simulator behind PX4 and ArduPilot SITL and Nav2 demos, with IMU, NavSat (GNSS), magnetometer, altimeter, air pressure, cameras and LiDAR, so you can fly or drive a vehicle and cut its GNSS on cue.        --- ---    Install   Binary per the gazebosim.org getting-started guide (README defers there): e.g. Harmonic on Ubuntu 24.04 via the OSRF apt repo ( sudo apt install gz-harmonic ). With ROS 2, install the matching  ros-$ROS_DISTRO-ros-gz  packages. Library-only install: gazebosim.org/api/sim/9/install.html. Usually you get it indirectly from PX4 ( make px4_sitl gz_x500 ) or  ardupilot_gazebo .     Runs on   Ubuntu (CI: Noble amd64), macOS via Homebrew, Windows via Conda (server and GUI in separate terminals,  gz sim -s  /  gz sim -g ). GPU strongly preferred for camera / depth sensors (OGRE 2); headless server ( gz sim -s ) works without a display for non-rendering sensors.     Inputs   SDF world and model files ( .sdf ), models from Gazebo Fuel, plugin (system) configuration in SDF,  <spherical_coordinates  for the world's geodetic origin, commands over gz-transport topics/services ( gz topic ,  gz service ), ROS 2 topics through  ros_gz_bridge .     Outputs   gz-transport messages:  gz.msgs.IMU ,  gz.msgs.NavSat  (lat, lon, alt, velocity),  gz.msgs.Magnetometer ,  gz.msgs.Altimeter ,  gz.msgs.FluidPressure ,  gz.msgs.Image ,  gz.msgs.LaserScan , poses, odometry. Bridged to ROS 2 as  sensor_msgs/Imu ,  se

docs.s: The ROS 2 <=  Gazebo (gz-sim) glue:  parameter_bridge  maps Gazebo sensor topics (IMU, NavSat, magnetometer, altimeter, air pressure, cameras, LiDAR, odometry, clock) onto ROS 2 messages, plus launch files to start Gazebo and spawn models. This is what lets a ROS nav stack run against a simulated GNSS that you can degrade or cut.
docs.b: ros_gz - integration card The ROS 2 <=  Gazebo (gz-sim) glue:  parameter_bridge  maps Gazebo sensor topics (IMU, NavSat, magnetometer, altimeter, air pressure, cameras, LiDAR, odometry, clock) onto ROS 2 messages, plus launch files to start Gazebo and spawn models. This is what lets a ROS nav stack run against a simulated GNSS that you can degrade or cut.        --- ---    Install   Binary:  sudo apt install ros-$ROS_DISTRO-ros-gz  (README shows  ros-rolling-ros-gz ). Supported pairs from the README table, binaries on packages.ros.org: Humble + Fortress, Jazzy + Harmonic, Kilted + Ionic, Lyrical + Jetty, Rolling + Jetty. Humble + Harmonic (or Garden) binaries come from packages.osrfoundation.org. Other pairs are source-only:  git clone https://github.com/gazebosim/ros_gz.git -b <branch  into  ~/ws/src ,  rosdep install -r --from-paths src -i -y --rosdistro <distro ,  colcon build . Branches:  humble ,  jazzy ,  kilted ,  ros2  (Rolling); ROS 1 is on  noetic .     Runs on   Ubuntu with ROS 2 (source build documented for Linux and macOS). CPU for the bridge; GPU needed by Gazebo for camera / GPU-LiDAR sensors, not by the bridge.     Inputs   Gazebo Transport topics ( gz.msgs. ) and ROS 2 topics; bridge spec on the command line or a YAML array ( topic_name  or  ros_topic_name / gz_topic_name ,  ros_type_name ,  gz_type_name ,  direction ,  lazy , queue sizes, QoS).     Outputs   Nav-relevant mappings (bridge README table):  sensor_msgs/msg/Imu  <=   gz.msgs.IMU ,  sensor_msgs/ms

docs.b: OSMnx - integration card One-line: one Python call turns an OSM area into a NetworkX road/path graph with lengths, speeds and travel times - fastest way to prototype ground-vehicle route planning, task allocation or road-constrained map matching in a notebook.        --- ---    Install    pip install osmnx  (PyPI 2.1.1, 2026-07-21, MIT, requires Python  =3.11). Extras:  osmnx[neighbors]  (scikit-learn + scipy for nearest-node/edge search),  osmnx[raster]  (rasterio for DEM elevations),  osmnx[visualization]  (matplotlib),  osmnx[all]  (pyproject.toml). Python 3.9/3.10: last compatible line is 2.0.x (2.0.7 requires  =3.9).     Runs on   Pure Python on top of geopandas, shapely, networkx, pandas, numpy, requests; any OS/arch with wheels for those. No GPU.     Inputs   Place names (Nominatim geocode),  (lat, lon)  point + distance, bbox  (left, bottom, right, top)  in EPSG:4326, shapely polygon, or an OSM XML file. Online by default: Overpass API ( settings.overpass_url = "https://overpass-api.de/api" ) and Nominatim.     Outputs    networkx.MultiDiGraph  with node  x / y  (lon/lat), edge  length  (m), optional  speed_kph ,  travel_time  (s),  grade ; GeoDataFrames of nodes/edges; GraphML / GeoPackage / OSM XML files; matplotlib plots.     Key API / entry points    ox.graph_from_place(query, network_type="drive") ;  ox.graph_from_point((lat, lon), dist, network_type=...) ;  ox.graph_from_bbox((left, bottom, right, top), network_type=...) ;  ox.graph_from_xml(path) ;  ox.distance

docs.b: pymap3d - integration card Pure-Python geodetic / ECEF / ENU / NED / AER / ECI conversions with a Matlab-like API: the glue for turning GNSS lat/lon/alt into the local metric frame your filter, map or simulator works in, and back.        --- ---    Install    python3 -m pip install pymap3d  (PyPI 3.2.0,  requires-python  =3.9 ). Numpy optional (needed for arrays), AstroPy optional (higher-accuracy ECI / sky conversions). Body-frame functions need  pip install git+https://github.com/geospace-code/pymap3d  (see Gotchas).     Runs on   Anything that runs Python; no compiled deps. Stdlib-only mode handles scalars.     Inputs   Geodetic lat/lon in degrees by default ( deg=False  for radians), heights in metres above the ellipsoid; ECEF/ENU/NED/AER in metres and degrees; scalars or N-D numpy arrays;  ell=Ellipsoid.from_name('wgs84')  etc.;  datetime  for ECI.     Outputs   Tuples of the same shape as the input:  (x, y, z) ,  (e, n, u) ,  (n, e, d) ,  (az, el, srange) ,  (lat, lon, alt) . Rotation matrices via  _matrix  helpers.     Key API / entry points    geodetic2ecef(lat, lon, alt, ell=None, deg=True) ,  ecef2geodetic(x, y, z, ell=None, deg=True) ,  geodetic2enu(lat, lon, h, lat0, lon0, h0, ...) ,  enu2geodetic(e, n, u, lat0, lon0, h0, ...) ,  geodetic2ned  /  ned2geodetic ,  geodetic2aer  /  aer2geodetic ,  ecef2enuv  (vectors),  ecef2enu_matrix(lat0, lon0) ,  Ellipsoid.from_name(name) ,  pymap3d.vincenty.vdist  /  vreckon ; CLI  python -m pymap3d geodetic2ecef 40 -105 1600 .

In a hackathon use it only to produce  files  that a software receiver (GNSS-SDR) processes offline: repeatable test vectors for receiver, integrity and spoofing-detector development with no RF involved.
docs.b: GPS-SDR-SIM - integration card Generates GPS L1 C/A baseband IQ sample files for a chosen static position or trajectory and time. In a hackathon use it only to produce  files  that a software receiver (GNSS-SDR) processes offline: repeatable test vectors for receiver, integrity and spoofing-detector development with no RF involved.    Legal boundary.  Radiating GNSS signals over the air without authorization is illegal in practically every jurisdiction (in the US under FCC rules and federal law; in the EU/UK under national radio law) and endangers aviation and other users. This card covers file generation and offline processing only. Any hardware test must be cabled into the receiver under test through attenuation, or done in a certified shielded enclosure under the relevant authorization. Read docs/export-control-and-ethics.md first. The repo README includes SDR playback commands; they are deliberately not reproduced here.        --- ---    Install   No release tags.  git clone https://github.com/osqzss/gps-sdr-sim && cd gps-sdr-sim && gcc gpssim.c -lm -O3 -o gps-sdr-sim  (README). For trajectories longer than the default:  make USER_MOTION_SIZE=4000  or  -DUSER_MOTION_SIZE=4000 . Windows: Visual Studio project with  gpssim.c  +  getopt.c .     Runs on   Any OS with a C compiler (single C file, libm). No GPU. Repo archived (read-only) since 2025; last push 2025-01-26. Run the Micro XRCE-DDS Agent ( MicroXRCEAgent udp4 -p 8888 ) next to PX4 SITL. Install details are delegated to the PX4 uXRCE-DDS and ROS 2 guide (README).     Runs on   ROS 2 (Humble/Jazzy per PX4 docs), Linux. Depends directly on  px4_msgs .     Inputs   PX4 uORB topics bridged as  /fmu/out/  (e.g.  sensor_combined ,  vehicle_gps_position ,  vehicle_odometry ,  vehicle_status ).     Outputs   Example publishers to  /fmu/in/offboard_control_mode ,  /fmu/in/trajectory_setpoint ,  /fmu/in/vehicle_command ,  debug_vect . docs.s: One-line: the Python front-end to PROJ - correct datum, projection, UTM, ECEF and vertical (geoid) transformations plus ellipsoidal geodesics, with self-contained wheels; the default answer to "convert these coordinates" in a Python nav stack.
docs.b: pyproj - integration card One-line: the Python front-end to PROJ - correct datum, projection, UTM, ECEF and vertical (geoid) transformations plus ellipsoidal geodesics, with self-contained wheels; the default answer to "convert these coordinates" in a Python nav stack.        --- ---    Install    pip install pyproj  (PyPI 3.8.0, 2026-09-05, MIT, requires Python  =3.12). Wheels bundle PROJ 9.8.1 (history.rst 3.8.0) for manylinux_2_28 and musllinux x86_64/aarch64, macOS arm64 and x86_64, Windows x64/x86/arm64. Older Pythons: 3.7.2 needs  =3.11, 3.7.0/3.7.1 need  =3.10, 3.6.1 needs  =3.9. Optional  pyproj[shapely]  is on  main  only (unreleased).     Runs on   Any platform with a wheel; source builds need PROJ (env  PROJ_DIR ,  PROJ_VERSION ). Free-threaded Python classified "2 - Beta". No GPU.     Inputs   CRS as EPSG codes ( "EPSG:4326" ,  "EPSG:4978"  ECEF,  "EPSG:326zz"  UTM north), WKT, PROJ strings, PROJJSON, or PROJ pipelines; numeric scalars, lists or numpy arrays; optional  AreaOfInterest . Units follow the CRS (degrees, metres).     Outputs   Transformed coordinates (same shape as input), forward/back azimuths and distances (m) from  Geod , CRS metadata (axis info, area of use, datum), transformation descriptions and accuracy.     Key API / entry points    Transformer.from_crs(crs_from, crs_to, always_xy=False, area_of_interest=None, ...) ;  transformer.transform(xx, yy[, zz], direction=...)  and  itransform ;  Transformer.from_pipeline(pipeline, always_xy=False) ;  T

docs.s: One-line: pip-installable GeoTIFF/DEM reader that turns a map tile into a numpy array plus an affine transform, so a nav filter can look up terrain height or orthophoto pixels by world coordinate.
docs.b: Rasterio - integration card One-line: pip-installable GeoTIFF/DEM reader that turns a map tile into a numpy array plus an affine transform, so a nav filter can look up terrain height or orthophoto pixels by world coordinate.        --- ---    Install    pip install rasterio  (wheels bundle libgdal; latest release 1.5.2). Conda alternative:  conda install -c conda-forge rasterio  for more format drivers. Source build against system GDAL:  GDAL_CONFIG=/path/to/gdal-config python -m pip install --no-binary rasterio rasterio .     Runs on   Linux, macOS, Windows (official wheels per README). Rasterio 1.5+ needs Python  = 3.12, numpy  = 2, GDAL  = 3.8. No GPU.     Inputs   Any GDAL raster the bundled build supports: GeoTIFF/COG, VRT, JPEG2000, HDF5, netCDF (wheels include these per README); remote via  /vsicurl/  or  s3://  URLs.     Outputs    numpy  arrays (optionally masked),  Affine  transforms,  CRS  objects, written GeoTIFFs.     Key API / entry points    rasterio.open(path, mode="r") ;  DatasetReader.read(indexes=None, window=None, masked=False, ...) ;  DatasetReader.sample(xy, indexes=None, masked=False) ;  rasterio.windows.from_bounds(left, bottom, right, top, transform=None, ...) ;  rasterio.transform.xy(transform, rows, cols, offset="center")  /  rowcol(transform, xs, ys) ;  rasterio.warp.transform(src_crs, dst_crs, xs, ys) ,  reproject(...) ,  calculate_default_transform(...) ;  rasterio.vrt.WarpedVRT(src, crs=..., resampling=...) ; CLI  rio info ,  rio insp . docs.b: FilterPy - integration card Readable NumPy implementations of KF, EKF, UKF, CKF, IMM, ensemble, information, square-root and fading-memory filters plus RTS / fixed-lag smoothers: the fastest way to stand up a prototype GNSS/INS or tracking filter in Python and tune it in a notebook.        --- ---    Install    pip install filterpy  (PyPI 2.0.0, released 2026-10-26; deps numpy, scipy, matplotlib). docs.s: Pretrained visual navigation policies that drive a ground robot from a single RGB camera along a recorded image "topological map" (no metric map, no GNSS), plus NoMaD undirected exploration; ROS 1 deployment and PyTorch training code.
docs.b: GNM / ViNT / NoMaD (visualnav-transformer) - integration card Pretrained visual navigation policies that drive a ground robot from a single RGB camera along a recorded image "topological map" (no metric map, no GNSS), plus NoMaD undirected exploration; ROS 1 deployment and PyTorch training code.        --- ---    Install   No PyPI package. README ( deployment/ ): ROS Noetic,  sudo apt-get install ros-noetic-usb-cam ros-noetic-joy ,  conda env create -f deployment/deployment_environment.yaml && conda activate vint_deployment ,  pip install -e train/  (installs package  vint_train  0.1.0 from  train/setup.py ), then  git clone  real-stanford/diffusion_policy and  pip install -e diffusion_policy/ . Training:  train/train_environment.yml  per README. Only tag:  code_release  (2023-10-06).     Runs on   Tested on a LoCoBot with Ubuntu 20.04 and Jetson Orin Nano (README). NVIDIA GPU expected (conda env pins Python 3.8.5,  cudatoolkit ,  diffusers==0.11.1 ). Others report Jackal, Tello, Unitree A1, TurtleBot2 and CARLA (README).     Inputs   Camera images on  /usb_cam/image_raw  ( deployment/src/topic_names.py ), resized per model config; a topomap = folder of images  deployment/topomaps/images/<dir /0..N  created from a rosbag at  --dt 1  s spacing; model choice from  deployment/config/models.yaml  ( vint ,  late_fusion ,  gnm ,  nomad ).     Outputs    /waypoint  (std_msgs/Float32MultiArray; 2 or 4 values: dx, dy and optionally heading as cos/sin, robot frame) and  /topoplan/reach

docs.s: One-line: MCP server that gives an LLM client (Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Cursor...) discovery and pub/sub/service/action/param access to any ROS 1 or ROS 2 robot through rosbridge, with no changes to robot code; useful for an agent that inspects a nav stack ("is VIO publishing? what is the EKF covariance?") in a demo.
docs.b: ROS MCP Server - integration card One-line: MCP server that gives an LLM client (Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Cursor...) discovery and pub/sub/service/action/param access to any ROS 1 or ROS 2 robot through rosbridge, with no changes to robot code; useful for an agent that inspects a nav stack ("is VIO publishing? what is the EKF covariance?") in a demo.        --- ---    Install   Client side:  claude mcp add ros-mcp -- uvx ros-mcp --transport=stdio  (PyPI package  ros-mcp , v3.1.2 at time of writing, Python  = 3.10). Robot side:  sudo apt install ros-<distro -rosbridge-server  and  ros2 launch rosbridge_server rosbridge_websocket_launch.xml .     Runs on   Any host with Python 3.10+/uv for the server; robot needs ROS with rosbridge (ROS 2 Jazzy, Humble and others; ROS 1 too, per README).     Inputs   rosbridge WebSocket, default  127.0.0.1:9090  ( ros_mcp/main.py ); the LLM can call  connect_to_robot  to change IP/port.     Outputs   MCP tool results as JSON; images via  tools/images.py .     Key API / entry points   Tools in  ros_mcp/tools/ : topics  get_topics ,  get_topic_type ,  get_topic_details ,  get_message_details ,  subscribe_once ,  subscribe_for_duration ,  publish_once ,  publish_for_durations ; services  get_services ,  get_service_type ,  get_service_details ,  call_service ; connection  connect_to_robot ,  ping_robots ; plus  actions.py ,  nodes.py ,  parameters.py ,  robot_config.py . Resources  robot_specs ,  ros_metadata .     Time to first result

docs.s: One-line: a complete ROS 2 ground-robot navigation stack (localization, costmaps, planners, controllers, behavior trees, GPS waypoint following) you can drive from a short Python script, so you spend the hackathon on localization under degraded PNT rather than on path following.
docs.b: Nav2 (ROS 2 Navigation) - integration card One-line: a complete ROS 2 ground-robot navigation stack (localization, costmaps, planners, controllers, behavior trees, GPS waypoint following) you can drive from a short Python script, so you spend the hackathon on localization under degraded PNT rather than on path following.        --- ---    Install   Binary:  sudo apt install ros-$ROS_DISTRO-navigation2 ros-$ROS_DISTRO-nav2-bringup  (per docs.nav2.org Getting Started). Source: colcon build of the distro branch ( humble ,  jazzy , ...), or the prebuilt containers at  ghcr.io/ros-navigation/navigation2 . README build table lists humble, jazzy and lyrical Debian builds.     Runs on   Ubuntu with ROS 2 (Humble on 22.04, Jazzy on 24.04 per the build table; main targets the newest distro). amd64 binaries confirmed in the build table; arm64 not checked here. No GPU required. Simulation demos use Gazebo (gz-sim) or the built-in  nav2_loopback_sim  (no physics; on  jazzy  and  main , not on  humble ).     Inputs   TF tree  map =  odom =  base_link  (REP-105),  nav_msgs/Odometry ,  sensor_msgs/LaserScan  /  PointCloud2  for costmaps,  nav_msgs/OccupancyGrid  map from  nav2_map_server  (YAML + PGM), goals as  geometry_msgs/PoseStamped  or  geographic_msgs/GeoPose  (GPS waypoints). Parameters in one YAML file.     Outputs    cmd_vel  ( geometry_msgs/Twist  or  TwistStamped  depending on distro), planned paths ( nav_msgs/Path ), costmaps, action results/feedback on  navigate_to_pose ,  foll

docs.s: The fastest path from receiver logs or public RINEX to an SPP / RTK / PPK / PPP position file, plus  str2str  and  rtkrcv  for live NTRIP corrections and real-time RTK. Tuned for low-cost receivers (u-blox F9P and friends).
docs.b: RTKLIB demo5 / RTKLIB-EX - integration card The fastest path from receiver logs or public RINEX to an SPP / RTK / PPK / PPP position file, plus  str2str  and  rtkrcv  for live NTRIP corrections and real-time RTK. Tuned for low-cost receivers (u-blox F9P and friends).        --- ---    Install   Windows: prebuilt binaries on the GitHub releases page (latest tag  v2.5.1 ). Linux/macOS CLI:  git clone --depth 1 --branch v2.5.1 https://github.com/rtklibexplorer/RTKLIB.git && cmake -S RTKLIB -B RTKLIB/build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release && cmake --build RTKLIB/build -j  (README:  mkdir build; cd build; cmake ..; make; make test ). Qt5/6 needed only for the GUIs. Old per-app  gcc  makefiles still exist but are marked deprecated. Pre-built Linux packages via openSUSE OBS ( home:ReimannJens/rtklib-qt ), per README.     Runs on   Linux, Windows, macOS (CMake). Plain C, no GPU. Runs fine on a Raspberry Pi class board for  rtkrcv / str2str  (common community use, not stated in README).     Inputs   RINEX 2/3 OBS + NAV (also SP3, CLK, SBAS logs); raw receiver binaries (u-blox UBX, Septentrio SBF, NovAtel, etc.) via  convbin ; RTCM2/3 streams over serial, TCP, NTRIP for live work. Hatanaka  .crx / .d  needs  crx2rnx  on PATH.     Outputs    .pos  text solutions (llh, ECEF xyz or ENU baseline; Q flag 1=fix, 2=float, 5=single), NMEA GGA ( -n ), solution status/residual files ( -y ), KML/GPX via  pos2kml .  str2str  relays/converts streams (e.g. NTRIP =  serial to feed a receiver RTCM). docs.s: CLI and Python glue for GNSS streams: log or forward any receiver stream ( gnssstreamer ), pull RTCM corrections from an NTRIP caster ( gnssntripclient ), run your own caster ( gnssserver ), and convert u-blox raw logs to RINEX ( pyrinexconv ).
docs.b: pygnssutils - integration card CLI and Python glue for GNSS streams: log or forward any receiver stream ( gnssstreamer ), pull RTCM corrections from an NTRIP caster ( gnssntripclient ), run your own caster ( gnssserver ), and convert u-blox raw logs to RINEX ( pyrinexconv ).        --- ---    Install    python3 -m pip install --upgrade pygnssutils  (latest GitHub release v1.3.1;  =3.10 ). Pulls pyubx2 =1.4.0, pyrtcm, pynmeagps, pyspartn, pysbf2, pyunigps, pyqgc, pyubxutils, pyserial, certifi. Also on conda-forge.     Runs on   Any OS with Python 3.10+; pure Python except  cryptography  (via pyspartn), which can fail to build on 32-bit Linux.     Inputs   Serial port, TCP socket, binary file, or NTRIP caster (HTTP/HTTPS). Protocols NMEA, UBX, SBF (Septentrio), UNI (Unicore), QGC, RTCM3, SPARTN. NTRIP credentials via flags or env  PYGPSCLIENT_USER  /  PYGPSCLIENT_PASSWORD .     Outputs   Parsed text, JSON, raw binary to file/socket/serial, or a Python lambda per message. RTCM3 written back into the receiver for RTK. RINEX 3.05 / 4.02 obs + nav files.     Key API / entry points   CLIs from  pyproject.toml :  gnssstreamer ,  gnssserver ,  gnssntripclient ,  pyrinexconv . Classes:  GNSSReader( kwargs)  (multi-protocol reader),  GNSSStreamer( kwargs) ,  GNSSNTRIPClient(app=None,  kwargs) ,  GNSSSocketServer( kwargs) ,  RinexConvertor(app, rinex_version, rinex_type, gnssfilter, obsfilter, minobs, verbosity, logtofile,  kwargs) .     Time to first result   Estimate: 5 min to see RTCM

docs.b: PyGPSClient - integration card One-line: pure-Python tkinter GUI for GNSS receivers (u-blox, Septentrio, Unicore, Quectel, NMEA) - live C/N0, sky view, RF spectrum, position scatter, NTRIP client/caster and receiver config - the bench tool for jamming and RTK tests.        --- ---    Install    python3 -m venv pygpsclient && source pygpsclient/bin/activate && python3 -m pip install --upgrade pygpsclient  (PyPI  pygpsclient  1.8.0,  requires_python  =3.10 ). Needs Tk  = 8.6: Debian/Ubuntu/Pi OS  sudo apt install python3-tk python3-pil python3-pil.imagetk  (INSTALLATION.md lists more). Runs on   Any desktop with a window system: Windows 10+, macOS 13+ (Intel and Apple Silicon, python.org installer recommended), Linux incl. Raspberry Pi OS. INSTALLATION.md asks for  = 500 MB memory and  = 640x480 screen. No GPU.     Inputs   Serial (USB/UART), TCP/UDP socket (optional TLS), binary log file ( .log , u-center  .ubx ), NTRIP caster (RTCM3 or SPARTN). Protocols NMEA, UBX, SBF, UNI, QGC, RTCM3, SPARTN, TTY. Optional fixed reference position for the scatterplot.     Outputs   GUI widgets; binary datalog; GPX track; spatialite database; socket server re-broadcasting the live stream (default port 50012, unauthenticated) or an NTRIP caster (mountpoint  pygnssutils ); RTCM/SPARTN written back to the receiver for RTK; receiver config commands (UBX CFG-VALSET etc.). docs.s: One-line: zero-dependency Python parser/generator for NMEA 0183 - the quickest way to turn any receiver's serial/TCP/log NMEA into typed lat/lon/fix-quality/DOP values, or to emit fake NMEA for a test rig.
docs.b: pynmeagps - integration card One-line: zero-dependency Python parser/generator for NMEA 0183 - the quickest way to turn any receiver's serial/TCP/log NMEA into typed lat/lon/fix-quality/DOP values, or to emit fake NMEA for a test rig.        --- ---    Install    python3 -m pip install --upgrade pynmeagps  (PyPI latest 1.1.8,  requires_python  =3.10 ,  dependencies = [] ). Also  conda install -c conda-forge pynmeagps . Add  pyserial  yourself for live ports. Installing  pyubx2  pulls it in automatically.     Runs on   Any OS with Python 3.10+, pure Python, no GPU. Fine on Raspberry Pi / Jetson.     Inputs   Any object with  read(n) -  bytes  /  readline() : serial port, file opened  rb , or a socket (wrapped internally by  SocketWrapper ). Single sentences as  str / bytes  via  parse() . Talkers GP/GN/GL/GA/GB etc.; proprietary sentences (u-blox PUBX, Quectel PAIR, others in  nmeatypes_get_prop.py ) plus user-defined dicts.     Outputs    (raw_bytes, NMEAMessage)  tuples. Attributes per message ID: GGA =   lat ,  lon  (signed decimal degrees),  quality ,  numSV ,  HDOP ,  alt  (m MSL),  sep ,  diffAge ; GST =   stdLat ,  stdLong ,  stdAlt ; RMC =   spd  (knots),  cog ,  date . Repeating groups get 2-digit suffixes ( svid_01 ). Outbound:  msg.serialize()  bytes with checksum and CRLF.     Key API / entry points    NMEAReader(stream, msgmode=GET, nmeaonly=False, validate=VALCKSUM, quitonerror=ERR_LOG, userdefined=None) ;  NMEAReader.read() -  (bytes, NMEAMessage)  and iteration

docs.b: x-io Fusion - integration card One-line: a small, dependency-free C AHRS (gyro + accel [+ mag or external heading] =  quaternion) with a matching Python package, so the attitude you prototype on a laptop is the attitude your MCU computes.        --- ---    Install   Python:  pip install imufusion==1.3.3  (latest on PyPI as of 2026-11-06). Runs on   Anything with a C compiler, including MCUs without an FPU (fast inverse square root is on by default). Python wheels per PyPI; no ROS.     Inputs   Gyroscope in deg/s, accelerometer in g, magnetometer in any consistent unit (only direction is used), all as 3-vectors in the sensor frame. Optional external heading in degrees ( UpdateExternalHeading , e.g. GNSS course). Sample rate in Hz, or measured period per sample via  FusionAhrsSetSamplePeriod .     Outputs   Orientation quaternion (sensor relative to earth), gravity vector (sensor frame), linear acceleration (gravity removed, sensor frame), earth acceleration (earth frame, gravity removed). Earth convention selectable: NWU, ENU or NED. Internal states (accel/mag error in degrees, ignored flags, recovery triggers) and flags (startup, overrange, recovery).     Key API / entry points   C:  FusionAhrsInitialise(FusionAhrs ) ,  FusionAhrsSetSettings(FusionAhrs , const FusionAhrsSettings ) ,  FusionAhrsUpdate(ahrs, gyro, accel, mag) ,  FusionAhrsUp

Jittor (Tsinghua framework) for the  anti_uav_jittor/  code, PyTorch for  Codes/  and  Eval/ . Not tested on Jetson or macOS by the README.     Inputs   Video sequences, each a folder with  IR.mp4  and/or  RGB.mp4  plus  IR_label.json  /  RGB_label.json  ( Eval/test.py ). Labels:  gt_rect  (per-frame box  [x, y, w, h] ) and  exist  (per-frame 0/1 visibility). Datasets: Anti-UAV300 (RGB + IR), Anti-UAV410 and Anti-UAV600 (IR only). docs.s: Synthetic low-altitude quadcopter flights from the University of Liege (Fonder and Van Droogenbroeck, CVPR Workshops 2019). Each trajectory is rendered under several weather and season setups, with simulated IMU and GPS alongside dense vision ground truth. One of few public sets that pairs drone imagery with a (simulated) GPS stream.

docs.s: Two place-recognition datasets from SNU RPM Robotics Lab (Korea). MulRan (Kim et al., ICRA 2020): radar + lidar on repeated urban routes with month-level gaps and reverse revisits. HeLiPR (Jung et al., IJRR 2024): the same kind of routes with four different lidars (spinning, solid-state, FMCW) for cross-lidar place recognition, with sequences aligned to MulRan routes 4 years later.

docs.n: NRC UAV vs bird radar tracks (CUAS-sensing-dataset)
docs.s: Real radar tracks of small drones, birds, people and vehicles from an Echodyne EchoGuard (MESA, K-band) radar, recorded by the National Research Council Canada in eight field trials in Quebec, October 2019 to March 2021. docs.s: Two off-road ground-vehicle datasets. RELLIS-3D (Texas A&M + US Army CCDC ARL, 2020): Clearpath Warthog on the RELLIS campus with lidar and camera semantic labels. TartanDrive (CMU AirLab, ICRA 2022): instrumented ATV driven aggressively off-road, aimed at learning vehicle dynamics. Neither is a precision-navigation benchmark; both are the go-to real data for off-road autonomy and traversability.

docs.s: OpenAerialMap (OAM, run by HOT) is an open catalogue of user-contributed aerial and drone orthophotos, CC BY 4.0, stored as Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs on a public S3 bucket. Coverage is patchy (wherever someone uploaded a survey), but it gives real centimetre-level drone orthos outside the US with no login. No index id of its own; the marker names the sample that uses it.

docs.n: Remote ID and DJI DroneID sample captures
docs.s: There is no large public Remote ID dataset. What exists are small sample captures shipped with decoders: raw SDR IQ of DJI DroneID (OcuSync 2.0) bursts, and pcaps of ASTM F3411 / ASD-STAN Open Drone ID over Wi-Fi and Bluetooth. Enough to build and test a passive "who is flying near us" receiver.

docs.n: RoNIN - Robust Neural Inertial Navigation dataset
docs.s: Smartphone IMU dataset for learned pedestrian dead reckoning (Yan, Herath, Furukawa, ICRA 2020). A body-mounted Tango phone gives the trajectory while a second phone is carried naturally and records IMU.

docs.s: Synthetic SLAM dataset rendered in Unreal Engine / AirSim by CMU AirLab. v1 (Wang et al., IROS 2020) is stereo + depth + flow + pose over 30 environments; v2 adds a six-camera rig, lidar, IMU with a noise model, event cameras and customizable lenses, managed by the  tartanair  Python package. Perfect ground truth, hard motion and lighting.

docs.s: Handheld stereo + IMU benchmark from the TUM Computer Vision Group (Schubert et al., IROS 2018), with photometric calibration and long indoor/outdoor sequences. The standard test for long-horizon VIO drift, because most sequences end where they started.
docs.b: TUM-VI Handheld stereo + IMU benchmark from the TUM Computer Vision Group (Schubert et al., IROS 2018), with photometric calibration and long indoor/outdoor sequences. docs.n: UTIL - UWB TDoA indoor localization dataset (U. Toronto)
docs.s: University of Toronto Dynamic Systems Lab dataset of UWB time-difference-of-arrival measurements from Bitcraze's Loco Positioning System, with LOS/NLOS identification experiments and about 150 min of quadrotor flights. Published in IJRR 43(10), 2024 (Zhao, Goudar, Qiao, Schoellig). An older, smaller TDoA2-only release from the same author is also indexed.
docs.b: UTIL - UWB TDoA indoor localization dataset (U. Toronto) University of Toronto Dynamic Systems Lab dataset of UWB time-difference-of-arrival measurements from Bitcraze's Loco Positioning System, with LOS/NLOS identification experiments and about 150 min of quadrotor flights. Published in IJRR 43(10), 2024 (Zhao, Goudar, Qiao, Schoellig). An older, smaller TDoA2-only release from the same author is also indexed.   Field   Value    --- ---    Platform   Custom quadrotor on Crazyflie Bolt with LPS UWB tag (DWM1000), flow deck, ToF ranger, SD-card logger (flight set); static tag + 2 anchors (identification set)     Environment   7.0 x 8.0 x 3.5 m indoor arena; 8 anchors per constellation, 4 constellations; constellation 4 adds static and dynamic (metal) obstacles     Sensors and rates   UWB TDoA2 (centralized) and TDoA3 (decentralized), IMU accel/gyro, optical flow, ToF laser, barometer; event-stream logging with microsecond timestamps. docs.b: UZH-FPV Drone Racing Aggressive FPV quadrotor flights flown by an expert pilot, UZH Robotics and Perception Group (Delmerico et al., ICRA 2019), with frame camera, event camera and IMU. Problem A scalar magnetometer in an aircraft cabin measures the Earth core field ("25,000-65,000 nT"), the crustal anomaly field ("typically less than 1000 nT") and the aircraft's own interference field, all summed. MagNav needs the anomaly field alone to match against a map. The challenge asks for a model that removes the aircraft field from cabin magnetometers, where classical Tolles-Lawson (TL) compensation "does not produce a compensated signal with sufficiently accurate results".   Method This is a challenge-problem definition, not a method paper. What it fixes: - Task: map uncompensated cabin scalar magnetometers plus auxiliary sensors =  compensated anomaly signal. - Truth:  mag_1_c , the professionally compensated tail-stinger magnetometer. Chosen over an anomaly map to avoid position interpolation error and to share weather conditions with the cabin sensors. - Metric: standard deviation of the error between model output and truth, per flight line. - Hold-out: line 1003.10 of Flight 1003 is the evaluation line; the other lines are the build set. - Allowed inputs: diurnal, IGR

docs.b: AirIO - paper digest  AirIO: Learning Inertial Odometry with Enhanced IMU Feature Observability  - Qiu, Xu, Chen, Zhao, Geng, Scherer, IEEE RA-L 2025 (accepted per arXiv v2). paper   code   Read: full text, arXiv HTML v2 (16 Jun 2025)   Problem Learned inertial odometry (RoNIN, TLIO style) works for pedestrians but transfers badly to multirotor UAVs, whose motion is agile and not periodic. Existing UAV variants often need extra inputs (thrust, rotor speed). The paper asks why, and how to get IMU-only learned odometry on drones.   Method - Core claim: the usual practice of rotating IMU data into a global (gravity-aligned) frame couples attitude nonlinearly with the motion force and hides features the network needs. Keeping IMU data in the  body frame  keeps attitude linearly coupled with gravity and more observable. - Supported by latent-feature analysis: PCA reaches 95% energy with k=5 (body) vs k=8 (global) on Blackbird, k=15 vs k=40 on Pegasus; t-SNE separates velocity levels better in body frame. -  Attitude encoding : orientation mapped to so(3), passed through a CNN encoder, concatenated with the IMU encoder output, then bi-directional GRUs. - Two MLP heads: body-frame  velocity  and its uncertainty (diag covariance). Loss: Huber (delta 0.005) plus an uncertainty term weighted lambda 1e-4. - Training uses ground-truth orientation for the attitude input; test uses EKF-estimated orientation. -  EKF : state = rotation, global velocity, position, gyro/accel biases. (CMU, IIIT Hyderabad, MIT, Adelaide), IEEE RA-L 2023 (venue per repo README bibtex). paper   code   Read: full text via ar5iv rendering of arXiv 2308.00688, plus repo README   Problem State-of-the-art VPR models are trained on urban street imagery and break in unstructured domains (indoor, subterranean, aerial, underwater). The paper asks whether off-the-shelf foundation-model features plus unsupervised aggregation give one VPR method that works everywhere without VPR-specific training.   Method - Backbone: DINOv2 ViT-G14, frozen, features from layer 31, "value" facet; per-patch features, CLS token discarded (Sec. III-B, IV-B2). - Aggregation: hard-assignment VLAD with 32 clusters (AnyLoc-VLAD-DINOv2), or GeM (AnyLoc-GeM-DINOv2). Hard assignment beat soft and is ~1.4x faster (Sec. V-C3, Table VII). - Vocabulary (VLAD cluster centers) is built without labels from database images. Three options compared: map-specific, domain-specific (pooled over maps of the same domain, e.g. all aerial), global (Table V). Domain-specific is best. - Optional PCA-whitening down to 512-d for a ~100x smaller descriptor at similar recall (Sec. V-A1). - No training, no fine-tuning; "training-free" still needs reference-database statistics for the vocabulary and PCA.   Data and sensors - Monocular RGB only. - Structured (Table III): Baidu Mall, Gardens Point, 17 Places, Pittsburgh-30k, St Lucia, Oxford RobotCar

Pure integration drifts with t^2 from bias.   Method -  Right-invariant EKF on SE2(3) , 21-dim error state: orientation, velocity, position, gyro and accel biases, plus car-to-IMU misalignment rotation and lever arm (both near-constant random walks). -  Pseudo-measurements : lateral and vertical velocity in the  car  frame are about zero (non-holonomic constraint). Fed as y = 0 with covariance N_n. Car-frame vertical is argued to be more general than world-frame zero vertical velocity. -  Noise adapter : a small 1D CNN reads a window of N=15 raw IMU samples (no state) and outputs z_lat, z_up. Q is learned but fixed in time. - Training: Adam lr 1e-4, batches of nine 1-minute sub-sequences at random starts, Gaussian noise std 1e-4, dropout 0.5, grad clip 1, 400 epochs. docs.b: Factor Graphs for Robot Perception - paper digest  Factor Graphs for Robot Perception  - Dellaert, Kaess, Foundations and Trends in Robotics Vol. 6, No. 1-2, 2017 (DOI 10.1561/2300000043), about 139 pages. paper   code   Read: full text extracted from the free author PDF (figures not viewed). This is a monograph: "headline results" below are its key worked examples and claims, not benchmarks.   Problem How to model and solve large-scale inference in robotics (SLAM, aided navigation, mapping) in one framework that is both a clean modeling language and an efficient solver. The monograph argues factor graphs fit because each sensor measurement maps to one factor.   Method Chapters, in order: - 1 Introduction: Bayes nets as generative models, MAP inference, factor graphs as the posterior p(X Z). Running toy example: 3 poses, 2 landmarks, bearing measurements (Fig. 1.1-1.3). - 2 Smoothing and Mapping: nonlinear least squares; linearization; Gauss-Newton, Levenberg-Marquardt, Dogleg. - 3 Exploiting Sparsity: the sparse Jacobian is the factor graph; QR / Cholesky = variable elimination; the Cholesky factor is a Bayes net, back-substitution solves it. - 4 Elimination Ordering: fill-in, minimum degree (COLAMD), nested dissection, block-level ordering. - 5 Incremental Smoothing and Mapping: Givens updates, marginalization, fixed-lag smoothing, Kalman filter / smoother as special cases, Bayes tree, iSAM2. - 6 Optimization on Manifolds: rotations, exponential map, local coordinates, Pose

Thermal cameras see through these but give noisy, low-contrast, texture-poor images, and flat-field correction (FFC/NUC) shutter events interrupt the stream and change image appearance. Corner trackers struggle on such images.   Method - Front end: extract edges from thermal images (Difference of Gaussians, gradient threshold, sub-pixel refinement =  binary edge image). - DT-KLT: track features on the distance transform of the edge image rather than raw intensity, with pyramids - robust to intensity changes between frames. - ADT-KLT: adaptive switch between plain KLT and DT-KLT using a score combining change in edge count and IMU-preintegrated rotation angle. Threshold value not given in the text. - Back end: VINS-style sliding-window MAP optimization (IMU preintegration + reprojection on the unit sphere + marginalization prior, Huber loss, Ceres). Inverse-depth point features. - No explicit FFC/NUC compensation step described; edges are the robustness mechanism.   Data and sensors - Sensors: monocular thermal (own rig: Gobi+ 640, 640x480 @ 50 Hz) + IMU (MTi-G-710 @ 200 Hz). Ground truth from VLP-16 lidar + No

docs.b: FAST-LIO2 - paper digest  FAST-LIO2: Fast Direct LiDAR-inertial Odometry  - Xu, Cai, He, Lin, Zhang (HKU MaRS), arXiv 2107.06829, 2021 (arXiv lists no journal-ref; venue not verified here). paper   code   Read: full text, ar5iv HTML of arXiv v1 (appendix Table VIII not read)   Problem LiDAR-inertial odometry has to run on small onboard computers, cope with motion distortion, and work with both spinning and small-FoV solid-state LiDARs where hand-crafted edge/plane features break down. Maintaining a dense, updatable map in realtime is the main compute cost.   Method - Tightly coupled iterated Kalman filter on manifold (from FAST-LIO), 24-dim state, online LiDAR-IMU extrinsic calibration. Kalman gain computed with a state-dimension inverse, not measurement-dimension. - Direct registration: raw (downsampled) points matched to the map; plane fitted to 5 nearest map neighbours per point; no feature extraction. - Motion compensation by IMU back-propagation of every point to scan-end time. - ikd-Tree: incremental k-d tree with point insertion + on-tree downsampling, box-wise deletion via lazy labels, and parallel re-balancing; O(log n) insert and k-NN. - Map kept as a local cube moving with the sensor (default L = 1000 m); 0.5 m spatial downsampling; 1:4 temporal point downsampling. - Pure odometry: no loop closure.   Data and sensors - LiDAR + IMU. Evaluated with Livox Horizon (solid-state, 81.7 x 25.1 deg FoV), VLP-16, Velodyne HDL-32E; IMUs from 50 Hz to 1000 Hz. - Datasets: lili

docs.b: IMU preintegration (Forster) - paper digest  On-Manifold Preintegration for Real-Time Visual-Inertial Odometry  - Forster, Carlone, Dellaert, Scaramuzza, IEEE Transactions on Robotics 2016 (DOI 10.1109/TRO.2016.2597321; arXiv 2015). paper   code   Read: full text via ar5iv HTML render of arXiv 1512.02363 (two passes, whole page)   Problem Optimization-based VIO is more accurate than filtering but gets too slow as the trajectory grows, and a 200-800 Hz IMU would add a state per sample. Earlier preintegration (Lupton and Sukkarieh) used Euler angles, which are not frame-invariant and break near gimbal lock.   Method -  Preintegration on SO(3) : all IMU samples between two keyframes are summarized into one relative-motion measurement (delta rotation, delta velocity, delta position) that does not depend on the absolute start state, so it is computed once. - Analytic residuals and Jacobians are derived on the manifold (exponential map, right Jacobians). -  Noise propagation : preintegrated noise treated as zero-mean Gaussian to first order; its covariance is propagated iteratively sample by sample (appendix). -  Bias correction : when the bias estimate changes, the preintegrated delta is updated with a first-order Jacobian instead of re-integrating raw samples. -  Structureless vision factors : 3D landmarks eliminated linearly (Schur-style), so each landmark becomes one factor over the keyframes that see it. - Backend: factor graph solved incrementally with iSAM2, keyframe-based;

Problem Civil GNSS navigation data can be forged, for example with false ephemeris or clock data from a simulator spoofer. OSNMA lets a receiver cryptographically verify that the Galileo E1-B I/NAV navigation data came from Galileo and was not modified (RG 1.2). The chain key that produced them is disclosed later, and keys go out in reverse order of generation (ICD 1.4, 5.5.2). Submitted to IJRR" (text extracted from the PDF; figures not viewed). Final IJRR page numbers may differ.   Problem Online SLAM / sensor fusion needs the full smoothing solution (all past poses) updated every step. Batch sparse factorization gets too expensive as the graph grows. The original iSAM updates the linear system incrementally but needs periodic batch steps for variable reordering and relinearization, which cause spikes and fill-in.   Method -  Bayes tree : a directed tree of cliques encoding the factored density; maps to the square-root information matrix (like a clique tree but directed). Adding a factor only touches the cliques on the path from the affected variables to the root. - Incremental update = detach the affected top of the tree, re-eliminate it into a factor graph, re-insert orphaned subtrees. No matrix-level bookkeeping. -  Incremental variable reordering : the re-eliminated top is reordered with constrained COLAMD (CCOLAMD), forcing the most recent variables to the root so future updates stay cheap. -  Fluid relinearization : only variables whose delta exceeds threshold beta are relinearized, and only their cliques and ancestors are redone. Tracking and large-scale mapping need low latency. LightGlue keeps SuperGlue's robustness while cutting run time and training cost.   Method - Input: two sets of sparse keypoints + descriptors from any extractor (trained for SuperPoint, DISK, SIFT; ALIKED weights added later in the repo). - 9 layers (L=9), each one self-attention + one bidirectional cross-attention unit, 4 heads, d=256 (Sec. 4). - Relative (rotary) positional encoding added in every self-attention unit instead of SuperGlue's absolute MLP encoding. - Light assignment head: pairwise similarity plus a separate per-point "matchability" score replaces Sinkhorn optimal transport and the dustbin. - Deep supervision: a match prediction after every layer. A small confidence classifier decides when to stop (exit when a ratio alpha of points is confident, Eq. 10). - Point pruning: points confidently unmatchable (e.g. outside covisible area) are dropped between layers, so attention cost shrinks on low-overlap pairs. - Training: pre-train on synthetic homographies (1M images), fine-tune on MegaDepth. Equations came out garbled, tables and prose legible.   Problem 2D matchers fail under extreme viewpoint change (up to 180 deg, opposite-facing views). DUSt3R, a pointmap-regression 3D reconstruction network, is very robust to this but its correspondences are imprecise. MASt3R adds explicit matching to DUSt3R to get both robustness and pixel accuracy.   Method - Backbone: DUSt3R (ViT-Large encoder, ViT-Base decoder, cross-attention between the two views), initialized from the public DUSt3R checkpoint (Sec. 4.1). - Per pixel it outputs a 3D point (pointmap in camera 1 frame), a confidence, and a new 24-D local descriptor from an added MLP head (Sec. 3.2, App. D). - Losses: DUSt3R confidence-weighted 3D regression (made metric when ground truth is metric) + InfoNCE matching loss over ground-truth correspondences, weight 1. - Fast reciprocal matching: start from k sparse seed pixels, iterate NN back and forth until cycles (mutual matches) form. Complexity O(kWH) instead of quadratic; also improves pose accuracy because it samples matches more evenly (App. B). - Coarse-to-fine: network works at 512 px max; for high-res images, match at low res, then match overlapping 512 px window crops covering 90% of coarse match

Problem In 2016 COTS civil receivers had no spoofing defenses, even though receiver-spoofers and cheap programmable simulators existed. This survey lays out the attack modes and the detection techniques, then builds a cost-ranked attack/defense matrix. The goal is to tell receiver makers which defenses buy the most security per dollar.   Method - Common signal model for authentic and spoofed signals (Eqs. 1-3). Each attack is described by how its amplitude, code phase and carrier phase differ from the authentic signal. - Attack taxonomy (Sec. II): - self-consistent spoofers (simulator, receiver-spoofer); - meaconing (record and replay); - security code estimation and replay (SCER); - nulling of the true signal; - multi-antenna and motion-matched spoofers; - cooperative victims, e.g. a fisherman defeating his own tracker. - Defense taxonomy (Sec. III): - single-antenna signal processing: observable jumps, received power monitoring (RPM) with AGC, correlation-function distortion, continuous re-acquisition search for duplicate signals; - encryption: NMA, delayed-key spread-spectrum security codes (SSSC), dual-receiver c

RoMa targets robustness: matching pairs where most methods fail (the WxBS benchmark).   Method - Built on DKM (dense kernelized matching): global coarse match, then a stack of ConvNet refiners at strides 8/4/2/1 that predict warp residuals and certainty. - Coarse features: frozen DINOv2 (foundation model). Table 1 shows DINOv2 features are much more robust than VGG19/ResNet50 for coarse matching. - Fine features: a separate specialized VGG19 ConvNet, because DINOv2 patches are too coarse to localize. Not sharing weights between coarse and fine features helped (Table 2, setup II). - Transformer match decoder that predicts anchor probabilities (classification over coarse cells) instead of regressing coordinates, so the coarse stage can express multimodal hypotheses. - Loss: regression-by-classification for the coarse stage, robust (generalized Charbonnier) regression for refinement. - Output: a dense warp A= B plus per-pixel certainty; matches are sampled from it (10,000 matches with balanced sampling in the paper, Sec. 4.3). - Trained on MegaDepth + ScanNet at 560x560 (Sec. 4.2).   Data and sensors Monocular RGB pairs. Evaluated on IMC20

Prior work leans on polar transforms, special aggregation modules or multi-stage refinement, and triplet loss struggles with hard negatives (can collapse). The paper asks how far a plain shared encoder gets with a better loss and better negative sampling. Problem Quaternion and rotation formulas are scattered across conventions (Hamilton vs JPL, local vs global perturbations, active vs passive), and mixing them silently breaks IMU filters. The note collects one consistent set and derives a full IMU-driven error-state Kalman filter (ESKF) from it.   Method - Sec. 1-2: quaternion algebra, SO(3), exponential / log maps, Rodrigues formula, composition, SLERP; quaternion and rotation-matrix forms side by side. - Sec. 3: conventions. Table 2 lists the 4 binary choices (component order, algebra / handedness, passive function, direction of right-to-left products). Author picks  Hamilton  (scalar first, ij = k, right-handed, local-to-global), matching Eigen, ROS, Ceres. - Sec. 4: perturbations, derivatives, Jacobians (right Jacobian and its inverse), local vs global perturbations, time derivatives, zeroth- and first-order integration of rates. - Sec. 5: ESKF kinematics. docs.b: STGL (thermal geo-localization) - paper digest  Long-range UAV Thermal Geo-localization with Satellite Imagery  - Xiao, Tortei, Roura, Loianno (NYU, TII), IROS 2023. paper   code   Read: full text, arXiv HTML v3; repo README   Problem Locate a UAV at night, when RGB cameras are useless, by matching downward thermal images against daytime RGB satellite imagery. Two obstacles: paired thermal-satellite data is scarce, and thermal images over desert are low-contrast and self-similar.   Method - SGM (geo-localization module): image retrieval. The satellite map is tiled into a database (512x512 crops, 35 px stride); the thermal query is embedded and matched by nearest neighbour. ResNet-18 backbone + compression conv + NetVLAD (4096-d), triplet loss (margin 0.1). Positives within 35 m, negatives beyond 50 m. - TGM (thermal generative module): pix2pix GAN that turns satellite tiles into synthetic thermal tiles, giving 79,950 extra pseudo-pairs for SGM training. - Domain adaptation: DANN with gradient reversal (weight 0.1). Best variant applies it to positives only; using negatives fights the triplet loss. - Contrast enhancement: linear scaling of thermal images, factor 3. Turns out to be critical (see Table II). - Output: position = center of the best-matching tile, so precision is bounded by tile stride, and the query must be roughly north-aligned and at the map's scale.   Data and sensors - Sensors: nadir FLIR Boson thermal camera (640p, 8.7 mm, 50 deg HFOV), about 1 m/px after ort

Reject when all corner stds exceed a threshold s_c. - Deep Ensembles (model uncertainty): N_m models trained with different seeds, std across models. - Merge: CropTTA and DE combined by max (default), min or add. - Early stopping: run all samples only for the first k refinement iterations to estimate uncertainty, then continue with one sample - cuts latency. - Training: 100k steps, then 200k fine-tuning with CropTTA augmentation; 5 samples at evaluation. - Evaluation of rejection: ROC with predictions above 25 m MACE treated as should-reject.
